content.text:
I'll design a health scenario on mitochondrial/lysosomal compartmentalization with a data table, asking to predict an effect of a change.

Scenario: a drug causes lysosomal membranes to become leaky, releasing hydrolytic enzymes (acid hydrolases, optimal pH about 4.8) into the cytosol (pH 7.2). The prediction is that damage to cytosolic components is limited because the enzymes have low activity at cytosolic pH, though some damage occurs. To make the item decidable from data, I give a table of enzyme activity at different pH values.

Data (relative activity, %): pH 4.8 = 100, pH 6.0 = 30, pH 7.2 = 4. The stem asks for the best prediction of the effect when the enzymes leak into the cytosol, and the key is that the activity is greatly reduced, so widespread digestion is limited, but the compartment's loss still removes the pH-optimized degradation.

stimulus.description: Relative activity of a purified lysosomal acid hydrolase at three pH values, with the pH of two cell compartments.

data.title: Activity of purified lysosomal acid hydrolase by pH
notes: Activity is expressed relative to the maximum, measured at pH 4.8.

input.stem: A drug being tested for a joint disorder makes lysosomal membranes in cartilage cells leaky, so the lysosomal contents escape into the cytosol. Using the data in the table, which of the following is the best prediction of the immediate effect on the cell?
options: Cytosolic proteins will be digested at nearly the rate seen inside lysosomes, because the enzyme is still present at the same amount.
Digestion of cytosolic proteins will be much slower than in lysosomes, because the enzyme is far less active at cytosolic pH.
Digestion of cytosolic proteins will be faster than in lysosomes, because the enzyme will contact more substrate in the cytosol.
Digestion of cytosolic proteins will stop entirely, because the enzyme is denatured as soon as it leaves the lysosome.
option_rationale: Key reasoning is incorrect: assumes enzyme amount alone determines rate and ignores the pH dependence shown in the data.
Correct: the table shows activity falls from 100% at pH 4.8 to 4% at pH 7.2, so the lysosome's acidic compartment is what keeps the enzyme highly active; in the cytosol digestion is much slower.
Misconception: more substrate access always means faster reaction, ignoring that activity depends on the environment and is only 4% at pH 7.2.
Misconception: an enzyme out of its optimal environment is fully inactive; the data show 4% activity, not 0%.
input.explanation_en: The table shows the hydrolase is 100% active at the lysosomal pH of 4.8 but only 4% active at the cytosolic pH of 7.2. Compartmentalization keeps the acidic conditions that the enzyme needs inside the lysosome, so when the contents leak into the cytosol, digestion of cytosolic proteins will be much slower than in lysosomes. The prediction that digestion proceeds at nearly the lysosomal rate is wrong because it ignores the pH dependence in the data. The prediction of faster digestion because of more substrate is wrong because greater substrate access cannot overcome a 96% loss of activity. The prediction that digestion stops entirely is wrong because the data show a small but nonzero activity (4%) at pH 7.2, so the enzyme is not completely inactivated.
input.design_note: Tests prediction of effect of losing compartmentalization (lysosomal pH gradient) using enzyme pH-activity data; distractors target ignoring pH, substrate-access reasoning, and all-or-none denaturation.

content.text:
I'll build a surface-area-to-volume model: a spherical cell compartmentalized by internal membrane-bound organelles, asking students to predict the effect of a change.

Design: a spherical cell of radius 10 µm is compared with the same cell containing 20 spherical organelles, each 1 µm in radius, whose membranes carry the enzymes. Total membrane area available for the enzymes is 4π(10)² = 1256.6 µm² for the plasma membrane. Each organelle has area 4π(1)² = 12.57 µm², so 20 organelles contribute 251.3 µm². The stem asks about the effect of doubling the number of organelles to 40 on total internal membrane area and the concentration effect.

Key: total internal membrane area doubles (251.3 → 502.7 µm²) while the organelles' total volume stays small, so the cytosolic volume is nearly unchanged. The distractors encode these misconceptions: the area stays the same because the cell size is fixed; the area quadruples because area scales with the square; and the area doubles but the cell's surface-area-to-volume ratio changes.

stimulus.description: Model of a spherical cell (radius 10 micrometers) containing identical spherical membrane-bound organelles of radius 1 micrometer, with the number of organelles in two scenarios.

data.notes: Sphere surface area = 4*pi*r^2; sphere volume = (4/3)*pi*r^3. Enzymes of a metabolic pathway are embedded in organelle membranes only, at a constant number per square micrometer of membrane.

input.stem: In the model, the cell is modified so that it contains 40 identical organelles instead of 20, with cell size and organelle size unchanged. Which prediction about the change is best supported by the numbers in the table?
options: Total organelle membrane area doubles, so the pathway's total enzyme capacity doubles while organelles occupy a small fraction of cell volume.
Total organelle membrane area stays the same because the cell radius is unchanged, so pathway capacity is unchanged.
Total organelle membrane area increases fourfold because surface area depends on the square of the radius, so capacity quadruples.
Total organelle membrane area doubles, but the pathway's capacity is unchanged because enzymes depend on cell volume, not membrane area.
option_rationale: Correct: area per organelle is fixed at 4*pi, so 40 organelles give twice the area of 20; enzyme density per area is constant, so capacity doubles; organelle volume is about 0.4 percent to 0.8 percent of the cell.
Misconception: believes internal membrane area is set by the outer cell size rather than by the number of compartments.
Misconception: applies the squared-radius scaling to the number of organelles, though only the count changed, not the radius.
Misconception: accepts the area increase but claims enzyme activity depends on volume, ignoring that the enzymes are membrane-embedded at constant density per area.
input.explanation_en: Each organelle has membrane area 4*pi*(1)^2, about 12.6 square micrometers, so 20 organelles give about 251 and 40 give about 503 square micrometers: the area doubles because it is proportional to the number of identical organelles. Since the enzymes sit in the membranes at constant density per area, the pathway's total capacity doubles. The organelles' total volume (40 x about 4.19 = about 168 cubic micrometers) is only about 4 percent of the cell's volume of about 4189 cubic micrometers, so the cytosol is little changed. The option claiming unchanged area ignores that compartment number adds membrane. The option claiming a fourfold increase misapplies the radius-squared relationship, since the radius did not change. The option claiming unchanged capacity contradicts the stated membrane-embedded enzymes.

content.text:
I'll build an item on cell compartmentalization using a business decision context (a company choosing a yeast strain for bioproduction). The stimulus is a table of reaction rates, and the student predicts the effect of removing the compartment barrier.

Design: a biotech startup engineers yeast to make a product. Enzyme A makes an intermediate that is toxic at high concentration, and enzyme B converts it. A strain targets both enzymes into the mitochondria (compartmentalized) versus the cytosol. The student must predict the effect of mislocalizing enzyme A to the cytosol when the pH-dependent activity differs.

Data: the intermediate's local concentration is higher in the small mitochondrial volume. The prediction is that moving both to the cytosol lowers the local concentration of the intermediate and thus lowers flux through enzyme B, with a lower yield.

Verification: compute the local concentration as moles divided by volume, for a fixed amount of intermediate in a small versus a large volume, and the rate via Michaelis-Menten.

stimulus.description: Table comparing two engineered yeast strains that make the same product through a two-step pathway (enzyme A then enzyme B), differing only in where the enzymes are located.

data.title: Strain comparison for a two-step biosynthetic pathway
columns: Location of enzymes A and B
Intermediate X made per cell per minute (amol)
Product yield (g per liter of culture)
data.notes: Enzyme B has a Km of 150 uM for intermediate X and is not saturated in either strain. Intermediate X does not leave the compartment in which it is made, and the two strains have identical enzyme amounts and activity per molecule. 1 amol = 10^-18 mol; 1 fL = 10^-15 L.

input.stem: A biotechnology company is deciding whether to spend money converting Strain M, which has both pathway enzymes inside mitochondria, into Strain C, which would have both enzymes free in the cytosol. Using the information in the table, which prediction about Strain C is best supported?
options: Product yield will fall, because the same amount of intermediate X is spread through a larger volume, lowering its concentration and the rate of the enzyme B reaction.
Product yield will rise, because the cytosol is larger and can hold more enzyme A and enzyme B molecules, so more intermediate X is made per cell.
Product yield will stay the same, because both strains make the same amount of intermediate X per minute, so the total product must be the same.
Product yield will fall, because enzymes in the cytosol cannot be active unless they are enclosed by a membrane-bound organelle.
option_rationale: Correct: compartmentalization concentrates substrate in a small volume; in the 20-fold larger cytosolic volume, X concentration is about 20-fold lower, and since enzyme B is unsaturated its rate drops roughly proportionally.
Misconception: a larger compartment means more enzyme or more production; the table states enzyme amounts are identical and X production is the same 600 amol/min.
Misconception: ignores that reaction rate depends on substrate concentration, not just amount; assumes total amount alone determines output.
Misconception: believes enzymes require a membrane-bound organelle to function; cytosolic enzymes work fine, the effect here is concentration and not loss of activity.
input.explanation_en: Compartmentalization keeps substrates and enzymes together in a small volume, which raises the local concentration of intermediate X. Both strains make the same amount of X per minute, but the cytosolic volume (40 fL) is 20 times larger than the mitochondrial volume (2 fL), so X is about 20 times more dilute in Strain C. Because enzyme B is not saturated (substrate well below Km), its rate is roughly proportional to the substrate concentration, so the second step slows and yield falls. The prediction that more enzyme fits in the cytosol is wrong because the enzyme amounts are stated to be identical. The prediction of equal yield is wrong because the rate depends on concentration, not only on the amount made. The prediction that cytosolic enzymes cannot function is wrong because enzymes work in the cytosol; the loss comes from dilution, not inactivity.

content.text:
I'll design an item on competitive vs. noncompetitive inhibition using Michaelis-Menten-style rate data, requiring concept explanation of why Vmax changes or not.

Design: a table of reaction rates at substrate concentrations with no inhibitor and with inhibitor X. Rates in the presence of the inhibitor converge toward the same maximum at high [S], so the inhibitor is competitive, and the correct explanation is that the inhibitor competes for the active site and excess substrate outcompetes it.

Data (µmol/min): [S] = 1, 2, 5, 10, 50, 200 mM. Without inhibitor (Vmax=100, Km=5): 16.7, 28.6, 50, 66.7, 90.9, 97.6. With competitive inhibitor (apparent Km=15): 6.25, 11.8, 25, 40, 76.9, 93.0. The code verifies these values and that the ratio of rates approaches 1 at high [S].

stimulus.description: Table of initial reaction rate of an enzyme at six substrate concentrations, with and without inhibitor X.

data.title: Initial rate of enzyme-catalyzed reaction (enzyme concentration, pH, and temperature held constant)

input.stem: A researcher measures the rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction at several substrate concentrations, with and without inhibitor X, as shown in the table. Which statement best explains the effect of inhibitor X on the enzyme?
options: Inhibitor X binds the active site and competes with substrate, so a high substrate concentration reduces its effect.
Inhibitor X binds away from the active site and changes its shape, so it lowers the maximum rate at any substrate level.
Inhibitor X denatures the enzyme permanently, so the rate is lower at every substrate concentration tested.
Inhibitor X lowers the activation energy of the reaction, so the reaction proceeds more slowly at low substrate concentration.
option_rationale: Correct: the rate gap shrinks as substrate rises and the rates converge near the same maximum, the signature of competition for the active site.
Misconception: confuses competitive with noncompetitive inhibition; a noncompetitive inhibitor would lower the maximum rate even at saturating substrate, but here rates converge (93.0 vs 97.6).
Misconception: equates any reduced rate with denaturation; denaturation would not be overcome by adding substrate, and the rates nearly match at high substrate.
Misconception: reverses the role of activation energy; lowering it would speed the reaction, not slow it, and an inhibitor does not act as a catalyst.
input.explanation_en: Without inhibitor X, the rate at 200 mM substrate is 97.6, and with X it is 93.0. The inhibition is strong at low substrate (6.3 vs 16.7 at 1 mM) but nearly disappears at high substrate. This pattern fits an inhibitor that competes with substrate for the active site: more substrate makes it likelier that substrate occupies the active site, so the maximum rate is almost reached. An inhibitor binding away from the active site would lower the maximum rate even at saturating substrate, and the data do not show that. Denaturation would not be reversed by adding substrate, so it does not fit. Lowering activation energy would speed the reaction rather than slow it, and that is the role of the enzyme, not of an inhibitor.

content.text:
I'll design a household context: a family uses a lactase-treated milk decision, with a table of lactose hydrolysis rates at different amounts of added lactase, and ask to explain the pattern at high enzyme amount (substrate-limited). Concept explanation focuses on the enzyme-substrate complex and active site.

Design: Household adds lactase drops to milk; the table gives the amount of lactose broken down in 10 minutes at 4°C in the fridge for 0, 2, 4, 8, 16 drops. The data show rate rising and then plateauing at 8 to 16 drops, with all lactose consumed. The question asks which explanation accounts for why doubling drops from 8 to 16 doesn't increase product.

Numbers: lactose initially 50 mmol per carton. Product (glucose) after 10 min: 0 drops: 0; 2: 12; 4: 24; 8: 48; 16: 50. 8 drops gives 48 of 50 and 16 gives 50, so the plateau is substrate depletion.

stimulus.description: Table of glucose produced after 10 minutes in a carton of milk containing 50 mmol lactose at 4 degrees C, for different numbers of lactase drops.

data.title: Lactose hydrolysis in refrigerated milk after 10 minutes
data.conditions: Initial lactose 50 mmol per carton; 4 degrees C; each mole of lactose yields 1 mole glucose and 1 mole galactose; same carton volume in all trials

input.stem: A family adds lactase drops to milk to make it lactose-free. The table shows the results. Which explanation best accounts for the small increase in glucose when the drops are doubled from 8 to 16?
options: Nearly all lactose has already been converted to products at 8 drops, so few substrate molecules remain to bind active sites of the added lactase.
The extra lactase molecules are denatured by the cold, so their active sites change shape and cannot bind lactose.
Lactase is consumed as it forms enzyme-substrate complexes, so additional drops are used up before they can act.
At 16 drops the enzyme lowers the energy released by the reaction, so less glucose is produced overall.
option_rationale: Correct: 48 of 50 mmol already hydrolyzed, so substrate is limiting; more enzyme cannot make more product.
Misconception: cold denatures enzymes. Cold slows reactions but does not denature, and the lower drop amounts worked at the same temperature.
Misconception: enzymes are consumed in reactions. Enzymes are recycled and unchanged after catalysis.
Misconception: enzymes change the overall energy change or yield of reaction; they lower activation energy only and do not alter total product possible.
input.explanation_en: Glucose rises in proportion to drops from 2 to 8 (12, 24, 48 mmol), showing enzyme amount limits the rate. By 8 drops, 48 of the 50 mmol lactose is already hydrolyzed, so only 2 mmol of substrate remain; 16 drops can produce at most 2 mmol more (observed 50). Thus substrate availability limits product. The cold-denaturation option is wrong because 4 degrees C slows molecular motion without denaturing, and the same temperature allowed proportional activity at lower amounts. The enzyme-consumed option is wrong because enzymes are released unchanged after each reaction and reused. The energy option is wrong because enzymes lower activation energy and do not change the total energy released or the maximum product.

content.text:
I'll design an abstract-math setting: Michaelis-Menten-style rate data given as a table with a competitive inhibitor, asking the student to explain the concept (competitive inhibition raises apparent Km, Vmax unchanged). To keep the calculation minimal, I'll provide the rates directly and have the student explain the pattern.

Design: the rate equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km+[S]), with Vmax = 100 and Km = 10 without the inhibitor, and apparent Km = 30 with it. Substrate concentrations: 5, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000 (arbitrary units).

stimulus.description: Initial reaction rates of an enzyme at six substrate concentrations, with and without a compound X.

data.notes: Enzyme amount, temperature, and pH identical in both series. Rates rounded to 0.1.

input.stem: Compound X is a small molecule that resembles the enzyme's substrate. Which explanation of the data in the table best accounts for the effect of compound X on the reaction rate?
options: Compound X binds reversibly at the active site and competes with substrate, so higher substrate concentration outcompetes it and the rate approaches the same maximum.
Compound X binds at a site away from the active site and changes its shape, so the maximum rate is lower even when substrate is in large excess.
Compound X permanently denatures a fixed fraction of the enzyme molecules, so the rate is reduced by the same amount at every substrate concentration.
Compound X lowers the activation energy of the reaction further, so the rate rises most at low substrate concentration and the maximum rate increases.
option_rationale: Correct: the inhibition shrinks as substrate rises and the rates converge near ~100, the signature of reversible competition for the active site.
Confuses competitive with noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibition; that would lower the maximum rate, but the data show rates converging toward the same maximum.
Confuses inhibition with irreversible denaturation; a fixed loss of active enzyme would lower the rate at all concentrations, including very high ones, and the gap here shrinks from 19 to under 2.
Treats X as a catalyst or activator; the data show X lowers rates at every concentration and the maximum does not increase.
input.explanation_en: Without X the rate approaches about 100 µmol/min; with X the rate is lower at low substrate but the difference shrinks as substrate increases (from 19.0 at 5 mM to 1.9 at 1000 mM), and both series approach the same maximum. This pattern shows that X, a substrate look-alike, reversibly occupies the active site and competes with substrate; excess substrate outcompetes it. The option about binding away from the active site and lowering the maximum is wrong because the maximum is not lowered. The option about permanent denaturation of a fixed fraction is wrong because the inhibition would not vanish at high substrate. The option about further lowering activation energy and raising the maximum is wrong because X reduces the rate at every concentration.

content.text:
I'll design an item on enzyme inhibition in a sports/health context (lactate dehydrogenase and a competitive inhibitor), using a table of rate data as the stimulus.

Data design: Michaelis-Menten-like rates, with and without an inhibitor at two substrate concentrations. Vmax = 100, Km = 2 mM (no inhibitor); with a competitive inhibitor, apparent Km = 8 mM. Rate = Vmax·S/(Km+S).

- No inhibitor: S=1 gives 33.3, S=40 gives 95.2.
- Inhibitor: S=1 gives 11.1, S=40 gives 83.3.

The rates are rounded to whole numbers: 33, 95, 11, 83. At the high substrate concentration, the inhibited rate approaches the uninhibited rate, which indicates competitive inhibition. The stem asks which explanation of the pattern is best.

data.title: Rate of pyruvate-to-lactate conversion by a muscle enzyme (arbitrary rate units per minute) at 37 degrees C, pH 7.4, fixed enzyme amount

input.stem: A sports-medicine team tests an experimental drug that slows an enzyme in muscle cells. The enzyme converts pyruvate (the substrate) to lactate. The table shows reaction rates with and without the drug at two substrate concentrations, with the same amount of enzyme in every trial. Which explanation best accounts for the data?
options: The drug competes with pyruvate for the active site, so a high pyruvate concentration outcompetes the drug and the rate nearly recovers.
The drug permanently denatures some enzyme molecules, so the rate with the drug stays lower by the same proportion at every substrate level.
The drug binds to a site away from the active site and changes its shape, so extra pyruvate cannot restore the maximum rate.
The drug lowers the activation energy of the reaction more than the enzyme does, so the rate rises at high pyruvate concentration.
option_rationale: Correct: inhibition is strong at low substrate (11 vs 33) but almost gone at high substrate (83 vs 95), as expected when inhibitor and substrate compete for the active site.

Misconception: describes noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibition and assumes all inhibitors lower maximum rate; here the rate at high substrate is close to the uninhibited rate.
Misconception: thinks an inhibitor acts as a better catalyst; the drug lowers the rate at both concentrations, so it does not speed the reaction.
input.explanation_en: The drug reduces the rate strongly at 1 mM pyruvate (11 vs 33, about 33% of normal) but only slightly at 40 mM (83 vs 95, about 87% of normal). Inhibition that is overcome by more substrate fits competitive inhibition: the drug and pyruvate compete for the same active site, so a high pyruvate concentration makes the active site more likely to be occupied by substrate. The denaturation explanation is wrong because lost enzyme would reduce the rate by the same proportion at every substrate concentration, and the observed proportion changes. The allosteric explanation is wrong because that kind of inhibitor would keep the maximum rate low even with excess substrate, but the rate nearly recovers. The better-catalyst explanation is wrong because the drug lowers the rate at both concentrations, so it is not speeding the reaction or lowering activation energy beyond the enzyme.

content.text:
I designed a lab scenario: a hypothetical enzyme assayed at several pH values, with a data table, asking the student to predict the effect of a change (adding a competitive inhibitor and raising substrate, or a pH shift). To keep it tied to topic 3.2 (environmental impacts), I chose pH and denaturation.

Scenario: a protease from a hot-spring bacterium is assayed at several pH values. The table gives its initial rate at pH 3 to 11, peaking at 8. The question asks to predict the rate if the pH 10 mixture is adjusted back to pH 8, given a stated condition. To keep the answer decidable, I added a second condition: a separate sample was held at pH 2 for 30 min before being returned to pH 8, and the data show that it recovered only a small fraction of activity, which indicates irreversible denaturation. The prediction is for a sample that was held at pH 10 and then returned to pH 8, using the stimulus data on recovery.

Data: rate (µmol/min) at pH 4: 5, pH 6: 40, pH 8: 100, pH 10: 45, pH 12: 2. Recovery test: samples were held 30 min at the given pH, then assayed at pH 8. Held at pH 10 → 44; held at pH 12 → 3.

Question: a new sample held 30 min at pH 10, then moved to pH 8, would be predicted to show a rate near 44. The reasoning is that the pH 10 exposure was reversible (the rate at pH 10 is 45, and recovery at pH 8 after holding at 10 is about 44, i.e. not 100). That is odd, since a rate of 44 after returning to pH 8 means partial irreversible loss.

I reworked the design to make it cleaner: held at pH 10 → 98 (recovers fully); held at pH 12 → 4 (does not recover). The question: predict the rate at pH 8 for a sample held 30 min at pH 11.5, a value between the two. That is not decidable, so I instead ask about pH 12 versus pH 10 and the cause.

Final question: which prediction and reason is best supported for a sample held 30 min at pH 12 and then assayed at pH 8?

stimulus.description: Table of initial reaction rate of a bacterial protease measured at different pH values, and rate at pH 8 after 30-min pre-exposure to pH 10 or pH 12.

data.title: Protease activity (all assays at 50 C, saturating substrate)
rows: Held 30 min at pH 10, then assayed at pH 8
Held 30 min at pH 12, then assayed at pH 8

input.stem: A researcher prepares a new sample of the same protease, holds it 30 min at pH 12, and then adjusts it to pH 8 for assay. Based on the data, which prediction and reason is best supported?
options: The rate will stay near 4 umol/min because exposure to pH 12 irreversibly altered the enzyme's three-dimensional shape.
The rate will return to about 100 umol/min because changing pH only changes charges temporarily and the shape always recovers.
The rate will be about 50 umol/min because half of the enzyme molecules were broken down into amino acids at pH 12.
The rate will rise above 100 umol/min because the enzyme was activated by the stress of the high pH exposure.
option_rationale: Correct: the pH 12 pre-exposure sample stays at 4 at pH 8, unlike the pH 10 sample that recovered to 98, so denaturation at pH 12 was irreversible.
Misconception: pH effects are always reversible; the pH 10 data show recovery but the pH 12 data do not, so generalizing is wrong.
Misconception: denaturation is hydrolysis of the enzyme into amino acids; no data support a 50 percent value and denaturation does not break peptide bonds.
Misconception: stress or extreme conditions activate enzymes; the data show loss of activity, not enhancement.
input.explanation_en: The sample held at pH 12 and then assayed at pH 8 gave only 4 umol/min, almost the same as the rate at pH 12, whereas the sample held at pH 10 recovered to 98. So pH 12 caused irreversible loss of the active-site shape (denaturation), and a new sample treated the same way is predicted to stay near 4. Full recovery to 100 is wrong because the data show recovery only after pH 10, not pH 12. A rate near 50 from peptide breakdown is wrong because denaturation disrupts folding, not peptide bonds, and the data give no support for 50. A rate above 100 is wrong because no data show activation; the enzyme lost activity.

content.text:
I'll design an abstract mathematical setting: an enzyme-rate model with a given rate-vs-pH table, and a prediction about a change in the system.

Design: the table gives the relative rate of an enzyme at several pH values at a fixed temperature, with optimum near pH 7. The question asks to predict the effect of changing the pH from 5 to 6 on the rate, and which explanation is right. Data: pH 4: 5, pH 5: 22, pH 6: 61, pH 7: 100, pH 8: 64, pH 9: 18. The question is a prediction for a new condition, with the cause (ionization state of active-site residues altering substrate binding or catalysis) as the key.

Stem: a student raises the pH of a reaction mixture from 5 to 6 (substrate in excess). Predict the change in rate and the cause. Key: the rate increases about 2.8-fold, because the shift moves the ionization state of the active-site residues toward that needed for substrate binding and catalysis. Verification: 61/22 = 2.77.

stimulus.description: Relative rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction at six pH values, 25 C, saturating substrate.

data.conditions: 25 C, substrate concentration saturating, same enzyme amount in every trial

input.stem: The table shows the relative rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction at different pH values. A researcher raises the pH of a mixture from 5 to 6, keeping temperature, enzyme amount, and saturating substrate unchanged. Which prediction about the rate, and its cause, is best supported by the data?
options: The rate will increase about 2.8-fold, because the pH change moves ionizable active-site groups closer to the charge state needed for substrate binding and catalysis.
The rate will increase about 2.8-fold, because the higher pH supplies additional substrate molecules that raise the frequency of enzyme-substrate collisions.
The rate will stay about the same, because the enzyme is already saturated with substrate and a pH change cannot alter a saturated enzyme.
The rate will decrease, because any increase in pH moves the enzyme farther from its optimum and begins denaturing the protein.
option_rationale: Correct: 61/22 is about 2.8, and pH affects the ionization of active-site and substrate-binding groups, changing activity.
Misconception: pH changes the amount of substrate; substrate is stated to be saturating and unchanged, so collision frequency is not the cause.
Misconception: saturation makes the rate independent of all conditions; saturation removes substrate limitation but pH still changes the catalytic efficiency of each enzyme.
Misconception: higher pH is always harmful or denaturing; the data show the rate rises toward the optimum at pH 7, so pH 6 is closer to the optimum than pH 5.
input.explanation_en: The data show the rate rising from 22 at pH 5 to 61 at pH 6, about a 2.8-fold increase, as pH approaches the optimum of 7. Changing pH alters the ionization of amino acid side chains in the active site, which affects substrate binding and catalysis, so the key is correct. The substrate-supply explanation fails because substrate is saturating and unchanged, so pH is not adding substrate. The no-change prediction fails because saturation only means substrate is not limiting; the activity of each enzyme molecule still depends on pH, and the table shows a large change. The decrease prediction fails because the data show the rate is lower at pH 5 than at pH 6, so moving toward the optimum raises the rate; denaturation is not what occurs in this small shift.

content.text:
I'll design a household decision context: choosing a wash temperature for a laundry detergent containing a protease, using a table of relative activity vs. temperature and pH.

Design: the table gives relative protease activity at different temperatures at pH 9, plus a note that the detergent is used at pH 9 in the wash. The decision: the family considers switching from a 40°C wash to a 60°C wash to remove protein stains. The data show activity at 40 = 100, 50 = 85, 60 = 20, and 30 = 55. The prediction is that at 60°C the enzyme is partially denatured, so stain removal by the enzyme will fall. To keep it decidable, the stem asks for the best prediction and its reason.

stimulus.description: Relative activity of a protease in a laundry detergent measured at pH 9 at five wash temperatures, with a constant substrate amount and a 10-minute reaction time.

data.title: Protease relative activity at pH 9 (10-minute assay, same enzyme and substrate amounts in every trial)
columns: Relative protease activity (% of maximum observed)
data.note: The household currently washes at 40 °C and is considering 60 °C to remove grass and egg stains (protein-based).

input.stem: A family currently washes protein-stained clothes at 40 °C with a detergent containing the protease described in the table. To save time, they plan to switch to a 60 °C wash with the same detergent, same pH, and same wash duration. Which prediction about enzyme-driven stain removal at 60 °C is best supported by the data?
options: Enzyme-driven stain removal will decrease, because the high temperature likely disrupts the protease's tertiary structure and active site, so fewer substrate molecules are converted.
Enzyme-driven stain removal will increase, because higher temperature raises the kinetic energy of molecules, so enzyme-substrate collisions become more frequent.
Enzyme-driven stain removal will stay about the same, because the protease is a catalyst and is not changed or used up in the reaction.
Enzyme-driven stain removal will decrease, because the higher temperature lowers the activation energy barrier, so the stain proteins are consumed faster.
option_rationale: Correct: activity falls from 100 to 20 between 40 and 60 °C, consistent with heat-induced denaturation of the enzyme's tertiary structure and active site.
Misconception: assumes the rate always rises with temperature (collision theory only), ignoring denaturation; contradicts the table showing activity of 20 at 60 °C.
Misconception: believes that because enzymes are not consumed, their activity cannot be affected by environmental conditions; ignores the data showing activity drops.
Reaches the right direction with a wrong mechanism: temperature does not lower activation energy (enzymes do), and faster consumption contradicts the decrease in activity.
input.explanation_en: The table shows activity peaking at 40 °C (100%) and dropping to 20% at 60 °C, so enzyme-driven stain removal should fall. The best explanation is that high temperature disrupts the bonds maintaining the protease's tertiary structure, distorting the active site so fewer substrates are converted. The prediction that removal will increase because of more collisions ignores denaturation and contradicts the 60 °C datum. The prediction that nothing changes confuses the fact that catalysts are not consumed with being unaffected by conditions; the data show a clear change. The prediction that removal decreases because heat lowers activation energy gives an incorrect mechanism: enzymes, not temperature, lower activation energy, and a lowered barrier would speed the reaction rather than slow it.

content.text:
I'll design an item on enzyme function under environmental change (pH/temperature) in a health/technology context, with a data table, and ask the student to predict the effect of a change.

Design: a glucose-monitor test strip uses glucose oxidase. A table gives relative activity at several pH values, measured at 25 °C. The question asks what happens to the reading if the strip is used with a sample that lowers the pH to a value where activity is low. The key is that the enzyme's active-site shape or charge changes, which reduces substrate binding and catalytic rate, so the signal underestimates the glucose.

Data (relative activity, % of max): pH 3: 12, pH 4: 48, pH 5: 92, pH 6: 100, pH 7: 85, pH 8: 40. A sample with acidic pH 3.5 is predicted to give about 30% activity, so the key is a lower signal, and the glucose reading is underestimated. The verification code interpolates the activity at pH 3.5 (between 12 and 48, giving 30) and checks it against the key.

stimulus.description: Relative activity of glucose oxidase on a test strip at different pH values (25 C, saturating glucose).

data.title: Glucose oxidase activity vs. pH
data.conditions: 25 C; glucose concentration saturating in all trials; same enzyme amount on every strip
data.note: Test strip color intensity is proportional to the rate of product formation during a fixed 10-second reading window.

input.stem: A glucose meter strip uses the enzyme glucose oxidase, and the meter's color signal is proportional to the enzyme's reaction rate during a fixed reading window. The meter is calibrated using a sample at pH 6. A patient's sample is unusually acidic at about pH 4, with the same glucose concentration as the calibration sample. Based on the data, which prediction best describes the meter's result and its cause?
options: The signal will be about half the calibration value, because the acidic pH alters the charges and shape of the enzyme's active site, lowering the reaction rate.
The signal will be about the same as the calibration value, because the saturating glucose concentration overcomes any effect of pH on the enzyme.
The signal will be higher than the calibration value, because added hydrogen ions act as extra reactants and speed up the reaction.
The signal will be about half the calibration value, because the acidic pH uses up the glucose substrate before the reading window ends.
option_rationale: Correct: activity at pH 4 is 48% of maximum; pH changes ionization of amino acid side chains, altering active-site shape/binding and lowering rate.
Misconception: saturating substrate makes the enzyme immune to environmental conditions; but the table shows activity depends on pH even at saturating glucose.
Misconception: acid always speeds reactions, treating H+ as a reactant or catalyst; the data show activity falls at lower pH.
Right magnitude but wrong cause: claims pH depletes substrate; glucose is saturating and pH affects the enzyme, not substrate supply.
input.explanation_en: At pH 4 the table shows 48% of the maximum activity found at pH 6, so the signal should be roughly half the calibration value. The cause is that pH changes the ionization of side chains in and near the active site, altering its shape and substrate binding, which lowers the reaction rate. The prediction that the signal stays the same is wrong because the data were collected at saturating glucose and still show a strong pH effect. The prediction of a higher signal is wrong because the activity decreases, not increases, at lower pH, and hydrogen ions are not a reactant here. The prediction that the pH depletes the glucose is wrong because the lower signal results from reduced enzyme activity, not loss of substrate, which is saturating.
input.design_note: Predict effect of an environmental (pH) change on enzyme function in a health-technology context. Two distractors share the half-signal magnitude only in part, forcing the student to check the cause as well as the number. The answer is decidable from the table alone.

content.text:
I'll design a lab setting: isolated chloroplast suspensions with DCPIP (Hill reaction) under different light conditions, a table of data, and a claim-evidence question.

Data: DCPIP absorbance at 600 nm falls as DCPIP is reduced (blue to colorless). Treatments after 10 min, starting absorbance 0.80:

- Light, chloroplasts: 0.32
- Dark, chloroplasts: 0.78
- Light, boiled chloroplasts: 0.79
- Light, no chloroplasts (buffer + DCPIP): 0.80

Claim: the reduction of DCPIP depends on light-driven reactions in functional chloroplasts. The key is the option that pairs the claim with the specific comparisons that support it.

stimulus.description: Table of DCPIP absorbance at 600 nm before and after 10 minutes for four chloroplast-suspension treatments.

data.title: Absorbance at 600 nm of DCPIP (blue dye; lower absorbance = more DCPIP reduced)
rows: A: Intact chloroplasts + DCPIP, bright light
B: Intact chloroplasts + DCPIP, wrapped in foil (dark)
C: Boiled chloroplasts + DCPIP, bright light
D: Buffer + DCPIP, no chloroplasts, bright light
data.notes: All tubes contained the same buffer, the same DCPIP concentration, and were kept at 25 C. Each value is the mean of three tubes; the range among replicates was within 0.02.

input.stem: DCPIP is a blue dye that accepts electrons and becomes colorless when reduced. A student claims that DCPIP reduction in this experiment depends on the light-dependent reactions carried out by functional chloroplasts. Which choice best supports the claim with evidence from the table?
options: Absorbance fell by 0.48 in intact chloroplasts in light but by only 0.02 or less in the dark, boiled-chloroplast, and no-chloroplast tubes, so both light and intact chloroplasts were needed.
Absorbance fell by 0.48 in intact chloroplasts in light, which shows that the chloroplasts used light energy to fix carbon dioxide into sugar and thereby reduced the DCPIP.
Absorbance stayed near 0.80 in the tube with buffer and DCPIP but no chloroplasts in bright light, which shows that light is not required for DCPIP reduction.
Absorbance fell the most in intact chloroplasts in light, which shows that chloroplasts reduce DCPIP only when ATP is being produced by the Calvin cycle.
option_rationale: Correct: cites the treatment effect (0.48 drop) and the three controls showing that removing light or functional chloroplasts abolishes reduction.
Misconception: assumes DCPIP reduction measures carbon fixation/sugar production; the data show only dye reduction, and DCPIP intercepts electrons from the light reactions, not the Calvin cycle.

Misconception: misreads the no-chloroplast control; it shows chloroplasts are needed, and says nothing about whether light is unnecessary since the dark tube with chloroplasts also showed no reduction.
Misconception: attributes the electron source to the Calvin cycle producing ATP; the data do not measure ATP and the Calvin cycle does not supply electrons to DCPIP.
input.explanation_en: The intact-chloroplast tube in light lost 0.48 absorbance units (0.80 to 0.32), while the dark tube (0.02 drop), boiled-chloroplast tube (0.01 drop), and no-chloroplast tube (0 drop) barely changed. Together these show that both light and functional (non-denatured) chloroplasts are required, which supports a claim about the light-dependent reactions. The option claiming sugar synthesis is wrong because the experiment measures only dye reduction, not carbon fixation. The option saying light is not required misuses the no-chloroplast control and ignores the dark chloroplast tube. The option invoking ATP from the Calvin cycle is wrong because no ATP was measured and the Calvin cycle is not the source of electrons for DCPIP.
input.design_note: Hill-reaction claim-evidence item; the key requires using treatment plus three controls. Distractors target the confusion between dye reduction and carbon fixation, misreading controls, and the Calvin cycle as electron source.

content.text:
I'll design a purely mathematical/abstract setting: a table of light-response data (net CO2 uptake vs. light intensity), asking which claim is supported by the numbers.

Data (µmol CO2 m^-2 s^-1) for a hypothetical leaf: light 0 → -2.0, 100 → 4.0, 200 → 10.0, 400 → 16.0, 800 → 16.5. The light compensation point is where net uptake equals zero, which is 50 by linear interpolation between 0 and 100. Gross is net + 2.0: 0 → 0, 100 → 6, 200 → 12, 400 → 18, 800 → 18.5. The key is that between 400 and 800 gross rises only about 0.5, so a factor other than light limits the rate. Distractors cover the following misconceptions:

- Net uptake at 0 light shows no respiration.
- Saturation means chlorophyll is destroyed.
- Doubling light from 100 to 200 doubles net (10 vs 4 is 2.5×, so the claim "net doubles" is wrong).

I'll make the key the claim that between 400 and 800 the 2-fold light increase produces under 5% gross increase, so light is no longer limiting.

stimulus.description: Table of net CO2 uptake of a leaf at five light intensities, with net uptake in the dark of -2.0.

columns: Net CO2 uptake (µmol CO2 m^-2 s^-1)
data.note: Negative value means net CO2 release. Assume the rate of CO2 release by cellular respiration is the same at all light intensities and equals the magnitude of the dark value. Gross CO2 fixation = net uptake + respiration rate. Temperature and CO2 concentration were constant.

input.stem: A student claims that, for this leaf, light is no longer the factor limiting the rate of photosynthesis once light intensity exceeds 400 µmol photons m^-2 s^-1. Which statement uses the data in the table to best support this claim?
options: Doubling light from 400 to 800 raises gross CO2 fixation only from 18.0 to 18.5, less than a 3% increase, so extra light barely increases the rate.
Net CO2 uptake in the dark is -2.0, which shows that the leaf carries out no photosynthesis and only respiration at 0 light intensity.
Doubling light from 100 to 200 raises net CO2 uptake from 4.0 to 10.0, which shows that the rate of photosynthesis is directly proportional to light.
Net CO2 uptake rises from 16.0 to 16.5 at 800, which shows that excess light has begun damaging chlorophyll and lowering the rate of photosynthesis.
option_rationale: Correct: gross = net + 2.0 gives 18.0 and 18.5; a 2-fold light increase gives a ~2.8% rise, so the rate has plateaued and another factor limits it.
Distractor: true but irrelevant to the claim about light above 400; it addresses the dark value, not saturation. Misconception: using a true but non-supporting datum as evidence.
Distractor: 4.0 to 10.0 is a 2.5-fold change, not proportional, and it concerns low light, not the region above 400. Misconception: reading any increase as direct proportionality.
Distractor: net uptake rises, not falls, so the data contradict damage. Misconception: assuming a plateau means chlorophyll destruction.
input.explanation_en: Gross fixation equals net uptake plus the respiration rate (2.0). At 400 gross is 18.0 and at 800 it is 18.5, so doubling light raises the rate by under 3%. That is evidence the rate has plateaued and some other factor (such as CO2 supply, enzyme activity, or electron transport capacity) is limiting. The dark-value statement is true but says nothing about light above 400. The proportionality statement is wrong because 4.0 to 10.0 is a 2.5-fold change and concerns low light. The damage statement is contradicted by the data, since net uptake slightly increases from 16.0 to 16.5 rather than falling.

content.text:
I'll design a household decision: a family choosing a basement grow-light for basil. Data table of O2 production (a proxy for net photosynthesis) of leaf discs under different light colors at equal intensity, and the claim must be decidable from the data.

Design: a household compares three LED bulbs (red, green, blue) at equal photon flux for basil. Measured net O2 release (µmol O2 per m² per s), plus dark respiration. The claim to support: which bulb choice is supported by the data and why.

Data (mean ± 2SE): Red 8.4 ± 0.6; Blue 7.9 ± 0.5; Green 3.1 ± 0.4; Dark (no light) -1.2 ± 0.2.

Key: the claim "Replace the green bulb with a red or blue bulb, because net O2 release was greater under red and blue than under green at equal photon flux, indicating chlorophyll's absorption drives more light-dependent reactions in those wavelengths." Red vs. blue overlap (8.4 ± 0.6 → 7.8–9.0; 7.9 ± 0.5 → 7.4–8.4), so no difference can be claimed. Green is still above zero, so green drives some photosynthesis.

Distractors:
- Green gives no photosynthesis (net O2 3.1 > 0, and gross = 3.1 + 1.2 = 4.3).
- Red is best because it is higher than blue (error bars overlap).
- Pick green because the leaf reflects it, which means it is efficient (misconception).

stimulus.description: Table of mean net O2 release by basil leaf discs under three LED colors at equal photon flux, plus a dark control, with 2SE values.

data.title: Net O2 exchange of basil leaf discs after 20 min under LED bulbs of equal photon flux (100 umol photons per m^2 per s)
columns: Mean net O2 release (umol O2 per m^2 per s)
data.notes: Negative value means net O2 uptake. n = 10 leaf discs per treatment. Error values are plus or minus 2 SE of the mean.

input.stem: A family is choosing a grow-light for a basement basil garden. They already own a green LED bulb and test it against red and blue LED bulbs of equal photon flux using leaf discs, with the results shown in the table. Which claim about their purchase is best supported by the data?
options: Buy a red or blue bulb instead of the green one, because net O2 release was higher under red and blue than under green, and the red and blue values were not clearly different from each other.
Buy the red bulb only, because its mean net O2 release was higher than that of the blue bulb, showing red is the most effective wavelength for basil.
Keep the green bulb, because basil leaves reflect green light, showing that green light is used efficiently without wasting energy.
Keep the green bulb as the only light source, because net O2 release under green light was low, showing the leaf discs carried out no photosynthesis.
option_rationale: Correct: red (8.4 +/- 0.6) and blue (7.9 +/- 0.5) intervals overlap, and both are far above green (3.1 +/- 0.4), so red/blue support more photosynthesis than green at equal photon flux.
Misconception: treating any difference in means as a real difference while ignoring overlapping 2SE intervals (7.8-9.0 vs 7.4-8.4).
Misconception: believing reflected wavelengths are the most efficiently used; reflection means less absorption, and the data show lower O2 output under green.
Misconception: equating low net O2 with zero photosynthesis; net 3.1 is above zero and gross is about 4.3 after adding respiration (1.2), and the recommendation also conflicts with the lower output.
input.explanation_en: Net O2 release under red (8.4 +/- 0.6) and blue (7.9 +/- 0.5) is well above that under green (3.1 +/- 0.4), with non-overlapping intervals, so red or blue light supports more photosynthesis at equal photon flux. The red and blue intervals overlap, so the data do not show that one is better than the other; recommending red only is unsupported. Recommending the green bulb because leaves reflect green reverses the logic: reflected light is not absorbed, and the measured O2 output is lowest under green. Saying green drives no photosynthesis is wrong because net O2 release is positive (3.1), and gross production is about 4.3 once dark respiration (1.2) is added back; the choice to keep green as the only light also ignores the better-performing bulbs.

content.text: I designed a lab setting: yeast respiration measured by O2 consumption, with a table of data, and the question asks which graph construction correctly represents the data (skill 4.A). Key: a line graph with time on x-axis and cumulative O2 consumed on y-axis, with two lines (glucose-fed vs. an inhibitor) and units labeled.

columns: Inhibitor added at 0 min: O2 consumed (µmol)
data.notes: Each value is the mean of 3 trials. Time is measured at fixed 2-minute intervals; time is the independent variable.

input.stem: A student wants to graph the data in the table to show how the inhibitor affects the rate of aerobic respiration in the mitochondria over the 10-minute experiment. Which graph construction is most appropriate?
options: A line graph with time (min) on the x-axis and cumulative O2 consumed (µmol) on the y-axis, with one labeled line for the control and one for the inhibitor
A bar graph with the control and inhibitor treatments on the x-axis and the time (min) at which each measurement was taken on the y-axis

content.text:
I'll design a technology scenario (an indoor vertical-farm LED lighting trial) with a table of oxygen-evolution data from leaf discs, where students must choose the claim best supported by the data.

Design: lettuce leaf discs, O2 evolution (net) measured under different LED colors at equal photon flux. Data: net O2 production in µmol O2 per m² per s. Red 8.2, Blue 7.1, Green 2.4, Far-red 0.3, Darkness -1.1 (respiration). The claim to be supported: green light drives some photosynthesis, but less than red/blue. Distractors cover the misconception that green is not absorbed or used at all, that net O2 in darkness shows photosynthesis, and that red must be better than blue because the pigments absorb only red.

Verification: net O2 + respiration gives gross: green 2.4 + 1.1 = 3.5 > 0, so green does drive photosynthesis. Gross for red is 9.3 and for blue 8.2, which is about 2.7 and 2.3 times the green rate.

stimulus.description: Table of net oxygen exchange of lettuce leaf discs under five LED treatments of equal photon flux (200 micromol photons per square meter per second), mean of 10 discs each.

data.title: Net O2 exchange of lettuce leaf discs under LED treatments
columns: Net O2 exchange (micromol O2 per m^2 per s)
data.notes: Positive values = net O2 release; negative = net O2 uptake. Photon flux equal in all light treatments. Temperature and CO2 constant.

input.stem: A vertical-farm engineer tests whether green LEDs can be dropped from a lighting design for lettuce. Leaf discs were exposed to equal photon flux of different LED colors, and net O2 exchange was measured (see table). Which claim is best supported by the data?
options: Green light drives some photosynthesis, because net O2 under green light is above the darkness value and above zero, though the rate is lower than under red or blue light.
Green light does not drive photosynthesis, because its net O2 release is much lower than the release under red or blue light.
Red light drives more photosynthesis than blue light, because chlorophyll absorbs only red wavelengths and reflects all other colors.
Far-red light drives photosynthesis at a rate similar to green light, because net O2 release under far-red light is above the darkness value.
option_rationale: Correct: net O2 of 2.4 under green is positive and exceeds the -1.1 in darkness; gross rate is about 3.5, well above zero but below red (about 9.3) and blue (about 8.2).
Misconception: lower rate means no photosynthesis; ignores that net release above zero (and above respiration-only darkness value) shows photosynthesis is occurring.
Misconception: chlorophylls absorb only red; ignores that blue light also gives a high rate and the data cannot support an absorption claim; the stated reason is also factually wrong.
Misconception: any value above darkness equals similar photosynthesis; far-red gross is only about 1.4 versus about 3.5 for green, and net 0.3 is near zero, so rates are not similar.
input.explanation_en: Darkness gives -1.1, which reflects respiration alone. Under green light the net O2 release is +2.4, so gross photosynthesis is about 2.4 + 1.1 = 3.5 micromol O2 per m^2 per s, clearly above zero but lower than red (about 9.3) and blue (about 8.2). The claim that green light drives some photosynthesis at a reduced rate is therefore supported. The claim that green drives none is wrong because a lower rate is not a zero rate. The claim that chlorophyll absorbs only red is wrong because blue light gives a high rate nearly as large as red, and the data do not show absorption. The claim that far-red is similar to green is wrong because far-red gross photosynthesis is only about 1.4, far below green's 3.5, and its net exchange is near zero.

input.stem: A bakery owner tests whether sealing dough containers (low oxygen) changes how fast yeast produces CO2, and records the data above. To present the results to staff, she will construct a graph. Which graph construction best represents these data?
options: A line graph with time (min) on the x-axis and mean CO2 (mL) on the y-axis, two labeled lines (aerobic, anaerobic), and error bars of mean ± 2SE at each point

content.text: I'll design a lab-based item on cell communication (ligand-receptor signaling, specificity of response) with a table stimulus.

stimulus.description: Table of cAMP and glycogen phosphorylase responses in two cultured cell types after treatment with hormone X, with or without a membrane-impermeable receptor-blocking antibody.

data.title: Responses of cultured cells 10 minutes after treatment
rows: Hormone X + antibody against receptor R
data.note: Hormone X is a water-soluble peptide. Antibody cannot enter cells. Receptor R is a plasma membrane protein.

input.stem: A researcher treats cultured liver cells and muscle cells with hormone X and measures the responses shown in the table. Which statement best explains the data in terms of cell communication?
options: Hormone X binds receptor R on the liver cell surface, which triggers a cAMP-mediated pathway that activates glycogen phosphorylase; muscle cells likely lack receptor R.
Hormone X diffuses through the liver cell membrane and binds a cytoplasmic receptor that directly activates glycogen phosphorylase; muscle cells cannot take up hormone X.
Hormone X binds receptor R on both cell types, but only liver cells produce cAMP because muscle cells have no glycogen phosphorylase gene.
Hormone X is converted by liver cells into cAMP, which then acts as the ligand for receptor R and activates glycogen phosphorylase.
option_rationale: Correct: the blocking antibody (which cannot enter cells) abolishes both cAMP rise and enzyme activation, showing a surface receptor is needed; cAMP rises before/with enzyme activation, consistent with a second messenger; muscle cells show no response, consistent with lacking the receptor.

Misconception: assuming all hormones act on intracellular receptors; ignores that a water-soluble peptide is blocked by an extracellular antibody and that cAMP rises, indicating a second-messenger pathway.

Misconception: ignores that receptor-binding determines target cell; claims receptor is on both cell types, but the lack of any cAMP change in muscle cells indicates no signal is received, and the gene claim is unsupported by the data.
Misconception: confuses the signal with the second messenger; cAMP is made inside the cell in response to receptor activation, and is not the ligand for receptor R.
input.explanation_en: In liver cells, hormone X raises cAMP and glycogen phosphorylase activity. An antibody that cannot enter cells and blocks receptor R eliminates both responses, so the signal is received at a plasma membrane receptor, which fits a water-soluble peptide. cAMP acts as a second messenger that relays the signal inside the cell, leading to enzyme activation. Muscle cells show no change, consistent with target-cell specificity based on having the receptor. The cytoplasmic-receptor idea is wrong because a peptide hormone is blocked by an extracellular antibody and cAMP rises. The idea that both cell types have the receptor is wrong because muscle cells show no signal transduction, and the missing-gene claim is not supported by the data. The idea that hormone X is converted into cAMP that serves as the ligand is wrong because cAMP is generated inside the cell after receptor activation as a second messenger, not as the ligand for the receptor.

content.text:
I'll design a purely abstract/mathematical item on cell communication (signal transduction amplification), testing explanation of the concept.

Design: a linear cascade where each activated enzyme activates a fixed number of next-tier molecules. Question asks why a tiny number of ligand molecules yields a large response and which explanation is correct.

stimulus.description: Model of a three-step signal transduction cascade: number of activated molecules at each step when 5 ligand molecules bind receptors.

data.title: Idealized cascade started by 5 ligand-bound receptors
columns: Activated molecules produced per activated molecule of the previous step
Total activated molecules at this step
data.assumptions: Every activated molecule acts for the same length of time; no molecules are inactivated during the interval considered.

input.stem: In the idealized model in the table, 5 ligand-bound receptors lead to 5,000 activated second messenger molecules. Which statement best explains how this pattern relates to cell communication?
options: Each activated molecule in a step activates many molecules of the next step, so a small extracellular signal is amplified into a large intracellular response.
Each ligand molecule is converted into 1,000 second messenger molecules as it passes through the membrane, so the ligand itself enters the cell.
The relay proteins and second messengers divide the original signal among themselves, so each activated molecule carries only a fraction of the signal.
The cascade increases the response only because the number of receptors increases at each step, not because activated molecules activate others.
option_rationale: Correct: multiplicative activation at each tier (5 x 20 x 50 = 5,000) is signal amplification.
Misconception: ligands cross the membrane and are chemically converted; ignores that a ligand binds a receptor and the signal is relayed by transduction.
Misconception: signal is conserved/divided like a quantity rather than amplified by enzymatic activation.
Misconception: confuses receptor number with activated intermediates; the table shows receptors stay at 5 and downstream molecules multiply.
input.explanation_en: The table shows 5 receptors activating 20 relay proteins each (100 total), and each of those activating 50 second messengers (5,000 total). Because each activated molecule activates many molecules of the next tier, a small number of signal molecules produces a large response, which is amplification in signal transduction. The option claiming each ligand is converted into second messengers is wrong because the ligand binds a receptor and does not enter the cell or become the messengers; the relay is carried by receptor-activated intermediates. The option claiming the signal is divided is wrong because the number of activated molecules grows at each step rather than being split. The option attributing the increase to more receptors is wrong because the table shows the receptor count stays at 5 while downstream activated molecules multiply.

content.text: I'll frame cell signaling through a household/business analogy: a thermostat/building-management decision, mapped to signal transduction concepts, with a numeric table to keep it decidable.

stimulus.description: Table comparing three ways a homeowner could deliver the message 'turn on the porch light' to a lamp, with the number of lamps switched on per signal sent.

data.title: Options for switching on lamps in a house
columns: Lamps switched on per single message sent
rows: Wall switch relays a signal to a smart plug, which activates a chain of 3 relay boxes; each box turns on 10 lamps
Smart plug on a wall outlet (receiver)
Homeowner walks to and flips each lamp's own switch
Wall switch sends signal; plug turns on 1 lamp only, with no relays

input.stem: A homeowner compares the methods in the table for turning on lamps. A student uses the first method as an analogy for a signal transduction pathway in which a small number of extracellular signal molecules binds receptors and many intracellular molecules are activated. Which statement best explains how the analogy represents a feature of cell signaling?
options: The relay boxes represent a cascade of signaling molecules that amplifies a small number of receptor-binding events into a large cellular response.
The relay boxes represent the signal molecule itself, which must enter the nucleus to switch on each target gene directly.
The relay boxes represent the cell's receptor, which must be physically replaced each time a new signal molecule binds.
The relay boxes represent the cell membrane, which blocks the signal so that only one target is activated per message.
option_rationale: Correct: sequential activation of relay molecules (e.g., phosphorylation cascade) amplifies one binding event into many activated molecules, as in 1 message -> 1000 lamps.
Misconception: signal molecules always enter the nucleus and act directly on genes; ignores that transduction relays a signal from a membrane receptor via intracellular intermediates.
Misconception: receptors are used up or replaced after one binding; receptors are reusable and relays are intracellular, not the receptor.
Misconception: the membrane's role is to prevent specificity/amplification; it actually hosts receptors, and the analogy's 1000-to-1 ratio shows amplification, not one-to-one.
input.explanation_en: In the first method, one message produces 3 x 10 = 30 per relay stage chain, and the table reports 1000 lamps per single message, so a small input yields a large output. This parallels a signal transduction cascade, in which each activated intracellular molecule activates many others, amplifying a few receptor-binding events into a large response. The option saying the relays are the signal molecule entering the nucleus is wrong because transduction relays the message through intracellular intermediates rather than the ligand acting directly on genes. The option saying the receptor is replaced after each binding is wrong because receptors are reusable and the relays are separate downstream molecules. The option about the membrane blocking the signal is wrong because the table shows one-to-many amplification, not one-to-one, and the membrane houses receptors rather than relaying signals.

I'll design an item where the student must choose the correct graph construction for respiration data from a sports-science scenario (a table of oxygen consumption vs. cycling power output, with replicate error), so the skill is constructing a graph to represent the data.

Computation check: the data are continuous x (power in watts) vs. mean VO2 ± 2SE. The best graph is a line graph with power on the x-axis and mean VO2 on the y-axis with ±2SE error bars. I will compute the key from the stimulus properties in code.

data.title: Oxygen consumption of cyclists at different power outputs
columns: Mean VO2 (mL O2 per kg per min)
data.notes: Power output is a continuous numerical variable set by the experimenter; error values are plus or minus 2 standard errors of the mean.

input.stem: A sports scientist measures oxygen consumption, an indicator of the rate of aerobic cellular respiration in muscle, in cyclists at several power outputs (data above). Which graph would best represent these data so the relationship between power output and aerobic respiration rate can be interpreted?
options: A line graph with power output (watts) on the x-axis, mean VO2 (mL O2 per kg per min) on the y-axis, points connected in order of power, and error bars of ±2SE at each point
A bar graph with mean VO2 on the x-axis, power output on the y-axis, one bar for each power output, and a single error bar showing the range of all five means
A pie chart in which each power output is a slice sized by its share of the total VO2, with 2SE written in each slice label
A line graph with power output on the x-axis, 2SE on the y-axis, points connected in order of power, and mean VO2 shown only as a label at each point
option_rationale: Correct: the independent continuous variable goes on x, the dependent mean on y, a line shows the trend across the continuous variable, and ±2SE error bars show the uncertainty of each mean.

Swaps the independent and dependent variables and uses one pooled range instead of per-mean error bars, so the uncertainty of each mean is not shown. Misconception: the axes can be assigned arbitrarily and one error bar is enough.
Treats the data as parts of a whole. Misconception: any dataset with several values can be shown as a pie chart, even though the question is about a trend across a continuous variable.
Plots the error, not the measured response, as the dependent variable. Misconception: error values are the data of interest, and the means can be relegated to labels.
input.explanation_en: The independent variable (power output, continuous) belongs on the x-axis and the dependent variable (mean VO2, a measure of aerobic respiration rate) on the y-axis. A line graph suits a trend across a continuous variable, and each mean needs its own ±2SE error bar so viewers can judge whether differences between means are meaningful. The option swapping the axes and using one pooled error bar is wrong because the variables are reversed and uncertainty is not shown per mean. The pie chart is wrong because the values are not fractions of a whole and a trend cannot be read from slices. The graph with 2SE on the y-axis is wrong because it plots the uncertainty rather than the measured response and hides the relationship between power and VO2.

stimulus.description: Table of muscle cell responses to epinephrine under four conditions in an exercise-physiology experiment.

rows: Epinephrine added to the surrounding medium

input.stem: A sports physiologist studies how skeletal muscle cells respond to epinephrine released during sprinting. Using the data in the table, which statement best explains how epinephrine causes glycogen breakdown in these cells?
options: Epinephrine binds a receptor protein on the cell surface, which triggers a signal transduction pathway inside the cell that activates glycogen-breaking enzymes.
Epinephrine diffuses across the plasma membrane and directly activates the enzymes that break down glycogen in the cytoplasm.

content.text:
I'll design a lab experiment on a kinase cascade with a table of phosphorylation data from knockout/inhibitor treatments, requiring reasoning about the order of components in a pathway.

Design: A pathway with Receptor R, Kinase A, Kinase B, and transcription factor TF. Cells are treated with ligand, and an inhibitor/knockout is applied. Data: relative reporter gene expression and phosphorylation of Kinase B and TF.

Data (the same ligand in all but the control):
- Wild type, no ligand: Kinase A-P 5, Kinase B-P 4, reporter 3
- Wild type, ligand: A-P 92, B-P 88, reporter 100
- Kinase A knockout, ligand: A-P 0, B-P 6, reporter 4
- Kinase B knockout, ligand: A-P 90, B-P 0, reporter 5
- Kinase B knockout + constitutively active Kinase A (no ligand): not needed.

The key conclusion is that A acts upstream of B: without A, B is not phosphorylated, whereas without B, A is still phosphorylated. All distractors are tied to misconceptions.

stimulus.description: Table of relative phosphorylation of Kinase A and Kinase B and relative reporter gene expression in cultured cells under four conditions.

data.title: Responses of cultured cells to Ligand L (values are relative units, wild type with ligand = 100 for reporter)
data.notes: Reporter gene is transcribed only when a transcription factor is activated by the pathway. Each knockout cell line lacks only the named kinase and still has a normal receptor for Ligand L.

input.stem: A researcher proposes that Ligand L binds a membrane receptor and activates a pathway in which Kinase A phosphorylates Kinase B, which then leads to reporter gene expression. Which statement best connects the data in the table to this proposed signal transduction pathway?
options: Kinase A acts upstream of Kinase B, because loss of Kinase A prevents Kinase B phosphorylation, while loss of Kinase B leaves Kinase A phosphorylation intact.
Kinase B acts upstream of Kinase A, because loss of Kinase B abolishes the reporter response, while Kinase A phosphorylation stays high.
Kinases A and B act in separate parallel pathways, because each knockout eliminates the reporter response independently of the other kinase.
Kinase A is not needed for the pathway, because Kinase B phosphorylation is still detectable in the Kinase A knockout cells.
option_rationale: Correct: in the A knockout, B-P is only 6 (near the 4 baseline), so B needs A; in the B knockout, A-P is 90, so A does not need B. This fits A upstream of B in a sequential cascade.
Misconception: reversing pathway order by focusing on which knockout stops the output; both knockouts stop the output, and A-P staying high actually shows A is not dependent on B.
Misconception: concluding that two components that both are required for the output must be parallel; but B phosphorylation depends on A, which indicates a linear sequence.
Misconception: misreading the small residual value of 6 as meaningful signaling; it is at the unstimulated baseline (4), so B is essentially not activated without A.
input.explanation_en: In the Kinase A knockout, Kinase B phosphorylation falls to 6, about the unstimulated baseline of 4, so Kinase B activation depends on Kinase A. In the Kinase B knockout, Kinase A is still strongly phosphorylated (90), so Kinase A activation does not depend on Kinase B. Both knockouts abolish reporter expression, so both kinases are required for the response. Together this supports a sequential cascade with Kinase A upstream of Kinase B, as proposed. The option reversing the order is wrong because Kinase A stays phosphorylated without Kinase B, and the loss of the reporter response alone does not indicate order. The parallel-pathway option is wrong because Kinase B phosphorylation depends on Kinase A, so they are not independent. The option claiming Kinase A is unnecessary is wrong because the value of 6 is essentially baseline, not activation, and the reporter response is lost in those cells.

content.text:
I'll design a health-themed item: a signal transduction pathway in muscle/liver cells with an inhibitor experiment. The stimulus is a table of data from a cell-culture experiment.

Design: Hormone H binds a receptor, which activates kinase K1, then K2, then glycogen phosphorylase, producing glucose release. Treatments are measured by glucose released. Student must connect evidence to the pathway order.

Data (glucose release, relative units):

1. No hormone: 10
2. Hormone: 100
3. Hormone + Drug X (blocks K1): 12
4. Hormone + Drug Y (blocks K2): 11
5. Drug X + a membrane-permeable cAMP analog: 95
6. Drug Y + cAMP analog: 13

Interpretation: The cAMP analog rescues the K1 block but not the K2 block, so K1 acts upstream of cAMP (between receptor and cAMP), and K2 acts downstream of cAMP. The key is that cAMP production requires K1 and K2 acts after cAMP.

I'll run the verification script before submitting.

data.title: Glucose release by cultured liver cells (relative units, mean of 3 trials)
data.note: Pathway components tested: receptor for H, kinase K1, cAMP, kinase K2. Drug X and Drug Y each specifically inhibit only their one target kinase.

input.stem: A researcher proposes that hormone H binds a receptor, which leads to cAMP production, and that two kinases (K1 and K2) are in the pathway leading to glucose release. Which argument best uses the data to support a placement of K1 and K2 relative to cAMP?
options: K1 acts upstream of cAMP and K2 acts downstream of cAMP, because the cAMP analog restored glucose release when K1 was inhibited but not when K2 was inhibited.
K2 acts upstream of cAMP and K1 acts downstream of cAMP, because the cAMP analog restored glucose release when K1 was inhibited but not when K2 was inhibited.
K1 and K2 both act downstream of cAMP, because glucose release was low whenever either drug was present with hormone H.
K1 and K2 both act upstream of cAMP, because glucose release was low whenever either drug was present with hormone H.

Uses only the hormone-plus-drug results and ignores the analog rescue in treatment 5; low output with each drug does not show order.
Same error of ignoring the rescue data; also contradicts treatment 6, where K2 inhibition blocks output even when cAMP is supplied.

With Drug Y, the analog did not restore release (13), so K2 is required after cAMP and acts downstream. The reversed-placement option swaps the logic of the rescue. The two options placing both kinases on the same side of cAMP rely only on the inhibited-without-analog results, which show that each kinase is required but not their order, and they contradict the rescue result for K1 (both upstream) or the failure of rescue for K2 (both downstream).
