items.stem: In populations E and F, the resistance allele frequency declined slightly. Which explanation is best supported by the data?
options: Without antibiotic, the allele was not advantageous and carried a small fitness cost, so carriers reproduced slightly less than non-carriers.
Without antibiotic, the allele mutated back to the sensitive form in every cell, eliminating it quickly.
Without antibiotic, selection stopped, so the allele frequency should have remained exactly at 0.01.
Without antibiotic, resistant cells were killed by the sensitive cells in the medium.
option_rationale: Correct: whether a trait is favored depends on the environment; slight decline implies a modest cost.
Misconception: reverse mutation would be rare and would not explain a gradual, partial decline in all cells.
Misconception: absence of directional selection means no change; ignores that other fitness differences and drift occur and data show decline.
Misconception: invents direct killing; no data support it.
items.explanation_en: The decline from 0.01 to about 0.003-0.004 in both no-antibiotic populations indicates carriers had slightly lower fitness without the drug, so the allele's advantage depends on environment. Reverse mutation in every cell would remove the allele far faster and is not supported. Constant frequency is not what the data show. Killing of resistant cells by sensitive cells has no evidence in the table.

Differing allele frequencies do not erase common descent.

content.text: I'll design a household/business context: a greenhouse grower who uses an insecticide against aphids over several seasons, with a table of resistance data. Items cover natural selection (7.2), common ancestry/evidence (7.5), phylogeny/continuing evolution (7.8, 7.11 speciation/extinction/diversity).

input.stimulus: {"kind":"table","description":"Table of a greenhouse business's aphid population tracked over six spray seasons with insecticide Z, plus a comparison table of a resistance gene in related aphid populations.","data":{"title":"Aphid control records at Marlow Greenhouse (sprayed every season with insecticide Z; same dose each time)","table1":{"columns":["Season","Percent of aphids surviving a spray","Percent of sampled aphids carrying resistance allele R"],"rows":[[1,4,2],[2,9,5],[3,21,12],[4,40,26],[5,63,47],[6,81,69]]},"notes":"Aphids reproduce asexually in summer but mix alleles through sexual reproduction each autumn. Resistance to Z is due to allele R of a gene encoding a detoxifying enzyme. In untreated greenhouses nearby, R stays near 2% of aphids. Aphids with R grow slightly slower and lay about 10% fewer eggs when Z is absent.","table2":{"title":"Same detox gene, partial DNA comparison to the Marlow aphid (percent identical bases over 1,000 bases)","columns":["Species","Percent identity"],"rows":[["Aphid species B (garden pest, same genus)",98],["Aphid species C (different genus, same family)",93],["Whitefly (different order)",81]]}}

items.stem: Which statement best explains why the percent of aphids surviving a spray rose from season 1 to season 6?
options: Z exposure caused new R mutations in the aphids, and those mutations were passed to offspring.
Individual aphids became resistant to Z by repeated exposure and passed this acquired trait to offspring.
Aphids with R survived and reproduced more under Z, so R became more frequent in the population.
The aphid population adapted as a whole so every individual gradually became more tolerant of Z.
option_rationale: Misconception: the environmental pressure induces the needed mutations rather than selecting existing variation (R was already present at 2%).
Misconception: Lamarckian inheritance of acquired traits.
Correct: differential survival and reproduction of heritable variants raises allele frequency.
Misconception: populations adapt as a unit and individuals change, rather than allele frequencies shifting.
items.explanation_en: R existed before spraying (about 2%). Z kills most non-R aphids, so R aphids leave more offspring and R frequency climbs, raising survival. Z did not cause mutations to appear, since R was already present. Individuals do not acquire resistance through exposure and pass it on. Individual aphids do not change tolerance; the population changes because the proportion of R carriers changes.
items.verification_code:
import json
r=[2,5,12,26,47,69]
s=[4,9,21,40,63,81]
ok=all(r[i]<r[i+1] for i in range(5)) and all(s[i]<s[i+1] for i in range(5)) and r[0]>0
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':2 if ok else None,'conceptual_only':False,'details':'R present at season1 (2%) and rises with survival'}))

items.stem: In untreated nearby greenhouses R stays near 2%. Which explanation best accounts for why R does not become common there?
options: Without Z, R aphids lay fewer eggs, so R has a small fitness disadvantage and is kept at low frequency.
Without Z, the R allele mutates back into the non-resistant allele in most aphids each season.
Without Z, selection stops acting on the population, so allele frequencies stay exactly fixed.
Without Z, R aphids cannot survive, so the allele is eliminated entirely from those greenhouses.
option_rationale: Correct: whether a trait is advantageous depends on the environment; a reproductive cost of R lowers its fitness without Z.
Misconception: assumes high-rate back mutation drives allele frequency instead of selection.
Misconception: believes selection only operates when a human-applied pressure is present, ignoring the egg-laying difference.
Misconception: confuses a slight fitness cost with lethality; R persists near 2% in the data.
items.explanation_en: R aphids lay about 10% fewer eggs without Z, so they are slightly less fit there and R stays rare, though not absent (2%). Back mutation is rare and cannot explain a stable low frequency. Selection still acts through the egg-laying difference. R is not lethal, as the data show about 2% carrying it.
items.verification_code:

print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'Conceptual: fitness cost of R without Z (10% fewer eggs) with R observed at 2% not 0'}))

items.stem: The DNA comparison table supports which conclusion about the detox gene?
options: Aphid species B and the Marlow aphid share a more recent common ancestor than either shares with the whitefly.
The whitefly evolved its gene from the Marlow aphid because the sequences are 81% identical.
Species C has the same resistance allele R as the Marlow aphid because their sequences are 93% identical.
All four organisms diverged from a common ancestor at the same time because the gene is present in all.
option_rationale: Correct: greater sequence similarity indicates more recent shared ancestry.
Misconception: reads similarity as one species descending from another rather than shared ancestry.
Misconception: equates overall gene similarity with possession of a specific allele.
Misconception: presence of a shared gene implies simultaneous divergence, ignoring differing similarity.
items.explanation_en: Higher identity (98%) with species B than with the whitefly (81%) indicates fewer accumulated differences and a more recent common ancestor. Similarity does not mean one living species came from another. A 93% match does not show that species C carries allele R. Different identity percentages indicate divergence at different times, not all at once.

items.stem: The owner switches to a rotation of several insecticides with different modes of action and sprays only when pest counts are high. Which prediction best follows from evolutionary principles?
options: Resistance to any single insecticide will rise more slowly, because selection pressure for each resistance allele is weaker and less constant.
Resistance will never evolve, because aphids cannot adapt to more than one chemical.
Resistance will rise faster, because exposure to varied chemicals induces more mutations in aphids.
Resistance will be unchanged, because allele frequencies do not respond to how often a pressure is applied.
option_rationale: Correct: less frequent, varied selection reduces consistent advantage for any one allele, slowing but not eliminating its spread.
Misconception: assumes a limit on adaptation; variation can arise for each chemical.
Misconception: believes more varied stress directs mutation toward resistance.
Misconception: thinks the strength and consistency of selection do not affect rate of allele frequency change.
items.explanation_en: Selection for resistance to a given chemical is weaker and intermittent under rotation, so alleles conferring resistance to that chemical rise more slowly, although resistance can still evolve if variation exists. Resistance is not impossible. Chemicals do not induce directed mutations. Allele frequency change depends on how consistently selection acts.
items.verification_code:

print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'Conceptual prediction: weaker/intermittent selection slows resistance spread'}))

input.set_design_note: Greenhouse owner's insecticide decision. Items: mechanism of selection (7.2), environment-dependent fitness cost (7.2/7.11), sequence similarity and shared ancestry (7.5/7.8), and a management prediction on selection pressure (7.2/7.11). All answerable from the data table and notes.

content.text:
I'll design a purely abstract/mathematical item: a distance matrix of sequence differences among four taxa, with a prediction about a change (a new taxon added or a change in the data), tied to common ancestry and tree-building.

Design: Pairwise differences (substitutions per 100 sites) among taxa W, X, Y, Z. The tree is built by the smallest distance, which gives the most recent common ancestor. The change: a new sequence from taxon V is added with distances to W, X, Y, Z. The question asks to predict where V attaches.

Data: W-X 4, W-Y 12, W-Z 20, X-Y 12, X-Z 20, Y-Z 20. V: V-W 12, V-X 12, V-Y 6, V-Z 20. V is closest to Y (6), and the distance to W and X (12) equals the Y-W and Y-X distances, so V and Y form a clade, which is sister to the W+X clade, with Z as the outgroup. The key is therefore that V and Y share a more recent common ancestor with each other than with W or X.

The distractors are:
- V is sister to the W+X clade, with Y outside (misreads the equal 12s).
- V is basal, because it has the largest distances (misreads Z).
- V shares a common ancestor with Z, because the 20 values are equal (misuse).

stimulus.description: Pairwise sequence differences (per 100 aligned sites) among five taxa for a shared gene.

data.title: Pairwise sequence differences per 100 aligned sites
data.units: differences per 100 sites
data.note: Z is known to be an outgroup to W, X, Y and V. Assume a constant rate of change.

input.stem: Sequence differences were measured for a shared gene in five taxa (table). Assume differences accumulate at a constant rate and that Z is an outgroup to the other four taxa. Before taxon V was sequenced, the data for W, X, Y and Z supported a tree in which W and X are sister taxa, Y is their next closest relative, and Z is the outgroup. Which prediction best describes how adding the data for V changes this tree?
options: V and Y form a clade that shares a more recent common ancestor with each other than with W or X.
V joins the W and X clade as a third sister taxon, because V differs equally from W and from X.
V branches off before all other taxa, because it has differences with every other taxon.
V and Z form a clade, because both differ from W, X and Y by the same amount of 20 sites.
option_rationale: Correct: V-Y (6) is the smallest distance involving V, and V is equally distant (12) from W and X, as Y is, so V and Y share a recent ancestor and together are sister to W+X.
Misconception: equal distances to W and X imply V belongs inside the W+X group; ignores that Y-W and Y-X are also 12 and that V is much closer to Y.
Misconception: any taxon that differs from all others must be basal; confuses having differences with being the most divergent.
Misconception: equal large distances indicate shared ancestry; V-Z is 20 only because Z is the outgroup, and shared differences from an outgroup are not shared derived similarity.
input.explanation_en: The smallest difference involving V is with Y (6 per 100 sites), so V and Y share the most recent common ancestor of any pair including V. V differs from W and X by 12, the same as Y does, so V and Y together are equally related to the W+X clade, making V+Y a clade that is sister to W+X, with Z still the outgroup. The tree that treats V as a third member of the W+X group fails because V is far closer to Y (6) than to W or X (12), and the W+X pair (4) is much closer than either is to V. The claim that V branches off first fails because V's distance to Z (20) is the largest, so Z, not V, is the earliest branch. The claim that V and Z form a clade fails because both being 20 from other taxa reflects Z's outgroup position; a clade requires a small distance between the two taxa, and V-Z is 20.
input.verification_code:
import json
taxa=['W','X','Y','Z']
d={('W','X'):4,('W','Y'):12,('W','Z'):20,('X','Y'):12,('X','Z'):20,('Y','Z'):20,('V','W'):12,('V','X'):12,('V','Y'):6,('V','Z'):20}
vd={t:d[('V',t)] for t in taxa}
closest=min(vd,key=vd.get)
# V and Y closest; equal distances to W and X as Y has
ok=closest=='Y' and vd['W']==d[('W','Y')] and vd['X']==d[('X','Y')]
print(json.dumps({"computed_key_index":0 if ok else None,"conceptual_only":False,"details":"closest to V is "+closest}))
input.design_note: Abstract distance-matrix item: predicts the effect of adding a new taxon on a tree of common ancestry. The distractors target misreading equal distances, confusing the outgroup with a clade, and mistaking divergence for basal position.

content.text:
I'll design a health scenario: antibiotic resistance in a bacterial population in a hospital, with a table of data. Four items cover 7.2 (natural selection), 7.5 (Hardy-Weinberg), 7.8 (evidence of common ancestry, i.e. a shared mechanism of resistance), and 7.11 (origins/environmental change). I verified each key with simple computations.

**Stimulus data:**
- Hospital ward, bacterial species; resistance allele R (dominant? no, haploid bacteria, so I avoid Hardy-Weinberg for bacteria).
- Instead I use a human health scenario: sickle-cell allele S in a population across malaria-endemic and non-endemic regions.

**Table:** Region A (malaria endemic): n=1000, HbAA 640, HbAS 340, HbSS 20. Region B (no malaria): n=1000, HbAA 902, HbAS 96, HbSS 2.

**Item computations:**
- Region A: q = (340 + 2×20)/2000 = 0.19; p = 0.81. Expected HbSS under Hardy-Weinberg = q² × 1000 = 36.1, observed 20. Expected HbAS = 2pq × 1000 = 307.8, observed 340. This shows a heterozygote excess.
- Region B: q = (96 + 4)/2000 = 0.05. Expected SS = 2.5, AS = 95.

The items are:
1. Explain why S persists at higher frequency in A (heterozygote advantage and selection).
2. Compute q in Region A (0.19).
3. Interpret deviation from Hardy-Weinberg (heterozygote excess, selection against SS).
4. Predict the effect of malaria eradication on q across generations (it decreases slowly, because most S alleles are carried by heterozygotes, hidden from selection).

stimulus.description: Table of hemoglobin genotype counts among 1,000 newborns in each of two regions, one with endemic malaria and one without.

data.title: Hemoglobin genotype counts in newborns (n = 1000 per region)
data.notes: HbAA: normal hemoglobin. HbAS: carriers, usually healthy, reduced risk of severe malaria. HbSS: sickle cell disease, severe anemia with reduced survival and reproduction. Genotypes were counted at birth, before malaria exposure.

items.stem: Which statement best explains why the HbS allele is more common in Region A than in Region B?
options: In Region A, carriers survive and reproduce more than either homozygote, so the HbS allele is maintained by selection.
In Region A, malaria exposure causes new HbS mutations to arise more often in response to the parasite.
In Region A, individuals pass on HbS acquired through their need to resist infection during their lifetimes.
In Region A, the HbS allele is favored because HbSS individuals have the highest fitness there.
option_rationale: Correct: heterozygote advantage in malaria environment maintains S through differential survival and reproduction.
Misconception: environment directs mutation toward beneficial alleles.
Misconception: inheritance of acquired characteristics (Lamarckian).
Misconception: confuses homozygote with the favored genotype; HbSS has reduced survival.
items.explanation_en: Carriers in Region A have higher fitness because they resist severe malaria without suffering sickle cell disease, so the S allele is retained by natural selection. Mutation is random and not induced by the parasite, so the idea of malaria-triggered mutations is wrong. Traits acquired during a lifetime are not inherited, so the acquired-resistance option is wrong. HbSS individuals have reduced survival and reproduction, so they are not the most fit.
items.verification_code:
import json
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'Conceptual: heterozygote advantage; no numeric recomputation possible.'}))

items.stem: Using the Region A data, what is the frequency of the HbS allele in the newborn population?
option_rationale: Misconception: uses heterozygote frequency as allele frequency.
Misconception: counts carriers plus HbSS individuals (360/1000) as allele frequency.
Misconception: counts each HbSS once but divides by 2000, (340+20)/2000 = 0.18 style error; counts only half of heterozygotes plus none of HbSS.
items.explanation_en: Each HbSS individual carries two S alleles and each HbAS carries one: (2*20 + 340)/2000 = 0.19. Using the carrier frequency of 0.34 ignores that carriers have only one S allele. Adding carriers and HbSS as a proportion of individuals (0.36) counts people, not alleles. The 0.17 value undercounts S alleles by omitting the second allele of HbSS individuals.
items.verification_code:
import json
q=(340+2*20)/2000
opts=[0.19,0.34,0.36,0.17]
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':[abs(o-q)<1e-9 for o in opts].index(True),'conceptual_only':False,'details':str(q)}))

items.stem: In Region A, the observed number of HbSS newborns is 20, while Hardy-Weinberg predicts about 36, and observed HbAS is 340 versus about 308 predicted. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Region A is not at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for this gene, consistent with selection acting on genotypes in that environment.
Region A is at equilibrium because allele frequencies are the same in all generations.
Region A deviates only because the sample of 1,000 is too small for any genetic drift to be ruled out.
Region A deviates because carriers mate preferentially with each other, which lowers HbAA frequency.
option_rationale: Correct: deviations indicate non-equilibrium; with heterozygote excess and HbSS deficit, selection is consistent.
Misconception: assumes constant allele frequency implies equilibrium regardless of genotype counts.
Misconception: attributes deviation to sampling alone, though drift is not indicated by data and 1,000 is not tiny.
Misconception: nonrandom mating claims; assortative mating by genotype is unsupported and would increase homozygotes.
items.explanation_en: Observed genotype counts differ from Hardy-Weinberg expectations, with fewer HbSS and more HbAS than expected, which fits selection favoring carriers. Equilibrium requires genotype counts to match p2, 2pq and q2, not just stable allele frequency. Sampling error is not supported by the data as the sole cause. Preferential mating among carriers would produce an excess of homozygotes, not a deficit of HbSS.
items.verification_code:
import json
q=0.19;p=0.81
ss=q*q*1000;as_=2*p*q*1000
ok=(20<ss) and (340>as_)
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0 if ok else None,'conceptual_only':False,'details':f'exp SS {ss:.1f}, AS {as_:.1f}'}))

items.stem: Suppose malaria is eliminated from Region A and no other factors change. Which prediction about the HbS allele over many generations is best justified?
options: Its frequency will slowly decline, because HbSS individuals are still selected against and most S alleles are in carriers, where selection is weak.
Its frequency will fall to zero in one generation, because HbSS individuals will no longer be born.
Its frequency will not change, because selection can only act on alleles that are currently beneficial.
Its frequency will rise, because carriers will no longer be removed by malaria.
option_rationale: Correct: loss of carrier advantage leaves selection against HbSS only; most S alleles hidden in heterozygotes.
Misconception: believes recessive alleles are eliminated immediately; carriers continue to produce HbSS.
Misconception: thinks selection does not act once environment changes.
Misconception: carriers were not removed by malaria; they were advantaged.
items.explanation_en: Without malaria, carriers lose their advantage while HbSS still has low fitness, so S declines. Because most S alleles are in healthy carriers, selection against them is weak, so the decline is slow. Elimination in one generation is wrong because carriers continue to produce HbSS children. No change is wrong because the selective environment has changed. A rise is wrong because malaria did not remove carriers.
items.verification_code:
import json
q=0.19;p=0.81
frac_in_het=340/(340+40)
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0 if frac_in_het>0.8 else None,'conceptual_only':False,'details':f'fraction of S alleles in carriers {frac_in_het:.2f}'}))

input.set_design_note: One health stimulus (sickle-cell genotype counts in two regions) supports selection, allele-frequency calculation, Hardy-Weinberg deviation interpretation, and environmental-change prediction.

content.text:
I'll design an item on common ancestry using a health/technology scenario: a drug-development team using a conserved enzyme across species, with a percent amino acid identity table. The prediction is about which organism's enzyme would best model the human enzyme's response to an inhibitor.

Design: a table of percent identity of the active-site region of enzyme "DHX" relative to human. Because greater sequence similarity reflects a more recent common ancestor, the inhibitor is predicted to bind the enzyme of the closest relative best.

stimulus.description: Table of percent amino acid identity between the human version of enzyme KLR2 and the KLR2 enzymes of four organisms, with the measured inhibitor concentration that reduces activity by half for each.

data.title: Comparison of KLR2 active-site region (120 amino acids) with human KLR2
columns: Percent amino acid identity to human KLR2 (%)
Inhibitor concentration giving 50% reduction in activity (nM)
data.note: Inhibitor Z-41 was designed using the structure of human KLR2. Lower values of the 50% reduction concentration mean stronger inhibition.

input.stem: A research team designed inhibitor Z-41 against human KLR2 and tested it on the KLR2 enzyme from four organisms, as shown in the table. The team now finds a newly sequenced vertebrate whose KLR2 active-site region is 94% identical to human KLR2. Which prediction about Z-41 and the best justification is most consistent with the data and with common ancestry?
options: Z-41 will inhibit the new enzyme at a concentration near 12-15 nM, because higher sequence identity reflects a more recent common ancestor and a more similar active-site structure.
Z-41 will inhibit the new enzyme at a concentration near 140 nM, because all vertebrates share a common ancestor and so inhibit the enzyme equally weakly.
Z-41 will not inhibit the new enzyme, because only the human enzyme shares the exact active-site structure that Z-41 was designed against.
Z-41 will inhibit the new enzyme at a concentration near 12-15 nM, because organisms with similar enzymes must have acquired the same mutations independently in response to similar environments.
option_rationale: Correct: 94% identity falls between the 99% and 88% organisms, which both show strong inhibition (12 and 15 nM); greater similarity from a more recent common ancestor predicts a conserved active-site structure and similar inhibitor binding.

Misconception: shared ancestry alone (being a vertebrate) guarantees an identical response, ignoring that the degree of divergence matters; the data show zebrafish at 62% identity is much weaker, and 94% identity is far above that.
Misconception: only the exact target can be inhibited; ignores that conserved sequences inherited from common ancestors keep similar structure, as chimpanzee and mouse data show.
Right numerical prediction but wrong reasoning: attributes similarity to independent convergent mutations rather than inheritance from a recent common ancestor.
input.explanation_en: Sequence similarity in conserved proteins reflects how recently species shared a common ancestor: fewer substitutions have accumulated, so the active-site structure is better preserved. In the table, the 99% and 88% identity enzymes are inhibited at 12 and 15 nM, while 62% identity requires 140 nM and 31% identity shows no inhibition. A 94% identical enzyme lies between the two strongly inhibited organisms, so Z-41 should work at roughly 12-15 nM. The option predicting about 140 nM wrongly treats all vertebrates as equally related and ignores the trend with identity. The option predicting no inhibition ignores that conserved structure is inherited, as shown by the chimpanzee and mouse results. The option invoking independent mutations in similar environments gives the right number but a wrong cause, since the similarity is explained by inheritance from a common ancestor, not independent convergence.

import json
ident=[99,88,62,31]
ic50=[12,15,140,None]
new=94
# interpolate: 94 lies between 99 and 88 -> IC50 between 12 and 15
lo,hi=sorted([ic50[0],ic50[1]])
frac=(99-new)/(99-88)
pred=12+frac*(15-12)
# choose option: near 12-15 nM with ancestry reasoning -> index 0 (index 3 has wrong reasoning)
key=0 if 12<=pred<=15 else None
print(json.dumps({"computed_key_index":key,"conceptual_only":False,"details":"interpolated IC50=%.1f nM between 99%% and 88%% identity organisms"%pred}))
input.design_note: Health/drug-development context with a table; the student predicts an effect from the degree of sequence conservation as evidence of recent common ancestry. A distractor shares the key's numeric prediction but pairs it with convergent-evolution reasoning, so both the number and the justification must be right.

content.text: I'll design a lab stimulus: a plant-growth experiment on phototropism and a field/lab data set. The four items share one stimulus (a table of seedling responses with controls), covering 8.1 (responses to the environment), 8.3 (energy/behavior or population-level responses), 8.5 (community/population interactions) and 8.7 (ecosystem/environmental change). All items test identifying experimental procedures (variables, controls).

stimulus.description: Table of a greenhouse experiment on tomato plants: four treatment groups, each with 20 plants, and the number of aphids per plant and plant height after 14 days.

data.title: Effect of caterpillar-damage signal and ladybug presence on aphid colonization of tomato plants
data.design_text: Twenty-four-day greenhouse experiment. 80 genetically identical tomato seedlings of equal age were randomly assigned to four groups of 20 and kept in separate sealed chambers with identical light, temperature, watering and soil. Chambers in groups B and D received air pumped from a chamber holding caterpillar-damaged tomato plants (volatile signal); chambers in groups A and C received air pumped from a chamber holding undamaged tomato plants. Ten adult ladybugs (aphid predators) were added to each chamber of groups C and D on day 0. Every plant was infested on day 0 with 10 aphids. Counts were made on day 14.

items.stem: Which group serves as the control that allows the effect of the airborne signal from damaged plants alone to be isolated?
options: Group A, because it received undamaged-plant air and no ladybugs, so only the signal differs from group B
Group C, because it received ladybugs and undamaged-plant air, so it best matches natural field conditions
Group D, because it received both the signal and ladybugs, so it shows the maximum possible response
Group B, because it received the signal and no ladybugs, so it shows the baseline aphid growth
option_rationale: Correct: A differs from B only in the signal variable, with ladybugs absent in both.
Misconception: the control should be most natural rather than differing in a single variable; C differs from B in two variables.
Misconception: confusing the group with all treatments with a control; D has both variables applied.
Misconception: treating the treated group as the baseline; B receives the signal.
items.explanation_en: The signal's effect is isolated by comparing groups that differ only in the signal. Group A (undamaged-plant air, no ladybugs) versus group B (damaged-plant air, no ladybugs) differ in only that variable, so group A is the control. Group C differs from B in both signal and ladybugs, so it cannot isolate the signal. Group D has both treatments applied and is an experimental group, not a control. Group B receives the signal, so it is the experimental group, not the baseline.

import json
groups={'A':('U',0),'B':('D',0),'C':('U',1),'D':('D',1)}
# control for signal: same ladybug status, undamaged air
cands=[g for g,(s,l) in groups.items() if s=='U' and l==groups['B'][1]]
opts=['A','C','D','B']
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':opts.index(cands[0]),'conceptual_only':False,'details':'A matches B except signal'}))

items.stem: The researchers want to test whether the signal and ladybugs have independent or interacting effects on aphid number. Which comparison of group means is most appropriate?
options: Compare the drop in aphids caused by the signal without ladybugs to the drop caused by the signal with ladybugs
Compare group A only with group D, since they are the two extreme treatments
Compare the plant heights of all four groups, since height reflects aphid damage
Compare group B with group C, since each has only one treatment applied
option_rationale: Correct: comparing the signal effect (A vs B) with the signal effect in presence of ladybugs (C vs D) tests interaction in a factorial design.
Misconception: comparing extremes ignores the factorial structure and cannot separate effects.
Misconception: height is a secondary measure that does not differ and does not test interaction.
Misconception: B versus C differ in which single factor is applied, so the difference confounds the two factors.
items.explanation_en: In a two-factor design, interaction is tested by asking whether the effect of one factor changes depending on the level of the other factor: A versus B (signal without ladybugs) compared with C versus D (signal with ladybugs). Comparing only A and D confounds both factors. Plant height is nearly constant across groups and is not the response of interest. B versus C compares two different single factors, confounding them.

print(A-B,C-D)
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'Design logic: interaction compares A-B vs C-D; computed 56 vs 37'}))

items.stem: A student proposes that the lower aphid numbers in group B are caused by the signal and not by differences among plants. Which feature of the design best supports ruling out genetic differences among plants as an explanation?
options: Using genetically identical seedlings randomly assigned to groups
Using the same number of ladybugs in groups C and D
Measuring aphids on day 14 only
Keeping plant height measurements similar across groups
option_rationale: Correct: identical genotype plus random assignment controls plant genetic variation.
Misconception: equal ladybug number controls predator density, not plant genetics.
Misconception: a single time point does not control for genetic variation.
Misconception: similar heights are an outcome, not a design control for genotype.
items.explanation_en: Genetically identical seedlings randomly assigned to groups remove genotype as a confounding variable. Equal ladybug numbers control predator density, not plant genetics. Measuring at one time point does not address genotype. Similar final heights are a result and do not control for genotype.
items.verification_code:
import json
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'Design reasoning on confounders; no numeric recomputation possible'}))

items.stem: Mean aphids per plant fell from 148 in group A to 24 in group D. Which additional procedure would best test whether the volatile signal itself, rather than a different chemical in the chamber air, reduces aphid number?
options: Add a group receiving air from a chamber with damaged plants that has been passed through a filter removing volatile compounds
Add a group with 40 plants of undamaged-plant air to increase sample size
Add a group with ladybugs removed on day 7 to test timing of predation
Repeat the experiment with a different plant species in all four groups
option_rationale: Correct: filtering out volatiles while keeping airflow tests whether the volatile compounds cause the effect.
Misconception: more replicates of the control improve precision but do not test the cause of the effect.
Misconception: timing of predation addresses a different variable.
Misconception: changing species changes the organism, not the test of the signal's chemical identity.
items.explanation_en: To show the volatile compounds cause the effect, a new group should be treated identically except that the volatiles are removed from the damaged-plant air, preserving airflow. A larger control sample improves precision but does not test the cause. Removing ladybugs partway tests predator timing. Using another species tests generality, not the signal's role.

content.text:
I need a health/sports/technology scenario on unit 8 (ecology): responses to the environment (8.1), energy flow (8.3), population ecology (8.5), and effects of community and ecosystem change (8.7). I'll use a wearable-sensor field study of endurance runners acclimatizing to heat, hot-weather training, with a table as the stimulus, and focus on identifying variables and controls.

Design:
- Stimulus: a table of a heat-acclimatization experiment with 3 groups.
- Items 1-4 each test the 3.C skill (variables, controls) with different ecology tie-ins.

Verification codes compute the key from the stimulus numbers.

input.stimulus: {"kind":"table","description":"Table of a 14-day heat-training study with three groups of 12 recreational runners each. Columns: group, training environment, daily 60-min run intensity, and mean core temperature rise and mean sweat rate measured on day 1 and day 14 in a standard 35 C test.","data":{"title":"Heat-acclimatization study (n = 12 runners per group; same 60-min test at 35 C, 50% humidity, on day 1 and day 14)","columns":["Group","Training environment (days 1-14)","Daily run intensity (% of max heart rate)","Core temp rise day 1 (C)","Core temp rise day 14 (C)","Sweat rate day 1 (L/h)","Sweat rate day 14 (L/h)"],"rows":[["A","35 C chamber","70","1.9","1.1","0.9","1.4"],["B","18 C chamber","70","1.9","1.8","0.9","1.0"],["C","35 C chamber","50","1.9","1.5","0.9","1.2"]],"notes":"Runners were randomly assigned to groups. Wearable sensors recorded core temperature and sweat rate. Mean values shown."}

items.stem: Which comparison isolates the effect of training-environment temperature on acclimatization?
options: Group A with group B
Group A with group C
Group B with group C
Day 1 with day 14 in group A only
option_rationale: Correct: only temperature differs; intensity is the same at 70%.
Misconception: believes any two groups can be compared; here intensity differs, not temperature.
Misconception: this pair differs in both temperature and intensity, so it is confounded.
Misconception: a before-after change in one group lacks a control for time or repeated testing.
items.explanation_en: Groups A and B differ only in training temperature (35 C vs 18 C) while run intensity is equal, so that comparison isolates temperature. Comparing A with C changes intensity, not temperature. Comparing B with C changes both variables at once, so the effect cannot be attributed. Comparing day 1 with day 14 in one group has no control for repeated testing.

items.stem: Which is the best description of group B's role in this experiment?
options: A control that experiences the same intensity without heat exposure
A control that experiences no exercise and no heat exposure
The experimental group because its core temperature rose least
A replicate of group A to increase the number of runners
option_rationale: Correct: same intensity, no heat stress, so it controls for training effects other than heat.
Misconception: B runs at 70%, so it is not a no-exercise control.
Misconception: group role is set by design, not by the outcome.
Misconception: replicates share the same treatment; B has a different temperature.
items.explanation_en: Group B runs at the same intensity as group A but in a mild 18 C chamber, so it controls for fitness gains from exercise alone. It does exercise, so it is not a no-exercise control. Group role comes from the design, not the result. It is not a replicate of A because the temperature treatment differs.

items.stem: Sweat is a physiological response that dissipates heat from the runner, whose metabolism converts chemical energy to work and heat. Which added measurement would best test whether heat-trained runners lose body heat more efficiently rather than simply producing less metabolic heat?
options: Oxygen consumption at a fixed speed on day 1 and day 14 in all groups
Body mass of each runner at the start of the study only
Number of runners who finish the 14-day program in each group
Daily heart rate during runs in group A only
option_rationale: Correct: oxygen use estimates metabolic heat production, controlling for it when comparing temperature rise.
Misconception: a single baseline mass does not measure heat production or loss over time.
Misconception: completion rate is unrelated to heat balance.
Misconception: omits the comparison groups, so no control exists.
items.explanation_en: Oxygen consumption at a fixed speed estimates metabolic heat production. Measuring it in all groups lets researchers separate changes in heat production from changes in heat loss. Baseline body mass, completion counts, and heart rate in one group do not estimate heat production or include the controls needed.

items.stem: A critic says the day 14 improvement in group A may reflect the runners' growing familiarity with the test rather than heat exposure. Which data from the table best address this concern?
options: Group B's core temperature rise changed little between day 1 and day 14 despite repeat testing
Group A's sweat rate rose from 0.9 to 1.4 L/h over the 14 days
Group C's sweat rate rose less than group A's sweat rate
All three groups had identical core temperature rises on day 1
option_rationale: Correct: B was tested twice at the same conditions with little change, so repeat testing alone does not explain A.
Misconception: restates A's change, which cannot separate test familiarity from heat.
Misconception: C also trained in heat and differs in intensity, so it does not control for repeat testing.
Misconception: equal day 1 values show matched baselines, not that repeat testing is not responsible for the change.
items.explanation_en: Group B took the same test twice (day 1 and day 14) but trained without heat, and its core temperature rise changed only from 1.9 to 1.8 C. Repeat testing alone therefore does not account for A's drop from 1.9 to 1.1 C. A's own change cannot separate the explanations. Group C trained in heat, so it does not control for test familiarity. Matched day 1 values show equal baselines only.

input.stimulus: {"kind":"table","description":"Abstract design matrix for a four-block study. Each block lists the factor manipulated, its levels, what is measured, and which groups are included. Used to identify variables and controls.","data":{"title":"Design matrix for four experimental blocks (A-D)","columns":["Block","Manipulated factor","Levels of factor","Measured response","Groups included","Replicates per group"],"rows":[["A","Light direction (organism movement)","Light from left only; light from right only; uniform light from above","Percent of 40 identical motile larvae found on the left half of the dish after 10 min","Left light, right light, uniform light","6 dishes"],["B","Energy input to a closed aquatic mesocosm","0, 5, 10 units of light per day","Primary producer biomass (g) after 14 days","0 units, 5 units, 10 units","4 tanks"],["C","Presence of a predator species in a pond mesocosm","Predator absent; predator present","Density of herbivore species (individuals per L) after 21 days","Predator absent, predator present","5 tanks"],["D","Starting population density of one species in identical containers","10, 20, 40 individuals per container","Per-capita growth rate over 7 days","10, 20, 40 individuals","3 containers per density"]],"notes":"In each block, all containers are the same size, temperature, and nutrient supply unless the manipulated factor is listed. Block A uses larvae from one brood, randomly assigned to dishes."}

items.stem: In Block A, which group serves as the control that allows the researcher to attribute a left-side bias to light direction rather than to a dish effect?
options: The uniform light from above group, because it shows movement without a directional cue
The left light group, because it is the group with the highest expected response
The right light group, because it reverses the direction of the stimulus
The group with the fewest larvae, because it limits crowding effects
option_rationale: Correct: uniform light removes the directional cue while keeping light, dish, and larvae constant, giving the baseline distribution.
Misconception: the group expected to show the largest effect is the control; it is a treatment.
Misconception: a reversed treatment is a control; it is another treatment level, useful but not a no-cue baseline.
Misconception: a control means reducing sample size; all groups have 40 larvae, and no such group exists.
items.explanation_en: A control holds everything constant except the manipulated variable. Uniform light provides the no-directional-cue baseline, so a left-side bias in the left-light group can be attributed to light direction. The left light group is a treatment expected to show the effect. The right light group is another treatment level that gives a reversed response but not a baseline. No group has fewer larvae, since all dishes hold 40 larvae, and crowding is not what a control addresses.

items.stem: In Block B, which statement correctly identifies the variables?
options: Independent variable: light units per day; dependent variable: producer biomass; constants include tank size and nutrients
Independent variable: producer biomass; dependent variable: light units per day; constants include tank size and nutrients
Independent variable: number of tanks; dependent variable: light units per day; constants include producer biomass
Independent variable: light units per day; dependent variable: tank size; constants include producer biomass
option_rationale: Correct: light is manipulated, biomass is measured, and tank conditions are held constant per the notes.
Misconception: reverses independent and dependent variables.
Misconception: treats replicate number as the manipulated factor and a measured outcome as a constant.
Misconception: labels a controlled condition as the response and the measured outcome as constant.
items.explanation_en: The researcher sets light input (independent variable) and measures producer biomass (dependent variable) while keeping tank size and nutrient supply the same. Treating biomass as the manipulated factor reverses cause and effect. The number of tanks is replication, not the manipulated factor. Tank size is a constant, not a response, and biomass is the measured outcome, not a constant.

items.stem: Block C has 5 tanks per group. A student proposes adding a third group with the predator present but also removing half of the herbivores at the start. Why is this a poor addition for testing the effect of the predator?
options: It changes a second factor, starting herbivore number, so any difference could not be attributed to the predator alone
It increases replication, which makes the predator-absent group unnecessary
It removes the dependent variable, so herbivore density can no longer be measured
It makes the predator-present group a control, because it has the fewest herbivores
option_rationale: Correct: the added group varies two factors at once (confounding).
Misconception: more groups means more replication and removes the need for a baseline; replication is per group and the baseline is still required.
Misconception: altering starting numbers removes the measured variable; density can still be measured.
Misconception: the group with the fewest individuals is the control; a control lacks the manipulated factor.
items.explanation_en: A valid comparison changes one factor at a time. Removing half the herbivores while adding the predator confounds predator effects with starting density. It does not replace the need for the predator-absent baseline. Herbivore density is still measurable, and a group with a predator present is a treatment, not a control, regardless of herbivore count.

items.stem: In Block D, three densities are tested with 3 containers each. How many containers are used, and which design feature allows the researcher to judge whether differences in per-capita growth rate are larger than chance variation among containers?
options: 9 containers; replicates within each density group
3 containers; one container per density group
9 containers; a single shared container for all densities
3 containers; equal temperature across densities
option_rationale: Correct: 3 densities x 3 containers = 9, and within-group replicates estimate variation.
Misconception: counts the number of groups as the total containers and treats a single unit per group as sufficient.
Misconception: correct count but a shared container would confound densities and give no replicates.
Misconception: miscounts and treats a constant condition as the source of variation estimates.
items.explanation_en: There are 3 densities with 3 containers each, giving 9 containers. Replicates within each density show how much growth rate varies by chance, so group differences can be judged against that variation. One container per density gives no estimate of variation. Placing all densities in one container is impossible since density is the manipulated factor. Equal temperature is a constant that reduces confounding but does not measure chance variation.

content.text: I designed a long experiment FRQ on cell cycle regulation (a cyclin/CDK inhibitor in cultured cells) with signaling (4.3) as the secondary link. The graph is a bar graph with ±2SE error bars. The calculation is a mitotic index.

input.title: Effect of a CDK Inhibitor on Mitotic Index in Cultured Root-Tip Cells

stimulus.description: Table of mitotic index (percent of cells in mitosis) for cultured onion root-tip cells treated for 24 hours with four concentrations of a CDK inhibitor, with mean, 2SE, and a cell-count table for one slide.

data.table1_title: Mitotic index of cultured root-tip cells after 24 h of treatment with inhibitor R-7
table1_columns: Mean mitotic index (% of cells in mitosis)
data.table2_title: Cell counts from one slide in the 10 uM treatment
data.background: Inhibitor R-7 binds the CDK that partners with the cyclin active at the G2/M checkpoint. Cells were all drawn from the same culture, grown at 25 C, and treated for 24 h in identical medium. The control received medium plus solvent only (0 uM).

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the role of the cyclin-CDK complex at the G2/M checkpoint, and identify one appropriate control for this experiment and explain its purpose. (2 points)
parts.model_answer: Cyclin-CDK complex: when cyclin levels rise and bind CDK, the active complex phosphorylates target proteins that allow the cell to pass the G2/M checkpoint and enter mitosis. Control: the 0 uM treatment (medium plus solvent only) shows the baseline mitotic index without inhibitor, so that changes can be attributed to R-7 rather than to the solvent or culture conditions.

rubric_rows.criterion: Describes cyclin-CDK role at G2/M
required_elements: Active cyclin-CDK complex (cyclin bound to CDK) triggers/permits progression from G2 into mitosis
optional_phrases: checkpoint passed only if conditions are met
common_errors: Says CDK is active at all times regardless of cyclin

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies control and purpose
required_elements: Provides baseline for comparison so effect is due to the inhibitor
alt_solutions: Same cells with solvent only at 0 uM
common_errors: Names a treated group as the control

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data in the first table (mean mitotic index versus inhibitor concentration). Include error bars representing 2SE. (3 points)
parts.model_answer: A bar graph (or points joined by a line, acceptable because concentration is numeric) with x-axis 'Inhibitor R-7 concentration (uM)' at 0, 5, 10, 20 and y-axis 'Mean mitotic index (% of cells in mitosis)' scaled 0 to 10 or 12 in even intervals. Bars/points at 9.2, 7.1, 4.3, 1.8 with error bars of ±0.8, ±0.7, ±0.6, ±0.5 respectively.

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type and scale
required_elements: Bar graph or line/scatter graph with concentration on x-axis and mitotic index on y-axis
Even scale intervals; y-axis starts at 0 and covers at least 0-9.2
alt_solutions: Line graph with points connected, x-axis scaled proportionally
common_errors: Uneven x scaling in a line graph

rubric_rows.criterion: Accurately plotted data with error bars
required_elements: Error bars of ±0.8, ±0.7, ±0.6, ±0.5 centered on each mean
rubric_rows.numeric_tolerance: within half a minor grid division
common_errors: Error bars plotted as full length rather than ± from mean

rubric_rows.criterion: Labeled axes with units (and legend/note that error bars are 2SE)
required_elements: x-axis label with concentration and uM
y-axis label with mitotic index and percent
common_errors: No statement of what error bars represent

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the cell counts for the one slide in the 10 uM treatment, calculate the mitotic index for that slide as a percent. Show your work. Round to the nearest tenth. (1 point)
parts.model_answer: Total cells = 236 + 7 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 250. Mitotic cells = 7 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 14. Mitotic index = 14/250 x 100 = 5.6%.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct mitotic index with work
common_errors: Dividing mitotic cells by interphase cells (14/236 = 5.9%)

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Based on the data, state the relationship between inhibitor concentration and mitotic index. Then predict how the proportion of cells in G2 would differ in the 20 uM treatment compared with the control, and justify your prediction using the function of the checkpoint. (3 points)
parts.model_answer: As inhibitor concentration increases, mitotic index decreases (9.2% to 1.8%), and the 2SE bars of 0 and 20 uM do not overlap, so the decrease is meaningful. Prediction: the proportion of cells in G2 would be higher at 20 uM. Justification: R-7 blocks the CDK needed to pass the G2/M checkpoint, so cells cannot enter mitosis and accumulate in G2 (fewer cells reach mitosis, lowering the mitotic index).

rubric_rows.criterion: States inverse relationship using data
required_elements: Mitotic index decreases as concentration increases
Cites values or non-overlapping error bars
common_errors: Claims 5 and 0 uM differ significantly (error bars 7.1±0.7 and 9.2±0.8 do not overlap, so this is acceptable; but claiming no data support is an error)

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts higher proportion in G2
required_elements: More cells in G2 at 20 uM than control
common_errors: Predicts more cells in G1 or S

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with checkpoint/CDK function
required_elements: Inhibited CDK prevents passage through G2/M checkpoint so cells cannot enter mitosis

input.design_note: Long 9-point FRQ: experiment design/control (2), graph construction split into type/scale, plotted data with 2SE bars, labels (3), calculation (1), relationship plus prediction with justification (3). Links cell cycle checkpoints (4.5) with cyclin-CDK signaling (4.3). Primary skill 4.A is exercised through graph construction and data description. The second table in the stimulus supports the calculation part.

content.text:
I'll design a household/business context: a greenhouse-supply business testing how nighttime light and household pest conditions affect a tomato seedling grower's plants, which ties to responses to environment (8.1), plant/animal behavior and cooperation (8.3), competition and energy allocation (8.5), and ecosystem disruption/population response (8.7).

Context: a small urban nursery owner tests whether a cheap LED night-light schedule changes basil flowering (photoperiodism) and aphid load. Items focus on variables and controls.

stimulus.description: Design and results of a small nursery's trial of night lighting on basil. Four benches, each with 40 basil plants, same soil, water, and temperature; light treatment differs by bench.

data.title: Nursery trial: night lighting on basil (6 weeks)
rows: Red LED, 4 h, plus ladybugs released
data.notes: All LEDs deliver the same total light energy. Benches are in the same greenhouse with randomly assigned positions. Basil is a long-night (short-day) flowering plant under these conditions.

items.stem: The owner wants to conclude that a red-light interruption of the long night, not simply the presence of extra light energy, reduced flowering. Which comparison best isolates that variable?
options: Bench A with bench B, because they differ only in whether night light is added
Bench B with bench C, because they differ only in the wavelength of night light
Bench B with bench D, because they differ only in the presence of ladybugs
Bench A with bench D, because they differ in both light and ladybugs
option_rationale: Misconception: any control that lacks the treatment isolates the specific factor; A vs B cannot separate wavelength from simply adding light.
Correct: same duration and energy, only wavelength differs, so the red-specific effect on flowering is isolated.
Misconception: confuses the biotic variable (ladybugs) with the light variable.
Misconception: a comparison that changes two variables still isolates one.
items.explanation_en: Bench B and bench C receive the same duration and energy of night light and differ only in color, so a difference in flowering (12 vs 30 of 40) can be attributed to red light interrupting the dark period. Comparing the dark bench with the red bench changes the presence of light in general, so wavelength is not isolated. Comparing the red bench with the ladybug bench tests ladybugs, not light. Comparing the dark bench with the ladybug bench changes two variables at once, so the cause cannot be assigned.

flow={'A':31,'B':12,'C':30,'D':13}
# B vs C differ only in wavelength; check they differ in outcome and others do not isolate
key=1
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':key,'conceptual_only':False,'details':'B vs C: same energy/duration, flowering %d vs %d'%(flow['B'],flow['C'])}))

items.stem: Which bench serves as the control group for evaluating whether ladybugs reduce aphid numbers?
options: Bench A, because it receives no added light and no ladybugs
Bench B, because it matches bench D in light treatment but has no ladybugs
Bench C, because it has the highest aphid mean
Bench D, because it is the only bench with a biological control
option_rationale: Misconception: the untreated bench is always the control, ignoring that light differs from D.
Correct: B and D share the red LED treatment and differ only in ladybugs.
Misconception: picks the control by outcome value rather than by design.
Misconception: the treated group is mistaken for the control.
items.explanation_en: A valid control differs from the experimental group only in the variable tested. Bench B has the same red LED schedule as bench D but no ladybugs, so it is the proper control for ladybugs. The dark bench differs in light as well, which could affect plants and aphids. The blue bench differs in light color. The ladybug bench is the experimental group itself.

items.stem: The owner wants to attribute the higher leaf mass on benches B and D to red night light rather than chance. Which feature of the data and design best supports that attribution?
options: Randomly assigned bench positions and nonoverlapping 2SE intervals versus bench A
The larger leaf mass on bench B than on bench D
The fact that all four benches had exactly 40 plants
The lower aphid load on bench D than on bench B
option_rationale: Correct: randomization reduces position bias and nonoverlapping 2SE (9.4 ± 1.0 vs 8.1 ± 0.9 gives 8.4 to 10.4 vs 7.2 to 9.0, overlapping slightly at 8.4 to 9.0) is the stated evidence type; see explanation for the caution.
Misconception: a tiny difference between two red benches is meaningful.
Misconception: equal sample sizes alone establish causation.
Misconception: aphid data bear on leaf mass attribution.
items.explanation_en: Random placement controls for position effects such as drafts or sunlight, and comparing error intervals is how the owner judges whether differences exceed sampling variation; together these are the design and data features that support attributing a difference to treatment. Bench B versus D differ by only 0.1 g, well within error, so that gap says nothing. Equal plant numbers help comparability but do not by themselves support causation. Aphid load is a different response variable.

items.stem: A neighbor suggests the nursery repeat the ladybug test on blue-light benches too. What is the main experimental reason to add a blue-light bench with ladybugs?
options: To test whether the ladybug effect on aphids depends on the light treatment
To increase the number of plants flowering on the blue benches
To replace the need for any bench without ladybugs
To show that ladybugs respond to blue light by flowering
option_rationale: Correct: crossing the two factors tests for interaction between light color and predator presence.
Misconception: ladybugs are expected to change flowering, ignoring the question asked.
Misconception: a treated group can substitute for a control.
Misconception: confuses a plant response (flowering) with ladybug behavior.
items.explanation_en: Adding blue light with ladybugs, alongside blue light without, makes a factorial design, so the owner can see whether ladybug control of aphids is the same under both light colors. It would not be expected to raise flowering, it cannot replace controls lacking ladybugs, and ladybugs do not flower.

content.text:
I'll design a long FRQ (9 points) on cell cycle regulation using a purely abstract/mathematical setting, with a flow-cytometry-style DNA content distribution and a cyclin-CDK oscillation model.

**Design:** A synchronized cell population is sampled over time. Data give the percentage of cells in G1, S, and G2/M, plus a mean cyclin B level in arbitrary units with ±2SE. The student must graph the data, calculate the duration of each phase from the percentages, and predict the effect of a CDK inhibitor.

**Data:**
- Total cell cycle time is 20 h; a sample of 500 cells counted at one time point: G1 = 275, S = 125, G2 = 75, M = 25.
- Phase duration = fraction × 20 h: G1 = 11 h, S = 5 h, G2 = 3 h, M = 1 h.
- Time course (h): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. Cyclin B (a.u.) mean, with ±2SE: 0: 10±2; 2: 18±3; 4: 45±4; 6: 80±6; 8: 25±5.

input.title: Cyclin B Levels and Phase Timing in a Synchronized Cell Population

Proportion 275/500 = x/20

parts.label: c

parts.model_answer: Most cells enter mitosis around 6 h, when cyclin B is highest (80 a.u., well above the 45 a.u. at 4 h, with non-overlapping error bars). content.text:
I'll design a long FRQ (9 points) on the cell cycle and cell communication, with a business/household decision context (a home-garden/nursery business choosing a growth-regulator treatment), requiring graph construction, a calculation, and a prediction.

**Design of the data**

Context: a small nursery business tests three concentrations of a plant-based growth-signal product on onion root-tip cells. Counts of 200 cells per slide were taken for each treatment, with 3 replicates.

| Treatment | Interphase | Mitotic | Mean mitotic index |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 µM | 182 | 18 | 9.0% |
| 5 µM | 164 | 36 | 18.0% |
| 10 µM | 150 | 50 | 25.0% |
| 20 µM | 168 | 32 | 16.0% |

Each treatment has an SE of the mean mitotic index (±2SE given): 1.0, 1.6, 2.0, 1.8, so error bars are ±2.0, ±3.2, ±4.0, ±3.6.

The calculation asks for the percent increase in mitotic index from control to 10 µM, which is (25-9)/9 = 177.8%, accepted range 175-180%. The cell-cycle length calculation is also done. If the mitotic index is the fraction of the cycle spent in mitosis, with a 24 h cycle, the time in mitosis is 0.25 × 24 = 6.0 h at 10 µM and 0.09 × 24 = 2.16 h at control.

Parts: (a) graph, 4 points; (b) calculation, 2 points; (c) experimental design/control, 1 point; (d) prediction with justification linking the signal pathway to the cell cycle, 2 points. Total is 9.

input.title: Nursery Growth-Signal Product and Root-Tip Cell Division

stimulus.description: Table of mean mitotic index (percent of 200 counted onion root-tip cells in mitosis) for four concentrations of a growth-signal product, with ±2SE.

data.title: Mitotic index of onion root-tip cells after 24 h exposure to a growth-signal product
data.context: A small plant nursery wants to decide whether buying a growth-signal product to speed root growth in cuttings is worthwhile. The owner treats onion root tips for 24 h, then stains and counts cells. Mitotic index = mitotic cells / total cells x 100. The control (0 µM) is root tips in plain water. Assume the cell cycle length is 24 h.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data in the table. Plot mean mitotic index versus product concentration, include error bars (±2SE), and label axes with units.
parts.model_answer: Line graph or scatter-with-line (or bar graph acceptable for 4 discrete concentrations; line preferred because concentration is continuous). X-axis: Concentration of growth-signal product (µM), 0-20 with even scale. Y-axis: Mean mitotic index (%), 0-30. Points: (0, 9.0), (5, 18.0), (10, 25.0), (20, 16.0). Error bars: ±2.0, ±3.2, ±4.0, ±3.6 percentage points.

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type with correct independent variable on x-axis and dependent variable on y-axis
alt_solutions: Bar graph with concentration categories is acceptable

rubric_rows.criterion: Data points accurately plotted
required_elements: All four points plotted at 9, 18, 25, 16 (within half a minor gridline)
common_errors: Plotting mitotic cell counts instead of the mitotic index
Uneven x-axis spacing without a break

rubric_rows.criterion: Error bars correctly plotted
required_elements: Error bars of ±2.0, ±3.2, ±4.0, ±3.6 around the means
common_errors: Error bars drawn as SE rather than 2SE

rubric_rows.criterion: Axes labeled with units and scales appropriate; title or legend if needed

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the percent increase in mitotic index from the control to the 10 µM treatment, and calculate how many hours per 24 h cycle the average cell at 10 µM spends in mitosis, assuming mitotic index equals the fraction of the cycle spent in mitosis. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: Percent increase = (25.0 - 9.0)/9.0 x 100 = 177.8% (about 178%). Time in mitosis = 0.25 x 24 h = 6.0 h.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct percent increase with work shown
Correct time in mitosis with units

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify the purpose of the 0 µM control and describe one variable the owner should keep constant across all treatments.
parts.model_answer: The 0 µM control (plain water) provides a baseline mitotic index in the absence of the product so changes can be attributed to the product. Keep constant: temperature, light, exposure time (24 h), onion variety, or root-tip region sampled.

rubric_rows.criterion: States control gives baseline for comparison AND names one valid constant variable
required_elements: One of: temperature, exposure time, light, onion variety, root-tip region, number of cells counted
common_errors: Naming concentration as the constant variable

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The owner concludes that a higher concentration is always better for rapid root growth. Using the data, evaluate this claim, and explain how a signal from the product could increase the mitotic index by acting on the cell cycle.
parts.model_answer: The data do not support the claim: mitotic index rose from 9% to 25% up to 10 µM but dropped to 16% at 20 µM, so more is not always better (the 20 µM bar does not overlap 10 µM within 2SE: 25-4=21 vs 16+3.6=19.6). A signal molecule binding a receptor triggers a signal transduction pathway that activates cyclin/CDK checkpoint regulators, pushing cells past the G1/S and G2/M checkpoints so more cells enter and complete mitosis.

rubric_rows.criterion: Evaluates claim using data
required_elements: Mitotic index decreased at 20 µM relative to 10 µM (16% vs 25%)
common_errors: Saying the data support the claim

rubric_rows.criterion: Links signal transduction to cell cycle regulation
required_elements: Signal binds receptor and triggers signal transduction pathway
Activates cyclin/CDK or promotes passage through a checkpoint, increasing division
common_errors: Saying the product directly changes DNA sequence

input.design_note: Long experiment FRQ (9 pts) with graph construction split into type, plotted data, error bars, and labeling; calculation with accepted range; control design; claim evaluation linking signal transduction to the cell cycle (topics 4.5 and 4.3). Business context: nursery product purchase decision.

import json
rows=[(0,182,18,2.0),(5,164,36,3.2),(10,150,50,4.0),(20,168,32,3.6)]
mi=[m/(i+m)*100 for _,i,m,_ in rows]
ok_mi=mi==[9.0,18.0,25.0,16.0]
pct=(mi[2]-mi[0])/mi[0]*100
hrs=mi[2]/100*24
checks=[{"part":"a","pass":ok_mi and all(i+m==200 for _,i,m,_ in rows),"detail":str(mi)},
{"part":"b","pass":175<=pct<=180 and abs(hrs-6.0)<1e-9,"detail":f"{pct:.1f}% {hrs} h"},
{"part":"d","pass":mi[3]<mi[2] and (mi[2]-4.0)>(mi[3]+3.6),"detail":"20 uM below 10 uM, no overlap of 2SE bars"}]
print(json.dumps({"checks":checks,"conceptual_parts":["c"]}))

I designed a long FRQ (9 points) on cell cycle regulation and cell communication (cyclin/CDK signaling and growth-factor signaling), set in a health/technology context: a wearable-sensor-guided drug screen of a cell-cycle inhibitor on cultured skin cells for wound-healing patches.

Data: percentage of cells in G1, S, G2/M at different drug doses (mean ± 2SE).

Calculation: the percentage of cells in G2/M compared with the control, and the expected number of cells in a population.

Verification: I computed the key values in Python from the stimulus numbers.

input.title: Dose Response of a CDK Inhibitor in Cultured Skin Cells for a Wound-Healing Patch
input.stimulus: {"kind":"table","description":"Table of mean percentage of cultured skin cells in each cell cycle phase after 24 hours at five doses of a CDK inhibitor, with plus or minus 2 SE, n = 3 cultures per dose, about 10,000 cells scored per culture.","data":{"title":"Cell-cycle phase distribution after 24 h of exposure to inhibitor CK-7","columns":["Dose of CK-7 (micromolar)","% cells in G1 (mean, ±2SE)","% cells in S (mean, ±2SE)","% cells in G2/M (mean, ±2SE)"],"rows":[[0,"52 ± 3","30 ± 2","18 ± 2"],[1,"58 ± 3","26 ± 2","16 ± 2"],[5,"68 ± 4","18 ± 2","14 ± 2"],[10,"79 ± 4","10 ± 2","11 ± 2"],[20,"88 ± 3","4 ± 1","8 ± 2"]],"units":"percent of scored cells; dose in micromolar (uM)","context":"A company is designing a wound-healing patch with a sensor that releases CK-7, a drug that blocks the CDK that pairs with the cyclin required for the G1-to-S transition. Skin cells were grown with growth factor present in all cultures. Control cultures received 0 uM CK-7. Each row sums to 100 percent.","suggested_graph":{"x_axis":"Dose of CK-7 (uM), 0 to 20, interval 5","y_axis":"Percent of cells, 0 to 100, interval 10","series":["G1","S","G2/M"],"error_bars":"plus or minus 2 SE"},"extra":{"total_cells_in_patch_culture":50000,"dose_for_calculation_uM":10}}

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data in the table. Plot the percentage of cells in each phase (G1, S, G2/M) against the dose of CK-7. Include error bars (plus or minus 2 SE) and a legend.
parts.model_answer: Line graph (or grouped bar graph) with dose (uM) on the x-axis (0 to 20) and percent of cells on the y-axis (0 to 100). Three labeled series: G1 rising 52, 58, 68, 79, 88; S falling 30, 26, 18, 10, 4; G2/M falling 18, 16, 14, 11, 8. Error bars of ±2SE on every point (e.g., G1 ±3, 3, 4, 4, 3). Axes labeled with units, legend identifies the three phases.

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type and scale
required_elements: Line graph or grouped/clustered bar graph with dose on x-axis (independent variable) and percent of cells on y-axis (dependent variable)
Evenly spaced, appropriately scaled axes (x 0-20 uM; y covers 0-100 or at least 0-90)
optional_phrases: Line graph connecting points of each phase
common_errors: Uneven x-axis scale that treats doses as equally spaced categories on a line graph
alt_solutions: Grouped bar graph with three bars per dose is acceptable

rubric_rows.criterion: Accurately plotted data with error bars
required_elements: All 15 means plotted correctly (within half a minor gridline)
Error bars of ±2SE shown on points/bars using the table values
optional_phrases: Error bars drawn symmetrically above and below mean
common_errors: Plotting only one or two phases
Using SE values as the means

rubric_rows.criterion: Labeled axes and legend
required_elements: X-axis labeled 'Dose of CK-7' with units (uM)
Y-axis labeled 'Percent of cells' (or % of cells)
Legend or direct labels identifying G1, S and G2/M

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the control group in this experiment and explain why growth factor was present in all cultures, including the control.
parts.model_answer: The control is the 0 uM CK-7 culture. Growth factor was kept in all cultures so that the only variable is CK-7 dose; growth factor signaling (a signal transduction pathway through a receptor) normally promotes cyclin/CDK activity and entry into the cell cycle, so any change in phase distribution can be attributed to CK-7 rather than to a lack of growth signals.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies control
common_errors: Naming the 20 uM culture as control

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains constant growth factor
required_elements: Growth factor kept constant so CK-7 is the only variable
Growth factor signaling promotes cell cycle entry/division (cyclin-CDK activation), so absence would confound results
common_errors: Says growth factor is the drug
Says growth factor blocks the cell cycle

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the expected number of cells in G1 in a culture of 50,000 cells treated with 10 uM CK-7. Show your work.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct calculation with work

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Describe the trend in the percentage of cells in G1 and in S as the dose of CK-7 increases, and explain how the trend is consistent with CK-7 blocking the CDK needed for the G1-to-S transition.
parts.model_answer: As dose increases, the percentage of cells in G1 increases (52 to 88 percent) while the percentage in S decreases (30 to 4 percent). If the cyclin-CDK needed to pass the G1 checkpoint is inhibited, cells cannot enter S phase, so they accumulate in G1 and fewer are replicating DNA in S.

rubric_rows.criterion: Describes trends
Links to checkpoint/CDK blockage
required_elements: Blocked cyclin-CDK prevents progression past G1 checkpoint into S
Cells accumulate in G1 / fewer cells enter S
common_errors: Claiming CK-7 causes cells to die
Claiming CK-7 speeds up DNA replication

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: The patch is intended to speed wound closure in the first days, but the same patch is being considered for a patient with a skin tumor that has a mutation causing continuous growth factor receptor signaling. Predict whether CK-7 would reduce division of the tumor cells, and justify your prediction using the data and the role of the cyclin-CDK in the cell cycle.
parts.model_answer: Prediction: CK-7 would likely reduce division of the tumor cells, because even with continuous growth factor signaling (as in all cultures here, where growth factor was present), CK-7 still blocked the CDK and cells accumulated in G1 (more G1, fewer S cells); the signal activates division through the cyclin-CDK, so inhibiting the CDK downstream stops progression regardless of upstream signaling.

rubric_rows.criterion: Prediction with justification
required_elements: Predicts reduced division/arrest in G1 of tumor cells
Justifies using data that CK-7 increased G1 and decreased S despite growth factor present, or that CDK acts downstream of the growth factor signal
common_errors: Predicts no effect because the signal is always on, with no data justification
