content.text:
I'll design a long FRQ (9 points) on lac-operon-like regulation in a lab setting, tying to 6.7 (Mutations) through a promoter/operator/repressor mutant strain.

Design:
- Bacterial strains grown in lactose vs. glucose; β-galactosidase activity (Miller units), n=3 replicates, mean ± 2SE.
- The mutant has a mutation in the operator, so expression is constitutive.
- Parts: a) experimental design/controls (2), b) graph (3), c) calculation (1), d) claim-evidence about mutation (2), e) prediction with justification (1) = 9.

Data (mean β-gal activity, ± 2SE):
- Wild type, no lactose: 2.0 ± 0.6
- Wild type, + lactose: 180 ± 14
- Mutant O^c, no lactose: 165 ± 12
- Mutant O^c, + lactose: 172 ± 15

Calculation: fold induction for WT = 180/2.0 = 90. Accepted range: 88–92.

Prediction: a mutant with a lacI repressor that can't bind DNA gives constitutive expression, as does an operator mutation. For the prediction, a super-repressor (I^s) that cannot bind lactose would give low expression even with lactose.

input.title: Operator Mutation and Inducible Gene Expression in E. coli

stimulus.description: Table of mean beta-galactosidase activity (Miller units) with error bars of plus or minus 2 standard errors for wild-type and mutant E. coli grown with or without lactose.

data.title: Beta-galactosidase activity in E. coli cultures (n = 3 cultures per condition)
data.notes: Glycerol is used as the carbon source so catabolite repression by glucose is absent. Strain M1 carries a single-base substitution in the DNA sequence between the promoter and the lacZ gene; the lacI gene and the lacZ coding sequence in M1 are identical to wild type. Cultures were grown to the same optical density and assayed under identical conditions. Error bars represent mean plus or minus 2SE.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: A student claims that the lac operon in wild-type cells is induced by lactose. (i) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this experiment. (ii) Identify the control group that allows the student to evaluate the effect of lactose on wild-type cells, and explain why the cultures were grown to the same optical density.
parts.model_answer: (i) Independent variable: presence of lactose (and strain). Dependent variable: beta-galactosidase activity. (ii) Control: wild-type cells grown on glycerol without lactose. Same optical density ensures equal cell numbers/growth stage so differences in activity reflect gene expression per cell rather than different amounts of cells.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
Identifies control and justifies equal density
required_elements: Wild type without lactose is the control
Equal optical density standardizes cell number/growth so activity differences are due to treatment
common_errors: Naming mutant M1 as the control for the lactose effect in wild type

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct an appropriately labeled graph of the data in the table, including error bars that represent plus or minus 2SE.
parts.model_answer: Grouped (clustered) bar graph with strain on the x-axis (wild type, M1), two bars per strain (no lactose, with lactose), y-axis beta-galactosidase activity (Miller units) 0-200, bars at 2.0, 180, 165, 172 with error bars of ±0.6, ±14, ±12, ±15, and a legend.

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type
required_elements: Bar graph (grouped by strain, with lactose conditions distinguished) for categorical data

rubric_rows.criterion: Accurately plotted data with error bars
rubric_rows.numeric_tolerance: bar heights within about 5 Miller units on a 0-200 axis

rubric_rows.criterion: Labeled axes and legend
required_elements: Y-axis labeled with quantity and units (Miller units)
Legend or labels distinguishing lactose presence/absence

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold increase in mean beta-galactosidase activity caused by adding lactose to wild-type cells. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: 180 / 2.0 = 90-fold increase.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct ratio with work shown
alt_solutions: Percent increase of 8900% (89 x 100) accepted

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A second student claims that the mutation in M1 disrupted the ability of the cell to repress transcription of lacZ in the absence of lactose. Using the data AND your knowledge of gene regulation, (i) support the claim with specific evidence from the table, and (ii) explain how a single-base substitution in the DNA between the promoter and lacZ could produce this phenotype.
parts.model_answer: (i) Without lactose, M1 has 165 Miller units compared with 2.0 in wild type, so lacZ is expressed without inducer, and lactose barely changes it (172 vs 165, overlapping error bars). (ii) The substitution likely alters the operator sequence so the repressor protein can no longer bind; RNA polymerase is not blocked, so transcription occurs constitutively.

rubric_rows.criterion: Evidence from data
required_elements: M1 without lactose 165 versus wild type 2.0
Little/no change in M1 with lactose (172 vs 165, overlapping error bars)

rubric_rows.criterion: Mechanism linking mutation to phenotype
required_elements: Repressor cannot bind, so RNA polymerase transcribes without inducer
optional_phrases: changed nucleotide sequence changes protein-binding site
common_errors: Claiming lacI protein is altered although lacI is identical to wild type
Claiming the lacZ enzyme is more active rather than more expressed

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: A third strain, M2, has a mutation in the lacI gene that changes the repressor so it still binds the operator but can no longer bind the inducer (allolactose). Predict the beta-galactosidase activity of M2 grown with lactose relative to wild type grown with lactose, and justify your prediction.
parts.model_answer: Activity would be low (near 2 Miller units, much lower than wild type with lactose at 180) because the repressor stays bound to the operator even when lactose is present, so transcription remains blocked.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct prediction with justification
required_elements: Prediction: low activity, far below wild type with lactose
Justification: repressor cannot be inactivated by inducer and remains bound to operator, blocking transcription
common_errors: Predicting constitutive high expression like M1

Decidable from the data given; glycerol medium removes catabolite repression so only the lac repressor system is tested.

rubric_rows.criterion: Wild-type fold increase
Strain M1 fold increase
common_errors: Using the difference of 7 as a fold

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A manager claims: 'Strain M1 has a mutation that disrupts the repressor's ability to control the operon, so M1 makes enzyme constitutively.' Support or refute this claim using specific data from the table, and explain how the described mutation location accounts for the data.
parts.model_answer: The claim is supported. M1 makes 395 ± 30 units/mL without inducer versus 2 ± 1 in wild type, far outside overlapping error bars, so expression is no longer repressed. Adding inducer does not change M1 (402 ± 34 vs 395 ± 30, overlapping intervals). The mutation is in the operator-type sequence where the repressor binds, so the repressor cannot bind and block RNA polymerase/transcription, giving constitutive expression regardless of inducer.

rubric_rows.criterion: States a claim consistent with the data
required_elements: claim supported: M1 expresses enzyme constitutively

rubric_rows.criterion: Cites data with comparison
required_elements: 402 vs 395 with overlapping error bars or no inducer effect
common_errors: Citing only one number without comparison

rubric_rows.criterion: Links mutation location to mechanism
required_elements: repressor cannot bind mutated DNA site
transcription not blocked, so gene is on without inducer
common_errors: Saying the enzyme protein itself is altered

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data in the table for all three strains, with and without the inducer, including error bars (±2SE). Label axes with units and include a legend or labels distinguishing conditions.
parts.model_answer: Grouped (clustered) bar graph: x-axis strain (wild type, M1, M2); y-axis enzyme activity (units/mL) 0-450; two bars per strain (no inducer, with inducer) with legend; bars at 2, 410; 395, 402; 1, 6; error bars ±1, ±36; ±30, ±34; ±1, ±2.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Strain M2 makes almost no enzyme even with inducer. A student concludes that M2 has a defective repressor gene. Explain why the data do not support this conclusion, and predict how the activity of a strain carrying both the M2 mutation and the M1 mutation would compare with M1 alone, with justification.
parts.model_answer: If M2 had a defective repressor, expression would be constitutive (high without inducer), but M2 is low without inducer (1 unit/mL) and still low with inducer (6 ± 2), so regulation is not the problem. The M2 mutation is in the coding sequence, producing a nonfunctional enzyme. A double mutant would transcribe the gene constitutively (M1) but make nonfunctional enzyme (M2), so activity would be low, near M2 levels, not 395.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains why data do not support defective repressor
required_elements: defective repressor would give high activity without inducer
M2 low in both conditions, so enzyme itself is altered/nonfunctional

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts double mutant low activity with justification
required_elements: gene transcribed constitutively but active-site mutation makes enzyme nonfunctional
common_errors: Predicting high activity because M1 turns gene on

input.design_note: Part d is the graph-construction portion but is awarded 0 here to keep the total at 9, so the graph rows are folded into a separate scoring split below; see rubric note. Business context: inducer cost decision. Skill 6.B (claim with evidence) is exercised in parts c and e.
input.verification_code:
import json
wt0,wt1=2,410
m10,m11=395,402
f_wt=wt1/wt0
f_m1=m11/m10
checks=[{"part":"a","pass":wt0<10,"detail":"wt uninduced low"},
{"part":"b","pass":round(f_wt)==205 and round(f_m1,2)==1.02,"detail":f"{f_wt},{f_m1:.3f}"},
{"part":"c","pass":(m10-30)>(wt0+1) and abs(m11-m10)<(34+30),"detail":"M1 high uninduced; induction overlap (diff 7 < combined 2SE)"},
{"part":"e","pass":6+2<50,"detail":"M2 low both conditions"}]
print(json.dumps({"checks":checks,"conceptual_parts":["a","d","e"]}))

content.text: I'll build a short FRQ (4 points) on phototropism in a lab setting, focused on identifying variables and controls.

input.title: Blue Light and Seedling Bending in Oat Coleoptiles

stimulus.description: Table of coleoptile bending angles after 6 hours under four treatments, 20 seedlings per treatment, with mean and 2SE values.

data.setup: Oat (Avena sativa) seedlings were grown in complete darkness for 4 days at 22 C until coleoptiles were about 2 cm tall. Seedlings were then placed in identical growth chambers (22 C, same humidity) for 6 hours. Light came from one side only. Bending angle is measured from vertical (0 degrees = straight up); positive angles mean bending toward the light source.
rows: Tip covered with opaque foil cap
data.units: degrees from vertical
data.error_bars: plus or minus 2 standard errors of the mean

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in the comparison of treatment 1 with treatment 2.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: presence or absence of the coleoptile tip (intact vs. tip removed). Dependent variable: coleoptile bending angle (degrees from vertical).

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
required_elements: Independent: tip present vs. removed (tip status)
common_errors: Naming blue light as the independent variable (light is constant in treatments 1 and 2)

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the treatment that serves as the negative control for testing whether one-sided blue light causes bending, and explain what it controls for.
parts.model_answer: Treatment 4 (intact seedlings in darkness). It shows bending that occurs without directional light, such as spontaneous or handling-related curvature, so any bending in treatment 1 can be attributed to the light.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies treatment 4 and explains it shows baseline bending without the light stimulus
required_elements: Baseline/no bending without the directional light variable
optional_phrases: only the light differs from treatment 1
common_errors: Choosing treatment 2 or 3, which test the tip rather than the light

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the data, state which part of the seedling detects the light stimulus, and justify your claim with evidence from the table.
parts.model_answer: The tip detects the light. Covering the tip (3 degrees) or removing it (2 degrees) abolished bending compared with intact tips in blue light (38 degrees), with non-overlapping 2SE ranges, and the result is similar to darkness (1 degree).

rubric_rows.criterion: Claim that the tip senses light supported by data comparison
required_elements: Tip is the site of light detection
Cited values: 38 vs. about 3 (or 2) degrees, or non-overlap of error
optional_phrases: foil-covered tip still attached shows the tip is needed for sensing, not just for bending
common_errors: Claiming the tip removal alone shows detection (it cannot separate sensing from response); the foil treatment is needed

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A researcher proposes testing whether the foil cap itself harms the seedlings. Describe one additional treatment that would control for this and the result that would show the cap is not harmful.
parts.model_answer: Cap the tip with a transparent (clear) cap or foil placed on the base of the seedling, leaving the tip exposed, under one-sided blue light. If bending is about 38 degrees, similar to treatment 1, the cap or foil itself does not impair bending.

rubric_rows.criterion: Describes a valid control treatment and the expected result
required_elements: Treatment keeps cap/foil present but lets tip receive light (clear cap or foil on lower region)
Bending similar to treatment 1 indicates no harmful effect
common_errors: Describing darkness with cap, which does not test the cap effect on bending

input.design_note: Short FRQ ordered identify variables, identify control, evidence-based claim, design an additional control. Tests 3.C within topic 8.1 (phototropism as a response to environmental stimulus). All data are in the table; no outside knowledge of auxin is required.

content.text:
I designed a lac-operon-style regulation scenario presented as abstract mathematical data (a model of reporter output as a function of repressor and inducer levels), tied to topic 6.7 (changes in gene expression and mutation effects). I'm making it a 9-point long FRQ with a table-based stimulus.

Data: a reporter expression model has a baseline output of 2 units. The repressor reduces output to a fraction f = 1/(1+R/K), with K = 4. Inducer relieves repression. Expression E = 100·(1/(1+(R/K)(1/(1+I/Ki)))) is too heavy, so I give the measured table directly and keep the calculations simple.

Table, mean reporter units (n=3, ±2SE):
- Strain W (wild type), no inducer: 4 ±1
- Strain W, +inducer: 80 ±6
- Strain M1 (operator mutant), no inducer: 76 ±5
- Strain M1, +inducer: 78 ±6
- Strain M2 (repressor-gene deletion), no inducer: 82 ±7
- Strain M2, +inducer: 84 ±6

Calculations: the fold induction in W is 80/4 = 20. The percent of maximal expression in W without inducer is 4/80 = 5%.

The inducer response in M1 is 78/76 = 1.03, which is within error.

input.title: Reporter Output Under Repressor Control: Argument from Mutant Data

stimulus.description: Table of mean reporter protein output (arbitrary units, n=3 cultures, reported as mean ± 2SE) for three bacterial strains grown without and with an inducer molecule.

data.title: Reporter output (arbitrary units) by strain and condition
rows: Wild type: intact operator and repressor gene
Single mutation in operator DNA sequence; repressor gene intact
Deletion of repressor gene; operator intact
data.units: arbitrary reporter units
data.setting_note: Reporter gene is placed downstream of the operator and promoter in all strains. Inducer is a small molecule that binds the repressor protein.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and one control that is necessary for interpreting the experiment, and explain why that control is needed.
parts.model_answer: Independent variables: strain genotype (W, M1, M2) and presence/absence of inducer. Necessary control: wild-type strain W (with and without inducer) serves as the baseline showing normal regulation, so that mutant output can be compared with the normal repressed and induced states. (Also acceptable: a no-inducer condition for every strain.)

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies independent variable
Identifies control and justifies it
required_elements: wild type strain W or no-inducer condition

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold increase in reporter output caused by the inducer in strain W. Then calculate the no-inducer output of strain W as a percentage of its induced output. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: Fold increase = 80/4 = 20-fold. Percentage = 4/80 × 100 = 5%.

rubric_rows.criterion: Fold increase with work
Percentage with work

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student claims: 'The operator mutation in M1 prevents the repressor from binding, so repression is lost.' Use specific data from the table to support this claim, and explain why the data from M1 with and without inducer fit this claim.
parts.model_answer: M1 without inducer gives 76, far above W without inducer (4), so repression is lost even though the repressor gene is intact. Adding inducer changes M1 output only from 76 to 78, which is within the error (±5 and ±6, overlapping), so inducer has no effect. This fits a mutant operator where the repressor cannot bind; inducer acts by binding the repressor, so with no repressor binding to the operator there is nothing for the inducer to relieve.

rubric_rows.criterion: Cites data showing loss of repression
required_elements: M1 no inducer 76 vs W no inducer 4

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains why lack of inducer response fits the claim
required_elements: inducer acts through repressor, which is not bound to operator

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Strains M1 and M2 both show high output without inducer. Explain how the molecular cause differs between the two strains, and describe what kind of mutation (in DNA sequence terms) each strain carries relative to the regulatory system.
parts.model_answer: In M1 the repressor protein is made but its DNA binding site (operator) is altered, so it cannot bind: a cis-acting regulatory DNA sequence mutation. In M2 the operator is intact but no repressor protein is made because the gene is deleted: a loss of a trans-acting regulatory protein (gene deletion). Both lead to constitutive transcription of the reporter.

rubric_rows.criterion: M1 cause
M2 cause
required_elements: no repressor protein produced because gene deleted

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: A new strain M3 carries both the intact operator of W and a mutation in the repressor gene that changes the inducer-binding site so the repressor can no longer bind inducer but still binds the operator. Predict the reporter output of M3 without and with inducer, and justify your prediction using the data for W.
parts.model_answer: Prediction: low output (about 4 units) both without and with inducer. Justification: the repressor still binds the operator, and because it cannot bind inducer, it cannot be released, so the gene remains repressed, unlike W, where inducer raises output from 4 to 80.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct prediction with justification
required_elements: repressor binds operator but cannot be inactivated by inducer

input.design_note: Abstract-data presentation of operon regulation (6.5) with mutation effects (6.7); the argument is decidable from the table alone using ±2SE overlap. Part e is a novel-scenario prediction.
input.verification_code:
import json
W0,W1,M10,M11=4,80,76,78
fold=W1/W0
pct=W0/W1*100
overlap=(M11-6)<=(M10+5)
print(json.dumps({"checks":[{"part":"b","pass":fold==20 and pct==5.0,"detail":f"fold={fold}, pct={pct}"},{"part":"c","pass":overlap,"detail":"M1 +/- inducer ranges overlap"}],"conceptual_parts":["a","d","e"]}))

content.text:
I'm designing a short FRQ (4 points) on Unit 8, Topic 8.1 (responses to the environment: phototropism, tropism/taxis, behavior). The context is a household/business decision: a greenhouse grower or home gardener deciding on supplemental light for seedlings. The primary skill is 3.C (identify variables and controls).

Data: seedling stem curvature (degrees toward the light) after 48 h under different light treatments, n=12 per group, mean ± 2SE.

Treatments:
- A: white light from the left, 80 µmol/m²/s: 38.2 ± 4.0
- B: blue light from the left, same intensity: 41.5 ± 4.4
- C: red light from the left, same intensity: 3.1 ± 2.6
- D: white light from above (overhead), no side light: 1.4 ± 2.2

Parts:
- (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
- (b) Read the data: which wavelength is effective, and does the difference between white and blue exceed the error? The intervals overlap (38.2 ± 4.0 gives 34.2–42.2, and 41.5 ± 4.4 gives 37.1–45.9), so the difference is not clearly significant.
- (c) Predict and justify: covering the tips with foil caps.
- (d) Justify the control: which treatment serves as the control for the effect of directional light, and why.

The verification code recomputes the intervals and the overlap.

input.title: Choosing a Grow-Light Setup for Windowless Seedling Trays

stimulus.description: Table of mean stem curvature toward light (degrees) of seedlings after 48 hours under four light treatments, n = 12 per group, with ±2SE.

data.title: Stem curvature of bean seedlings after 48 h
columns: Intensity (umol photons per m2 per s)
data.notes: All seedlings are the same bean variety, same age (7 days), same soil, water, temperature (22 C) and tray position type. Curvature is the angle of the stem tip from vertical, measured toward the left side.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: A home grower wants to know which light setup makes seedlings bend toward a side light. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: the light treatment (color and direction of light). Dependent variable: stem curvature toward the light side (degrees).

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly names both variables
required_elements: Independent: light color and/or direction (light treatment)
Dependent: stem curvature (degrees) toward the light
common_errors: Naming intensity as the independent variable
Naming seedling number as the dependent variable

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using the data, identify which light color causes the bending response and state whether the data support a claim that blue light produces a larger curvature than white light. Support your answer with the values.
parts.model_answer: Blue (41.5 degrees) and white (38.2) cause strong curvature, while red (3.1) does not. The data do not clearly support blue being greater than white because the mean ± 2SE intervals overlap (34.2-42.2 vs 37.1-45.9).

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies blue (not red) as effective and concludes no clear white/blue difference using overlapping 2SE intervals
required_elements: Intervals overlap so difference not supported
common_errors: Claiming blue is greater because 41.5 > 38.2 without considering error

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Treatment D used white light from directly above. Explain what this treatment controls for, and what conclusion it allows about the cause of bending in treatment A.
parts.model_answer: D has the same color and intensity of white light but no direction difference, so it controls for light presence/intensity. The lack of bending in D shows that bending in A is caused by the directional (one-sided) light, not just by the presence of light.

rubric_rows.criterion: Links D to isolating direction of light as the cause
required_elements: Bending in A is due to unequal/directional light
common_errors: Saying D is a control for water or soil

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The grower suspects the stem tip detects the light. Describe one additional treatment to test this, including what is kept constant and the result predicted if the suspicion is correct.
parts.model_answer: Cover the tips of seedlings with opaque foil caps (control: seedlings with uncapped tips or transparent caps) under the same white side light at 80 umol/m2/s, same age and conditions. If the tip detects light, capped seedlings will show little curvature while uncapped ones bend.

rubric_rows.criterion: Valid treatment with control and correct prediction
required_elements: Opaque cap over tip vs uncapped/transparent control
Predicts capped seedlings bend much less
optional_phrases: cover below tip as additional control
common_errors: Changing light color at the same time

input.design_note: Four 1-point parts ordered variables, data reading, control logic, and experimental design. It targets 3.C using a household gardening decision.
input.verification_code:
import json
a=(38.2-4.0,38.2+4.0);b=(41.5-4.4,41.5+4.4)
overlap=a[1]>=b[0] and b[1]>=a[0]
print(json.dumps({"checks":[{"part":"b","pass":bool(overlap) and round(a[0],1)==34.2 and round(a[1],1)==42.2 and round(b[0],1)==37.1 and round(b[1],1)==45.9,"detail":"intervals overlap"}],"conceptual_parts":["a","c","d"]}))

content.text: I'll build a short FRQ (4 points, four 1-point parts) on Unit 8.1 (responses to the environment), testing the identification of variables and controls. The setting is an abstract/mathematical one: a table of data from a hypothetical design on plant phototropism, framed with generic variables and numbers.

input.title: Designing a Test of a Light-Response Model
input.stimulus: {"kind":"table","description":"Table of bending angle of seedling shoots after 6 hours under four treatments, 20 seedlings per treatment, with mean and standard error.","data":{"title":"Shoot bending angle after 6 hours","columns":["Treatment","Light source","Shoot tip","Number of seedlings","Mean bending angle toward light (degrees)","SE (degrees)"],"rows":[["1","Blue light from the left, 10 units of intensity","Intact","20",38.0,2.0],["2","Blue light from the left, 10 units of intensity","Tip removed","20",2.0,0.8],["3","Blue light from the left, 10 units of intensity","Tip covered with opaque cap","20",3.0,1.0],["4","No light (darkness)","Intact","20",1.0,0.6]],"fixed_conditions":"All seedlings are the same species and age, grown at 22 C with equal watering.","model_statement":"Model: the shoot tip detects light direction and causes elongation on the shaded side, producing bending toward light.","units":"degrees of bending from vertical; positive = toward the light source","error_bars":"SE; mean ± 2SE is the approximate 95% interval"}

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using the table, identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: the treatment of the shoot, i.e., light presence/direction and the condition of the shoot tip (intact, removed, covered). Dependent variable: mean bending angle toward the light (degrees).

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies both variables correctly
required_elements: Independent: light condition and/or tip condition (intact/removed/covered)
alt_solutions: Independent variable stated as shoot tip condition (with light held constant in treatments 1-3) is acceptable
common_errors: Naming the number of seedlings or temperature as independent variable

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify which treatment serves as the positive control (the condition expected to show the response) and explain what that control allows the researcher to conclude if the other treatments differ from it.
parts.model_answer: Treatment 1 (intact tip in blue light from the left) is the control showing the normal response (38 degrees). It shows the setup can produce bending, so lower bending in treatments 2 and 3 can be attributed to the tip manipulation rather than to the light or the seedlings.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies intact tip in light as control AND states its purpose as baseline for comparison
required_elements: Provides baseline/normal response so differences in other treatments can be attributed to the manipulated variable
alt_solutions: Treatment 4 named as a negative control is not credited for this positive control question unless treatment 1 is also named
common_errors: Choosing treatment 4 as the positive control
Naming control without stating its purpose

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Treatment 3 uses an opaque cap over the tip, whereas treatment 2 removes the tip. Explain why including treatment 3 in addition to treatment 2 strengthens the conclusion that the tip detects light.
parts.model_answer: Removing the tip could reduce bending because of wounding or loss of growth-promoting tissue rather than loss of light detection. The cap leaves the tip and shoot intact but blocks light to the tip, so low bending (3 degrees) there isolates light detection by the tip from the effect of damage.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains that removal confounds (damage/loss of tissue) with light detection and the cap separates them
required_elements: Tip removal introduces a confounding variable such as damage or loss of tissue
Cap keeps tissue intact while blocking light, isolating light detection
common_errors: Saying only that more treatments give more data
Claiming the cap increases sample size

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A student proposes adding a treatment in which only the tip is exposed to blue light from the left while the rest of the shoot is shielded from light. Predict the mean bending angle relative to treatment 1 and justify your prediction using the model statement.
parts.model_answer: Prediction: bending close to treatment 1 (about 38 degrees, much greater than 3 degrees). Justification: the model says the tip detects the light direction, so exposing only the tip should be sufficient to trigger elongation on the shaded side.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts substantial bending similar to treatment 1 and justifies with tip detection
required_elements: Prediction: large bending toward light, similar to intact control
Justification: tip is the site of light detection so tip exposure alone is sufficient
optional_phrases: asymmetric elongation on the shaded side
alt_solutions: Prediction of somewhat less than 38 degrees but clearly above 3 degrees with tip-detection justification is acceptable
common_errors: Predicting no bending because the rest of the shoot is shaded

input.design_note: Short FRQ ordered identify variables, control purpose, confounder reasoning, then prediction. Abstract model-testing framing with table data; skill 3.C (variables and controls) is exercised in every part. Decidable from the table and model statement alone.
input.verification_code:
import json
m={1:(38.0,2.0),2:(2.0,0.8),3:(3.0,1.0),4:(1.0,0.6)}
checks=[]
# a: conceptual; b: treatment 1 has max mean
checks.append({"part":"b","pass":max(m,key=lambda k:m[k][0])==1,"detail":"Treatment 1 has largest mean"})
# c: treatments 2 and 3 both far below 1 (beyond 2SE intervals)
lo1=m[1][0]-2*m[1][1]
ok=all(m[k][0]+2*m[k][1]<lo1 for k in (2,3,4))
checks.append({"part":"c","pass":ok,"detail":"Treatments 2,3,4 intervals do not overlap treatment 1"})
print(json.dumps({"checks":checks,"conceptual_parts":["a","d"]}))

content.text: I'll design a short FRQ (4 points) on responses to the environment (Unit 8, topic 8.1) in a sports/technology context: a wearable-sensor study of heart rate response to heat, focusing on identifying variables and controls.

input.title: Heart Rate Response of Cyclists to Ambient Temperature

stimulus.description: Table of mean heart rate and mean core body temperature change for four groups of trained cyclists after 30 minutes of cycling at a fixed workload in rooms at different air temperatures, with n=12 per group.

data.setup: A sports-science team used chest-strap heart monitors and ingestible temperature sensors. Forty-eight trained cyclists of similar age and fitness were randomly assigned to four groups (n=12 each). Each cyclist rode a stationary bike for 30 minutes at a fixed workload of 150 W in a climate chamber with 40% relative humidity. Each group rode in a chamber set to a different air temperature. All cyclists drank 500 mL of water 30 minutes before the ride and wore identical clothing. Group 1 (18 C) was designated the comparison group.
columns: Mean heart rate during minutes 25-30 (beats per minute)
SE of mean heart rate (beats per minute)
Mean rise in core body temperature (C)
data.error_bar_note: SE = standard error of the mean

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: chamber air temperature. Dependent variable: heart rate during minutes 25-30 (core temperature rise is also a measured response).

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
required_elements: Dependent variable = heart rate (beats per minute)
optional_phrases: core body temperature rise as an additional dependent variable
alt_solutions: Dependent variable stated as core body temperature rise in addition to or instead of heart rate is acceptable only if heart rate or core temperature is named as a measured response
common_errors: Naming workload or humidity as the independent variable

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify TWO variables that the researchers held constant and explain why holding them constant strengthens the conclusion that air temperature affects heart rate.
parts.model_answer: Workload (150 W), humidity (40%), pre-ride water intake, clothing, ride duration, or cyclist fitness/age are held constant. Holding them constant means these factors cannot be the cause of differences in heart rate, so the difference can be attributed to air temperature.

rubric_rows.criterion: Names two constants and links them to isolating the effect of temperature
required_elements: Two valid constants from: workload, humidity, water intake, clothing, duration, fitness, age
Explains that this removes alternative explanations/confounding so only temperature differs
alt_solutions: Any two of the listed constants
common_errors: Listing air temperature as a constant

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify which group serves as the comparison (control) group and describe what the comparison group allows the researchers to determine. Then state one data-based pattern showing how mean heart rate changes as temperature increases.
parts.model_answer: Group 1 (18 C) is the comparison group; it provides a baseline heart rate for the same exercise without heat so changes at higher temperatures can be attributed to temperature. Mean heart rate increases as chamber temperature increases, from 142 bpm at 18 C to 173 bpm at 40 C.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies Group 1 as baseline and states the increasing trend with data
required_elements: States heart rate increases with temperature, citing values (e.g., 142 to 173 bpm)
alt_solutions: Any correct pair of table values showing the increase

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The researchers want to test whether the heart rate increase is due to the body's response to rising core temperature rather than to the temperature of the air itself. Describe one additional measurement or experimental modification that would help test this, and predict the result if core temperature drives the response.
parts.model_answer: Compare heart rate with core temperature rise across individuals, or add a group that cools its core (e.g., cooling vest or cold-water ingestion) in the 40 C chamber. If core temperature drives the response, heart rate would correlate positively with core temperature rise, or the cooled group at 40 C would have a lower heart rate than the uncooled 40 C group despite identical air temperature.

rubric_rows.criterion: Proposes a valid modification/measurement and gives a consistent prediction
required_elements: Valid design: measure/correlate core temperature with heart rate, or manipulate core temperature at constant air temperature
Prediction consistent with core temperature driving heart rate (positive correlation or lower heart rate when core is cooled)
alt_solutions: Warm the core at 18 C and predict higher heart rate
common_errors: Changing air temperature again without isolating core temperature

input.design_note: Short FRQ ordered identify variables, constants/controls, comparison group plus data reading, then design extension; all parts exercise skill 3.C within topic 8.1 (physiological response to environmental temperature).
input.verification_code:
import json
hr=[142,149,161,173]
temps=[18,26,34,40]
inc=all(hr[i]<hr[i+1] for i in range(3))
print(json.dumps({"checks":[{"part":"c","pass":inc and hr[3]-hr[0]==31,"detail":"HR increases monotonically; 173-142=31"}],"conceptual_parts":["a","b","d"]}))

content.text:
I'll design a long FRQ (9 points) on an athlete's muscle adaptation to endurance training, covering lac operon-like regulation analogs: transcription factor regulation of gene expression (6.5) and changes in gene expression/phenotype due to environment, with a sports scenario (6.7 natural/artificial change in genetic information is approximated via a mutation in a regulatory element).

Design: the stimulus is a table of qPCR relative mRNA expression (mean ± 2SE) for gene VEGFA in cultured muscle cells under normoxia and hypoxia, in wild-type and a cell line with a mutated HRE (hypoxia response element) in the promoter. The calculation is fold change. Graph construction is in part (b). The claim-evidence part uses the data.

input.title: Endurance Training, Low Oxygen, and Regulation of a Capillary-Growth Gene

stimulus.description: Table of relative VEGFA mRNA levels (mean ± 2SE, n = 6 culture dishes per group) in cultured human muscle cells grown in 21% or 5% oxygen, for cells with a normal promoter or a promoter with a mutated hypoxia response element (HRE).

data.title: Relative VEGFA mRNA level (arbitrary units, normalized to a housekeeping gene) after 24 hours
data.units: arbitrary units (a.u.)
data.background: Endurance athletes training at high altitude show more capillaries in muscle. In low oxygen, the transcription factor HIF-1 is stabilized and enters the nucleus, where it binds the HRE, a DNA sequence in the promoter region of VEGFA, which encodes a protein that stimulates capillary growth. The mutated HRE line has a single base-pair substitution in the HRE only; the VEGFA coding sequence is identical in both lines. Error bars represent ±2SE.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the control group (by group number) that serves as the baseline for evaluating the effect of low oxygen on VEGFA expression in this experiment, and state one variable that should be kept constant across all groups.
parts.model_answer: Independent variables: oxygen level (21% vs 5%) and HRE status (normal vs mutated). Control/baseline: Group 1 (normal HRE, 21% oxygen). Constant: e.g., culture temperature, medium, cell number/density, 24 h duration, or mRNA measurement method.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies independent variable(s) and baseline control group
required_elements: oxygen concentration and/or HRE status as independent variable
optional_phrases: Group 3 as control for the mutation
alt_solutions: Group 1 as control for oxygen effect; Group 1 vs Group 3 for mutation effect
common_errors: naming VEGFA mRNA level as the independent variable

rubric_rows.criterion: Names a valid controlled variable
required_elements: one of: temperature, growth medium, cell density, time of exposure, qPCR method, cell type
common_errors: naming oxygen level as the constant

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct a graph of the data in the table. Include appropriate error bars, and label axes.
parts.model_answer: Bar graph with four bars (groups: normal HRE 21%, normal HRE 5%, mutated HRE 21%, mutated HRE 5%) at heights 1.0, 6.0, 0.9, 1.2 with error bars of ±0.2, ±0.8, ±0.2, ±0.3. X axis labeled with cell line and oxygen %; y axis labeled 'Relative VEGFA mRNA (a.u.)' with even scale 0-7.

rubric_rows.criterion: Appropriate graph type
required_elements: bar graph (categorical groups), grouped by cell line or oxygen level
alt_solutions: clustered bars with oxygen level as legend entries

rubric_rows.criterion: Accurately plotted data with error bars
required_elements: error bars ±0.2, ±0.8, ±0.2, ±0.3 centered on the means
common_errors: plotting error bars as 2SE total length incorrectly

rubric_rows.criterion: Labeled axes/legend with units and appropriate scale
required_elements: y axis labeled with VEGFA mRNA and a.u.
x axis labeled with groups/cell line and oxygen %

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold change in mean VEGFA mRNA caused by low oxygen (5% relative to 21%) in cells with the normal HRE, and in cells with the mutated HRE. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: Normal HRE: 6.0 / 1.0 = 6.0-fold. Mutated HRE: 1.2 / 0.9 = 1.33-fold (about 1.3).

rubric_rows.criterion: Fold change for normal HRE
alt_solutions: 5-fold increase (percent-style, 500% increase) if clearly stated as increase

rubric_rows.criterion: Fold change for mutated HRE

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Using the data, make a claim about the role of the HRE in the regulation of VEGFA expression, and support it with specific evidence and reasoning that connects transcription factor binding to the pattern of mRNA levels.
parts.model_answer: Claim: The HRE is required for the increase in VEGFA transcription in low oxygen. Evidence: with the normal HRE, mRNA rose from 1.0 to 6.0 a.u. (error bars do not overlap), but with the mutated HRE, mRNA stayed about 0.9 to 1.2 a.u. with overlapping error bars. Reasoning: HIF-1 must bind the HRE in the promoter to increase transcription; the mutation prevents binding (despite identical coding sequence), so low oxygen cannot upregulate transcription, showing regulation acts through this DNA regulatory sequence.

rubric_rows.criterion: Claim supported by specific data
required_elements: claim that HRE is needed for low-oxygen increase in VEGFA expression
cites values e.g., 1.0 to 6.0 vs 0.9 to 1.2
optional_phrases: error bars do not overlap for normal HRE; overlap for mutated
common_errors: claiming the mutation changes the VEGFA protein sequence
claiming low oxygen has no effect at all

rubric_rows.criterion: Reasoning linking HIF-1 binding to the HRE and transcription
required_elements: HIF-1 (transcription factor) binds HRE in promoter to increase transcription
mutated HRE prevents/reduces binding so no increase

input.design_note: Long 9-point FRQ. Tests 6.5 (transcription factor/regulatory DNA sequence controlling expression) with 6.7 (a base-pair change in a non-coding regulatory sequence alters phenotype/expression). Skill 6.B: claim-evidence in part d; parts a-c scaffold design, graphing and calculation. Rubric split follows the required graph/calc pattern. Calculator allowed; arithmetic is minimal.

f1=n5/n1
f2=m5/m1
checks=[{"part":"a","pass":True,"detail":"conceptual"},
{"part":"b","pass":True,"detail":"data heights 1.0,6.0,0.9,1.2; error 0.2,0.8,0.2,0.3"},

content.text:
I'll design a short FRQ (4 points, 1 each) using a graph of enzyme activity versus pH for two enzymes, with a data table, in a lab setting.

Design: Enzymes from a hot-spring bacterium vs. a soil fungus are tested at different pH values. Part (a) is describe/explain, (b) is a data read, (c) is a prediction, and (d) is a justification.

input.title: pH Profiles of Two Extracellular Enzymes in a Lab Assay

stimulus.description: Line graph of relative enzyme activity (percent of maximum) versus pH (2 to 10) for Enzyme P from a stomach-dwelling bacterium and Enzyme Q from a soil fungus, each assayed at 37 degrees C with excess substrate.

data.conditions: 37 degrees C, substrate in excess, same enzyme concentration for each assay
data.notes: Each point is the mean of three trials; activity measured as rate of product formation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using the graph, identify the optimal pH for each enzyme.
parts.model_answer: Enzyme P: pH 3. Enzyme Q: pH 7.

rubric_rows.criterion: Both optimal pH values read correctly from the graph
common_errors: Reporting the activity value (100%) instead of the pH

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how a pH of 9 reduces the activity of Enzyme Q, in terms of enzyme structure.
parts.model_answer: At pH 9 the altered H+ concentration changes the ionization of amino acid R groups, disrupting hydrogen and ionic bonds that maintain the tertiary structure. The active site changes shape (partial denaturation) so substrate binds poorly and the rate falls.

rubric_rows.criterion: Links pH change to altered R-group charges/bonds, changing protein shape and the active site, reducing substrate binding
required_elements: pH change alters ionization/charge of R groups or disrupts H/ionic bonds
active site or protein shape changes so substrate binds less effectively
common_errors: Saying the substrate is used up
Saying the enzyme is consumed or killed without structural explanation

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A third enzyme, Enzyme R, is isolated from the small intestine, where the pH is about 8. Predict the pH at which Enzyme R is most active and predict its relative activity at pH 3.
parts.model_answer: Enzyme R should have an optimum near pH 8 and very low (near zero) activity at pH 3, because the active site would be denatured or poorly shaped at strongly acidic pH.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts optimum near pH 8 AND low or near-zero activity at pH 3
required_elements: low or near-zero activity at pH 3
common_errors: Predicting optimum at pH 7 only with no activity statement

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A student claims that at pH 5 the two enzymes differ in activity because Enzyme P has a lower activation energy than Enzyme Q. Evaluate whether the graph supports this claim and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The graph does not support the claim. It shows only rates (P about 35%, Q about 60% at pH 5) and does not measure activation energy. The difference at pH 5 is better explained by the different pH sensitivity of each enzyme's active-site structure; also P has lower activity than Q, so lower activation energy would not be consistent with the data anyway.

rubric_rows.criterion: Rejects the claim with data-based justification: activity values at pH 5 (P lower than Q) and/or graph gives no activation-energy information; attributes difference to pH effect on shape
required_elements: cites P about 35% vs Q about 60% at pH 5 or notes activation energy was not measured
links difference to pH effect on enzyme structure/active site

input.design_note: Short FRQ ordered describe/read data, explain, predict, justify. Tests how environmental pH affects enzyme structure and function (3.2) using a graph model (skill 2.B). Claim in part d is decidable from graph data only.

{"part":"d","pass":P[5]==35 and Q[5]==60 and P[5]<Q[5],"detail":"pH5 P=35 Q=60"}]
print(json.dumps({"checks":checks,"conceptual_parts":["b","c"]}))

content.text: Design: a field setting (a community agricultural research station) with a fixed number of researcher-hours and a table of alternative uses. The question asks which statement best describes scarcity as shown. The key is that limited hours relative to wants force choices, so choosing one use means giving up another. Verification: total hours demanded by all projects exceeds the 120 available.

stimulus.description: Table of four field projects a research station wants to run this season, with the researcher-hours each requires. The station has 120 researcher-hours available.

data.title: Field projects requested at a university agricultural research station
data.units: researcher-hours per season

input.stem: A university agricultural research station has 120 researcher-hours available this season. The table shows the researcher-hours each of four requested field projects would require. Which of the following statements best describes how the table illustrates the economic concept of scarcity?
options: The projects together require more researcher-hours than are available, so running some projects means giving up others.
The station has too few researcher-hours to complete even one of the four projects, so no project can be run.
The irrigation trial requires the most hours, so it is the project that must be given up first.
Scarcity arises because the station could get more researcher-hours if it paid higher wages, so hours are not truly limited.
Researcher-hours are scarce only if every project is run, so scarcity would disappear once any two projects are chosen.
option_rationale: Key: total requested hours (155) exceed the 120 available, so wants exceed resources and choosing requires trade-offs.
Misconception: confuses scarcity with absolute lack of resources; each project needs 50 or fewer hours, so several can be run.
Misconception: believes scarcity dictates which good is dropped based on resource use alone, ignoring opportunity cost and the value of each project.
Misconception: thinks scarcity vanishes if more resources can be obtained at some price; scarcity is about limited resources relative to wants, even when purchasable.
Misconception: thinks scarcity depends on the particular choice made; in fact the resource is limited relative to wants regardless, and any choice still forgoes the other projects.
input.explanation_en: The projects require 40 + 35 + 50 + 30 = 155 researcher-hours, but only 120 are available. Wants exceed available resources, which is scarcity, so choosing some projects means forgoing others. The statement that no project can be run is wrong because each project needs fewer than 120 hours; scarcity does not mean having nothing. The statement that the irrigation trial must be dropped first is wrong because scarcity does not determine which project is dropped; that depends on the value of the alternatives forgone. The statement that hours are not truly limited if more could be bought is wrong because a resource is scarce whenever it is limited relative to wants, even if it can be obtained at a cost. The statement that scarcity disappears once two projects are chosen is wrong because the limit on hours persists and the unchosen projects are still forgone.
input.verification_code:
import json
hours=[40,35,50,30]
avail=120
total=sum(hours)
exceeds=total>avail
single_ok=all(h<=avail for h in hours)
key=0 if (exceeds and single_ok) else None
print(json.dumps({"computed_key_index":key,"conceptual_only":False,"details":f"total={total}, available={avail}, each project feasible alone={single_ok}"}))
input.design_note: Field-station setting with a table. It tests the definition of scarcity (limited resources versus wants) and the resulting trade-offs. Distractors target confusions between scarcity and absolute shortage, scarcity and a purchasable price, and scarcity and a particular choice.

content.text: I'll write a household decision item on scarcity (limited resources versus unlimited wants, forcing choices and opportunity costs), using a table stimulus.

stimulus.description: Table of a household's weekend plan options for a fixed budget of $120 and 10 hours of free time. The household cannot do all activities.

data.title: Okafor household weekend options

input.stem: The Okafor household has $120 and 10 hours of free time this weekend. The table lists four activities they would all like to do. Which statement best describes how the concept of scarcity applies to this household's situation?
options: The total cost of all four activities exceeds the household's budget, so choosing some activities means giving up others.
The household can afford each activity separately, so scarcity does not apply to the household's decision.
Scarcity exists only because the restaurant dinner costs more than the other three activities.
Scarcity would disappear if the household's budget rose enough to pay for the most expensive activity.
Scarcity applies only to the money budget and not to the household's limited free time.
option_rationale: Key: total cost is $170 > $120 and total time is 16 hours > 10 hours, so limited resources relative to wants force choices and trade-offs.
Misconception: scarcity requires being unable to afford any single item; ignores that the combined wants exceed the combined resources.
Misconception: scarcity is caused by one item being expensive rather than by limited resources relative to unlimited wants.
Misconception: scarcity can be eliminated by affording one more item; wants remain greater than resources, and time still constrains.
Misconception: scarcity is only about money; time is also a scarce resource, and total time needed (16 hours) exceeds 10 hours.
input.explanation_en: Scarcity means limited resources cannot satisfy all wants, so choices must be made. The four activities cost $70 + $50 + $30 + $20 = $170, above the $120 budget, and need 3 + 6 + 2 + 5 = 16 hours, above the 10 hours available. Therefore doing some activities requires giving up others, which is the statement about total cost exceeding the budget. The claim that each activity is affordable separately is wrong because scarcity concerns the combined wants against limited resources. The claim blaming the restaurant's high price is wrong because scarcity comes from limited resources relative to wants, not from one price. The claim that a bigger budget would end scarcity is wrong because wants would still exceed resources, and time remains limited. The claim that scarcity applies only to money is wrong because free time is also a scarce resource and also binds.
input.verification_code:
import json
cost=[70,50,30,20];time=[3,6,2,5]
ok = sum(cost)>120 and sum(time)>10 and all(c<=120 for c in cost)
print(json.dumps({"computed_key_index":0 if ok else None,"conceptual_only":False,"details":f"total cost {sum(cost)} vs 120; total time {sum(time)} vs 10"}))
input.design_note: Household context with table stimulus; tests the definition of scarcity (limited resources vs. wants) with both money and time constraints; distractors target common misconceptions about scarcity.

content.text: I'll design a short FRQ (4 points, four 1-point parts) on a sports-medicine scenario: lactate dehydrogenase activity in muscle as pH falls during intense exercise, shown as a graph. The data are fully specified, and the code recomputes the values read from the graph.

input.title: Muscle pH and Enzyme Activity During Sprint Training
input.stimulus: {"kind":"graph","description":"Line graph of relative activity of a muscle enzyme (percent of maximum) versus pH of the surrounding fluid, measured at 37 degrees C. Activity rises from low values at acidic pH to a peak near pH 7.0 and falls at lower and higher pH. Resting muscle pH (7.0) and pH after an all-out sprint (6.4) are marked with vertical dashed lines.","data":{"graph_type":"line with markers","x_axis":{"label":"pH of muscle fluid","min":5.0,"max":8.0,"major_tick":0.5,"units":"pH units"},"y_axis":{"label":"Relative enzyme activity (% of maximum)","min":0,"max":100,"major_tick":20,"units":"%"},"series":[{"legend":"Enzyme X at 37 C","points":[[5.0,5],[5.5,20],[6.0,55],[6.4,80],[6.5,86],[7.0,100],[7.5,70],[8.0,25]]}],"vertical_markers":[{"x":7.0,"label":"Resting muscle"},{"x":6.4,"label":"After all-out sprint"}],"context":"Intense sprinting produces lactic acid, lowering muscle fluid pH. Enzyme X is a muscle enzyme that catalyzes one step of ATP production."}

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe how the relative activity of enzyme X changes as pH decreases from 7.0 to 5.0.
parts.model_answer: Activity decreases as pH falls below 7.0, from 100% at pH 7.0 to about 5% at pH 5.0 (a steady decline).

rubric_rows.criterion: Describes decrease in activity with decreasing pH below the optimum, using the graph data
required_elements: activity decreases as pH decreases from 7.0 to 5.0
cites values or the direction from about 100% to about 5%
alt_solutions: Activity is highest at 7.0 and lower at every more acidic pH
common_errors: Says activity increases in acidic conditions
Describes only the pH 7.0 to 8.0 side

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using the graph, determine the percentage decrease in activity of enzyme X in muscle immediately after an all-out sprint (pH 6.4) compared with resting muscle (pH 7.0).
parts.model_answer: At pH 6.4 activity is 80% of max versus 100% at rest: (100-80)/100 = 20% decrease (answers 19-21% accepted if graph read as 79-81%).

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct percent decrease with values read from graph
alt_solutions: Activity is 0.8 of resting activity, so 20% lower
common_errors: Reports 20 percentage points without noting it is also 20%

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain, at the level of enzyme structure, why the activity of enzyme X is lower at pH 5.0 than at pH 7.0.
parts.model_answer: Excess H+ at low pH changes the ionization of R groups (amino acids) in the enzyme, disrupting hydrogen/ionic bonds that maintain its 3-D shape. The active site shape changes (denaturation), so substrate binds poorly and fewer reactions are catalyzed.

rubric_rows.criterion: Links pH to altered bonding/R-group charges, changed active site shape, and reduced substrate binding
required_elements: pH change alters R-group charge or ionic/hydrogen bonds
enzyme tertiary structure or active site shape changes
substrate binds less effectively so lower activity
common_errors: Says the enzyme is used up

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A trainer proposes a supplement that raises muscle pH after sprints by 0.5 units (for example, from 6.4 to 6.9). Predict the effect on enzyme X activity and justify your prediction using the graph.
parts.model_answer: Activity would increase, from about 80% to about 98-100% of maximum, because pH 6.9 is close to the optimum of 7.0 where the active site has its best shape for substrate binding.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts increased activity and justifies with graph values near optimum
required_elements: justification cites graph (about 80% rising to near 100%) or proximity to pH 7.0 optimum
alt_solutions: Activity would be close to maximum, about 95-100%
common_errors: Predicts decrease because higher pH is always worse

input.design_note: Short 4-point FRQ ordered describe, read data, explain mechanism, predict/justify. Sports context; line graph of pH vs enzyme activity; all values needed are in stimulus.data.

print(json.dumps({"checks":[{"part":"a","pass":ok_a,"detail":"activity monotonic increase from 5.0 to 7.0"},{"part":"b","pass":ok_b,"detail":"decrease %.1f%%"%dec},{"part":"d","pass":ok_d,"detail":"interpolated activity at 6.9 = %.1f"%a69}],"conceptual_parts":["c"]}))

content.text:
I'll design a household context (a home cook/baker using fresh pineapple in gelatin dessert, where bromelain is a protease that breaks down gelatin), with a graph of enzyme activity vs. temperature at two pH values.

Data design:
- Temperatures: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70 °C
- Relative activity (%), pH 6.0 (fresh): 15, 35, 65, 100, 70, 20, 2
- pH 4.0 (curve 2): 8, 18, 33, 52, 35, 10, 1

The parts are ordered describe/explain, then read data, then predict, then justify, each worth 1 point (4 total).

The model answers are:
- (a) The optimum is 40 °C at pH 6.0. Above it, heat disrupts the weak bonds (hydrogen and ionic) that hold the tertiary structure, so the active site changes shape and substrate no longer fits (denaturation).
- (b) At 40 °C, pH 4.0 activity is 52% against 100% at pH 6.0, a difference of 48 percentage points. A reduction of 48% relative to 100 is also accepted.
- (c) Pineapple heated to 70 °C would not stop the gelatin from setting. At 70 °C, activity is 2% or less, so the enzyme is denatured.
- (d) Adding acidic juice lowers the pH, which changes the charges on the R groups. This alters the ionic and hydrogen bonding at the active site, so the enzyme binds less well. Acid lowers the activity at every temperature, but the optimum stays at about 40 °C.

input.title: Fresh Pineapple in a Gelatin Dessert
input.stimulus: {"kind":"graph","description":"Line graph of relative bromelain activity (%) versus temperature (10 to 70 degrees C) at pH 6.0 and pH 4.0. Both curves peak at 40 degrees C; the pH 6.0 curve peaks at 100% and the pH 4.0 curve peaks at 52%.","data":{"chart_type":"line_with_markers","x_axis":{"label":"Temperature","units":"degrees C","range":[0,80],"ticks":[10,20,30,40,50,60,70]},"y_axis":{"label":"Relative bromelain activity","units":"% of maximum measured at pH 6.0","range":[0,110],"ticks":[0,20,40,60,80,100]},"series":[{"legend":"pH 6.0 (fresh pineapple juice)","points":[[10,15],[20,35],[30,65],[40,100],[50,70],[60,20],[70,2]]},{"legend":"pH 4.0 (juice acidified with lemon)","points":[[10,8],[20,18],[30,33],[40,52],[50,35],[60,10],[70,1]]}],"title":"Effect of temperature and pH on bromelain activity","context":"A home cook wants to make a gelatin dessert with fresh pineapple. Gelatin is a protein. Bromelain, a protease in raw pineapple, breaks down gelatin so that it will not set. Activity of bromelain was measured at several temperatures at two pH values."}

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using the graph, identify the temperature at which bromelain works best at pH 6.0, and explain, in terms of enzyme structure, why activity falls at temperatures above this optimum.
parts.model_answer: Optimum is 40 degrees C. Above it, heat disrupts the weak bonds (hydrogen/ionic) maintaining the enzyme's tertiary structure, changing the active site shape so substrate no longer fits (denaturation).

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies 40 degrees C AND links decline to disrupted bonds/3D shape changing the active site (denaturation).
required_elements: heat disrupts bonds or tertiary structure
active site shape changed or denatured
common_errors: Says the enzyme is killed or dies
Gives only 'enzyme slows down' without structure

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate how many percentage points lower the activity is at pH 4.0 than at pH 6.0 when both are at 40 degrees C.
parts.model_answer: 100 - 52 = 48 percentage points lower.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct difference of 48 (percentage points or %).
alt_solutions: 48% reduction relative to 100%
common_errors: Reads values at the wrong temperature

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The cook stirs fresh pineapple juice into the gelatin and heats the mixture to 70 degrees C before cooling it to set. Predict whether the gelatin will set, and justify your prediction using the graph.
parts.model_answer: The gelatin will set, because at 70 degrees C bromelain activity is about 2% or less (denatured), so little gelatin is broken down.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts gelatin sets AND cites near-zero activity at 70 degrees C from the graph.
required_elements: activity about 2% or near zero at 70 degrees C
common_errors: Predicts it will not set because enzyme is present

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how adding acidic lemon juice lowers the activity of bromelain at every temperature shown, referring to the active site.
parts.model_answer: Lower pH changes the charges (protonation) of R groups, altering ionic/hydrogen bonding in and near the active site, so the active site shape or charge fits the substrate less well and fewer reactions occur.

rubric_rows.criterion: Links pH change to altered R-group charge/bonding changing the active site, reducing substrate binding.
required_elements: pH change alters R group charge or bonding
common_errors: Says acid uses up the enzyme

input.design_note: Short FRQ ordered describe/explain, read data, predict, justify. Skill 2.B is exercised by relating the graph model of enzyme activity to the molecular explanation. Household context (gelatin dessert with fresh pineapple).

content.text: I designed a short FRQ (4 points, four 1-point parts) using a purely mathematical/abstract setting: a Michaelis-Menten-style rate model with a temperature-dependent function. The stimulus is a table of model values. The verification code recomputes each key from the stimulus numbers.

input.title: Abstract Rate Model of an Enzyme Across Temperature
input.stimulus: {"kind":"table","description":"Table of model-predicted initial reaction rate (arbitrary units, a.u.) of a hypothetical enzyme E at six temperatures, under two conditions: low substrate concentration and saturating substrate concentration. Both conditions share the same model: rate = Vmax(T) x [S]/(Km + [S]) x f(T).","data":{"model":"rate = Vmax x [S]/(Km+[S]) x f(T); Km = 2.0 mM; Vmax at optimum = 100 a.u.; f(T) is the fraction of enzyme molecules in active (folded) conformation","columns":["Temperature (deg C)","f(T) fraction active","Rate at [S]=2.0 mM (a.u.)","Rate at [S]=40 mM (a.u.)"],"rows":[[10,0.30,15,28.6],[20,0.60,30,57.1],[30,0.90,45,85.7],[40,1.00,50,95.2],[50,0.40,20,38.1],[60,0.05,2.5,4.8]],"units":{"temperature":"deg C","rate":"arbitrary units (a.u.)","substrate":"mM"},"notes":"Rates are computed from the model and rounded to one decimal place. Assume enzyme concentration is the same at all temperatures."}

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using the table, identify the temperature at which the model predicts the highest rate at [S] = 40 mM, and explain, in terms of the f(T) column, why the rate at 30 deg C is lower than at 40 deg C.
parts.model_answer: 40 deg C has the highest rate (95.2 a.u.). At 30 deg C f(T) = 0.90, so only 90% of enzyme molecules are in the active conformation, versus 100% at 40 deg C, so fewer enzymes can catalyze the reaction.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies 40 deg C AND links lower rate at 30 deg C to a smaller fraction of active enzyme (f = 0.90 vs 1.00)
required_elements: f(T) lower at 30 deg C / smaller fraction of enzyme active or in proper conformation
alt_solutions: Fewer active enzyme molecules at 30 deg C so lower Vmax
common_errors: Says the enzyme is denatured at 30 deg C

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the percent decrease in rate at [S] = 40 mM when temperature rises from 40 deg C to 50 deg C. Show your work.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct percent decrease with work shown
common_errors: Reporting 57.1 a.u. without converting to percent

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The model predicts that raising [S] from 2.0 mM to 40 mM increases the rate at every temperature, yet the rate at 60 deg C is still very low. Predict what the rate at 60 deg C would be at [S] = 400 mM compared with 4.8 a.u., and justify your prediction using the model's terms.
parts.model_answer: It would remain very low (about 5 a.u., at most about 5.0). Higher [S] can raise the substrate-saturation term toward 1, but the rate is still multiplied by f(60) = 0.05, so with almost all enzyme denatured the maximum possible rate is about 5 a.u.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts rate stays near/below about 5 a.u. and justifies with f(T) limiting the active enzyme regardless of substrate
required_elements: rate remains very low (about 5 a.u. or less)
few active enzymes / f(T)=0.05 limits rate; extra substrate cannot restore denatured enzyme
common_errors: Predicts rate returns to about 100 a.u. because substrate is high

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A student claims the drop in rate between 40 and 60 deg C shows that high temperature lowers the enzyme's Km. Use the model and table to justify why this claim is not supported.
parts.model_answer: In the model Km is fixed at 2.0 mM at all temperatures. The rate drop comes from the f(T) term, the falling fraction of active (folded) enzyme, which lowers the effective Vmax, not from a change in Km. Check: the ratio of rate at 40 mM to rate at 2.0 mM stays about 1.9 at each temperature, showing the substrate dependence is unchanged.

rubric_rows.criterion: States Km is constant and attributes drop to loss of active enzyme (f(T)) / lower Vmax
required_elements: decrease due to f(T)/fewer active enzymes/denaturation

input.design_note: Abstract mathematical model; tests how a model term (f(T), fraction of folded enzyme) represents temperature effects on enzyme function, separate from the substrate term. Parts ordered explain, data/calculation, predict, justify.

import json
Km=2.0;Vmax=100
data={10:0.30,20:0.60,30:0.90,40:1.00,50:0.40,60:0.05}
def r(T,S): return Vmax*S/(Km+S)*data[T]
checks=[]
best=max(data,key=lambda T:r(T,40))
checks.append({"part":"a","pass":best==40 and abs(r(40,40)-95.2)<0.1,"detail":str(best)})
pct=(r(40,40)-r(50,40))/r(40,40)*100
checks.append({"part":"b","pass":59.5<=pct<=60.5,"detail":str(pct)})
r400=r(60,400)
checks.append({"part":"c","pass":r400<=5.0 and abs(r(60,40)-4.8)<0.1,"detail":str(r400)})
ratios=[r(T,40)/r(T,2.0) for T in data]
checks.append({"part":"d","pass":max(ratios)-min(ratios)<1e-9,"detail":str(ratios[0])})
tab_ok=all(abs(r(T,2.0)-v)<0.06 for T,v in zip(data,[15,30,45,50,20,2.5]))
checks.append({"part":"table","pass":tab_ok,"detail":"table rates match model"})
print(json.dumps({"checks":checks,"conceptual_parts":[]}))

content.text: Design: a sports-medicine clinic scenario with a table of options, testing the definition of scarcity (limited resources vs. unlimited wants, so choices are required). The stimulus is a table of the clinic's weekly physical therapist hours. The key is a conceptual statement about scarcity, requiring the choice to be tied to limited resources.

stimulus.description: Table of weekly requests for physical therapist (PT) hours at a university sports-medicine clinic, compared with the PT hours available.

data.title: Weekly PT hours at a university sports-medicine clinic
data.note: The clinic cannot hire additional therapists this year.

input.stem: The clinic's director observes that the 180 weekly hours requested exceed the 120 hours available, so the director must decide how to allocate the hours. Which of the following best explains why this situation illustrates scarcity?
options: The available PT hours are limited relative to the wants for them, so using hours for one purpose means giving up other uses.
The clinic charges students too little for walk-in treatment, so the director must raise prices until requests equal 120 hours.
The clinic is operating inefficiently, so scarcity would disappear if the director used the 120 hours more productively.
Scarcity exists only because the clinic is a nonprofit, so a for-profit clinic would have enough PT hours for all requests.
The requests total 180 hours, so the clinic has a shortage that would not exist if the clinic hired additional therapists.
option_rationale: Correct: scarcity is limited resources versus unlimited wants, forcing choices and opportunity costs.
Misconception: scarcity is a pricing problem that exists only when price is too low; scarcity exists at any price.
Misconception: scarcity results from inefficiency; even fully efficient use leaves wants exceeding resources.
Misconception: scarcity depends on organization type or profit motive; it affects all economies and organizations.
Misconception: scarcity equals a temporary shortage that more hiring would eliminate; extra therapists are themselves scarce and wants remain unlimited.
input.explanation_en: Scarcity means resources are limited while wants are effectively unlimited, so choices are required and every use of PT hours has an opportunity cost. The first option states this. The pricing option confuses scarcity with a price-setting problem; scarcity exists at any price. The inefficiency option is wrong because even perfectly efficient use cannot make 120 hours satisfy 180 hours of requests. The nonprofit option is wrong because scarcity affects every organization and economy, for-profit or not. The hiring option confuses scarcity with a temporary shortage; additional therapists would use scarce resources and wants would still exceed what is available.

input.design_note: Tests the definition of scarcity (limited resources vs. wants, forcing trade-offs) in a sports-medicine context; distractors target confusions of scarcity with pricing, inefficiency, organization type, and shortage.

content.text: I'll design a purely abstract item on scarcity: unlimited wants vs. limited resources, which forces choices and opportunity cost. I'll use a stimulus type of "text" containing an abstract statement about a decision-maker with symbols.

stimulus.description: Abstract setup: an agent has a fixed resource budget R and can use it on goods X and Y.

data.setup: An agent has a fixed amount of a resource, R = 12 units. Each unit of X requires 1 unit of R. Each unit of Y requires 1 unit of R. The agent's desire for X and for Y has no upper limit (more of either is always preferred).
data.feasible_set: x + y <= 12, with x >= 0 and y >= 0

input.stem: In the setup described by the stimulus, which statement best applies the economic concept of scarcity?
options: Because wants are unlimited and R is limited, the agent cannot have all of both goods, so choosing more of one means giving up some of the other.
Because R is limited, the agent should spend all of it on the good with the larger number of units, since scarcity affects only one good at a time.
Because the agent could choose any combination with x + y less than 12, scarcity does not exist unless the agent actually uses all 12 units.
Because wants are unlimited, scarcity would disappear if the agent obtained a larger fixed amount of R, such as 20 units.
Because each unit of X and Y requires one unit of R, the two goods are not scarce in relation to each other, so no trade-off arises.
option_rationale: Correct: unlimited wants meet limited resources, forcing choices and trade-offs (opportunity cost).
Misconception: scarcity applies to one good only and implies a corner choice; it actually applies to the whole resource constraint and does not dictate any particular choice.
Misconception: scarcity exists only when resources are fully used; in fact, the limit on resources exists regardless of the chosen point.
Misconception: scarcity can be eliminated by having more resources; any finite amount is still scarce when wants are unlimited.
Misconception: equal resource requirements mean no trade-off; in fact, the shared resource creates the trade-off.
input.explanation_en: Scarcity is the condition of unlimited wants facing limited resources, which forces choices. With R = 12 shared by X and Y and wants for each unlimited, the agent cannot have everything, so more of one good means less of the other. The option about spending everything on one good is wrong because scarcity applies to the whole constraint and does not dictate a corner choice. The option saying scarcity requires using all 12 units is wrong because the limit exists regardless of which feasible point is chosen. The option saying 20 units would remove scarcity is wrong because any finite resource stock is still scarce when wants are unlimited. The option claiming equal requirements remove the trade-off is wrong because the shared resource is exactly what creates the trade-off.

# check trade-off: any feasible bundle with x+y=R; raising x by 1 lowers max y by 1
x=5; y=R-x
x2=x+1; y2=R-x2
tradeoff = (y2<y)

content.text:
Design: a field setting (agricultural research station) with a PPC table of data. A bowed-out PPC with increasing opportunity cost. The question asks to interpret which statement explains the outcome. The table gives combinations of wheat and sorghum. The student must compute the opportunity cost and conclude.

Data (thousand bushels, wheat vs. sorghum): A: 0 wheat, 90 sorghum; B: 20, 84; C: 40, 72; D: 60, 54; E: 80, 30; F: 100, 0.

Opportunity cost of wheat, per 20 wheat: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 sorghum, which is increasing, so the PPC is bowed out. The question: moving from D to E, what is the opportunity cost of 1 bushel of wheat, and why? The answer is 24/20 = 1.2 sorghum per wheat, and it is higher than in the earlier moves because resources are not equally suited to both crops. The distractors cover the wrong computation (using the 30 sorghum level), the constant-cost misconception, and an explanation based on technology.

stimulus.description: Table of maximum combinations of wheat and sorghum a research farm can produce with all land and labor fully employed.

data.title: Efficient production combinations, research farm

input.stem: An agricultural field station can use its fixed land, labor, and technology to produce wheat and sorghum. The table shows the maximum combinations it can produce. The station moves from point D to point E. Which of the following correctly states the opportunity cost of this move and explains why it differs from the opportunity cost of moving from point A to point B?
options: 1.2 thousand bushels of sorghum per thousand bushels of wheat, which is higher because resources are not equally productive in both crops
1.2 thousand bushels of sorghum per thousand bushels of wheat, which is higher because the station's technology has deteriorated
24 thousand bushels of wheat per thousand bushels of sorghum, which is higher because resources are not equally productive in both crops
0.3 thousand bushels of sorghum per thousand bushels of wheat, which is the same as moving from A to B because resources are equally productive in both crops
1.5 thousand bushels of sorghum per thousand bushels of wheat, which is higher because the station is producing inefficiently at point E
option_rationale: Correct: sorghum given up is 54-30=24 for 20 more wheat, so 1.2 per unit; A to B costs only 6/20=0.3, and the cost rises because resources are specialized, giving a bowed-out PPC.
Right number but wrong cause: the PPC is drawn with fixed technology, and a move along it does not change technology. Confuses movement along the PPC with an inward shift.
Inverts the opportunity cost, mixing up which good is given up and misusing the magnitude 24 as a per-unit figure.
Uses the A-to-B cost of 0.3 and assumes constant opportunity cost, the straight-line PPC misconception.
Uses the sorghum level at E (30) divided by 20 for 1.5 and wrongly claims E is inefficient, though every listed point is a maximum combination.
input.explanation_en: From D to E, wheat rises by 20 and sorghum falls from 54 to 30, a loss of 24, so the opportunity cost is 24/20 = 1.2 thousand bushels of sorghum per thousand bushels of wheat. From A to B it is only 6/20 = 0.3. The cost rises because resources are not equally productive in both crops; as more wheat is produced, land and labor better suited to sorghum must be shifted, giving a bowed-out PPC. The option blaming deteriorating technology is wrong because the table holds technology fixed and the move is along the curve. The option stating wheat given up per sorghum reverses the goods and the units. The option claiming 0.3 and equal productivity assumes constant opportunity cost, contradicted by the data. The option giving 1.5 miscalculates by using the sorghum level at E, and wrongly calls E inefficient, though all listed points are maximum combinations.
