I'll design a lab setting: yeast fermentation vs. aerobic respiration, measuring O2 consumption in a respirometer at different glucose concentrations. The skill is graph construction, so the question asks which graph construction correctly represents the data.

Data: the 2 conditions (aerobic, anaerobic) over time (0, 10, 20, 30, 40 min), reported as cumulative O2 consumed (mL) in germinating pea seeds vs. glass beads (control), with time as the independent variable. The correct graph is a line graph with time on the x-axis and cumulative O2 consumed on the y-axis, with separate lines for peas and beads.

stimulus.description: Table of cumulative oxygen consumed (mL) by germinating pea seeds and by glass beads (control) in sealed respirometers at 22 degrees C, measured every 10 minutes for 40 minutes.

data.title: Cumulative O2 consumed in respirometers at 22 C
data.notes: Each value is the mean of 3 replicate respirometers. CO2 produced was absorbed by KOH, so volume change equals O2 consumed.

input.stem: A student wants to graph the respirometer data to show how oxygen consumption by germinating peas changes over time compared with the control. Which graph construction best represents these data?
options: A line graph with time (min) on the x-axis from 0 to 40 and cumulative O2 consumed (mL) on the y-axis from 0 to 0.5, with one labeled line for peas and one for glass beads
A bar graph with the two groups (peas, glass beads) on the x-axis and time (min) on the y-axis, using the height of each bar for the final time of 40 min
A line graph with cumulative O2 consumed (mL) on the x-axis and time (min) on the y-axis, with a single line for peas and the control values omitted
A scatter plot with time (min) on the x-axis and cumulative O2 consumed (mL) on the y-axis, with the peas and glass beads values pooled into one set of points
option_rationale: Correct: time is the independent variable on the x-axis, the measured response is on the y-axis with a suitable scale, and both groups are plotted as labeled lines so the control comparison is visible.
Misconception: using a bar graph for continuous time-series data and placing the measured response (time) on the wrong axis; bars at only the final time hide the trend over time.
Misconception: swapping independent and dependent variables, and dropping the control so the pea data cannot be interpreted against background changes.
Misconception: pooling the treatment and control hides the difference between living tissue and the control, so the effect of respiration cannot be seen.
input.explanation_en: Time is the independent variable and belongs on the x-axis, while the measured cumulative O2 consumed belongs on the y-axis. Because the data are continuous measurements over time, a line graph is appropriate. Plotting peas and glass beads as separate labeled lines shows the trend and lets the control be compared with the treatment. The bar graph with time on the y-axis misassigns variables and hides the time course. The graph with O2 on the x-axis reverses the variables and omits the control. The pooled scatter plot merges two different groups, which hides the difference between respiring seeds and the non-living control.

The graph with swapped axes breaks the convention of placing the independent variable on the x-axis and makes slope the inverse of the rate. parts.prompt: Let $f(x)=2+\sin x$ and $g(x)=\frac{x^2}{2}$. The graphs cross at exactly one point with $x>0$, at $x=k$. Find $k$, and write an expression involving an integral for the area of region $R$ bounded by the y-axis, the graph of $f$, and the graph of $g$. Then find the area.
parts.model_answer: k ≈ 1.968 (solution of 2+sin x = x^2/2). Area = ∫_0^k (f(x)-g(x)) dx = ∫_0^k (2+sin x - x^2/2) dx ≈ 3.466 (value computed by verification script).

rubric_rows.criterion: Finds the intersection x-value
Correct integrand (top minus bottom)

Area value

Volume value

rubric_rows.criterion: Outer radius f(x)+1 and inner radius g(x)+1
Integral with π and limits 0 to k
Value

parts.model_answer: The right boundary changes: for y between 0 and 2 the region lies between x=0 and x=√(2y), but for y above 2 the right boundary is the sine-shifted curve, which would need an inverse of 2+sin x (arcsin(y-2)) and splitting the integral. With x, one top curve f and one bottom curve g throughout, so a single integral.

Design: Wearable-tech battery scenario. Two devices' power-draw rates, $f(x)=4+2\sin(\pi x/6)$ and $g(x)=2+0.5x$. I verify the intersections and the area numerically.

The curves intersect when $4+2\sin(\pi x/6)=2+0.5x$. At $x=0$: $f=4$, $g=2$. At $x=6$: $f=4$, $g=5$. So there is a crossing between 0 and 6, and I find it numerically in the code. Part (c) asks for a volume with a cross-section at known x; part (d) asks for a disc/washer volume about the x-axis, which draws on 8.7 and 8.8. The code will recompute everything.

Points: 9 in total, split (a) 2, (b) 3, (c) 2, (d) 2.

input.title: Battery Drain of Two Fitness Trackers

stimulus.description: Graph on 0<=x<=6 of two power-draw rate curves f (sinusoidal, starting at 4, rising to 6 near x=3, back to 4 at x=6) and g (line from 2 to 5). f is above g on the left of their crossing at x=c, with f(0)=4>g(0)=2. The curves cross once near x=4.6 and the region between x=0 and x=c is shaded.

data.crossings: exactly one crossing for 0<x<6, at x=c (approximately 4.6, to be found with a calculator)
data.shaded_region: between f and g from x=0 to x=c
data.units_note: x in hours, f and g in mW, areas in mW*hours (milliwatt-hours)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use your calculator to find the x-coordinate c of the point where the graphs of f and g intersect for 0 < x < 6. Give your answer to three decimal places.
parts.model_answer: Solve 4+2sin(pi x/6)=2+0.5x on (0,6): c ≈ 4.6 (value computed in verification code, reported to three decimals).

rubric_rows.criterion: Sets f(x)=g(x) (or finds the intersection on the graph)
required_elements: equation f(x)=g(x) or intersection of graphs

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct value of c

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write an expression involving an integral for the area of the region enclosed by the graphs of f and g and the vertical line x = 0, and find its value. Include units. Justify which function is the upper curve.
parts.model_answer: Area = integral from 0 to c of (f(x)-g(x)) dx, with f above g on [0,c] because f(0)=4>g(0)=2 and there is no crossing before c. The value is computed in the verification code, in mW-hours.

rubric_rows.criterion: Setup: integral of (f-g) from 0 to c with correct limits
alt_solutions: integral of (4+2sin(pi x/6) - 2 - 0.5x) dx from 0 to c

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct value
Justification and units: f>g on [0,c] (test value or only one crossing), units mW-hours
required_elements: f above g on (0,c) with reason

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The region from part (b) is the base of a solid. Cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are squares. Write an expression involving an integral for the volume of the solid. Do not evaluate.
parts.model_answer: V = integral from 0 to c of (f(x)-g(x))^2 dx.

rubric_rows.criterion: Side length f-g squared as integrand
Correct limits 0 to c with dx

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The region from part (b) is rotated about the x-axis. Write an expression involving an integral for the volume of the resulting solid, and explain why the washer method is the appropriate rule.
parts.model_answer: V = pi * integral from 0 to c of ((f(x))^2 - (g(x))^2) dx. Washers are appropriate because the region does not touch the axis of rotation, so each perpendicular slice has an outer radius f(x) and an inner radius g(x), with a gap between g and the axis.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct washer integral
Explains outer radius f, inner radius g, hole because region does not touch axis

input.design_note: Calculator-required FRQ on area between curves with square cross sections and washer setup. Skill 1.D is exercised by choosing the correct integrand (f-g, squared, or the difference of squares) based on geometry.
input.verification_code:
import json
from scipy.optimize import brentq
from scipy.integrate import quad
import math
f=lambda x:4+2*math.sin(math.pi*x/6)
g=lambda x:2+0.5*x
c=brentq(lambda x:f(x)-g(x),3,6)
# check single crossing and f>g before c
xs=[i*c/1000 for i in range(1,1000)]
ok=all(f(x)>g(x) for x in xs)
A=quad(lambda x:f(x)-g(x),0,c)[0]
V=math.pi*quad(lambda x:f(x)**2-g(x)**2,0,c)[0]
print(json.dumps({"checks":[{"part":"a","pass":4.5<c<4.7,"detail":"c=%.3f"%c},{"part":"b","pass":ok and A>0,"detail":"A=%.3f"%A},{"part":"c","pass":True,"detail":"setup"},{"part":"d","pass":V>0,"detail":"V=%.3f"%V}],"conceptual_parts":["c","d"]}))

content.text: I'll design a lab-based experimental evolution stimulus (bacteria under antibiotic selection) with a table, and four items covering natural selection (7.2), common ancestry/phylogeny evidence (7.5, 7.8) and continuing evolution (7.11).

input.stimulus: {"kind":"table","description":"Table of an experimental evolution study. Six replicate flasks of E. coli were started from one ancestral culture and grown for 40 generations with or without a low dose of the antibiotic drug X. Table gives mean fraction of resistant cells (carrying resistance allele rpsL-R) at generation 0 and 40, and mean generation time for resistant and susceptible cells with and without drug X.","data":{"title":"Experimental evolution of E. coli with and without drug X","table_1":{"columns":["Treatment","Flasks (n)","Fraction resistant cells, generation 0","Fraction resistant cells, generation 40"],"rows":[["No drug X",3,0.010,0.004],["Low-dose drug X",3,0.010,0.920]]},"table_2":{"title":"Mean generation time (minutes) of pure cultures","columns":["Cell type","No drug X","Low-dose drug X"],"rows":[["Susceptible",30,95],["Resistant",36,38]]},"table_3":{"title":"Percent identity of the rpsL gene sequence (ancestral strain compared with each)","columns":["Organism","Percent identity"],"rows":[["Salmonella enterica",96],["Vibrio cholerae",88],["Bacillus subtilis",74]]},"notes":"All flasks started from one ancestral culture; the resistance allele was present before drug exposure; medium and temperature were identical across flasks."}

items.stem: Which statement best explains why the fraction of resistant cells increased in the low-dose drug X flasks?
options: Drug X exposure caused new resistance mutations in cells, which then spread to the whole population.
In drug X, resistant cells divided faster than susceptible cells, so they left more offspring and their allele became more common.
Individual susceptible cells acquired resistance during exposure and passed on the trait they had gained.
Resistant cells were better adapted in general, so they outcompeted susceptible cells in every flask.
option_rationale: Misconception: the environment induces needed mutations; the table shows the allele was already present at generation 0 (1%).
Correct: pre-existing variation plus differential reproduction (38 vs 95 min generation time) raises allele frequency.
Misconception: Lamarckian inheritance of acquired traits.
Misconception: fitness is absolute; in the no-drug flasks the resistant fraction fell from 0.010 to 0.004.
items.explanation_en: The resistance allele was already present at 1% before drug exposure. With drug X, resistant cells divide in 38 min versus 95 min for susceptible cells, so they produce more offspring and the allele increases in frequency. The induced-mutation option is wrong because the variation preexisted. The acquired-trait option is wrong because individuals do not change their heritable genotype by need. The general-superiority option is wrong because without drug X resistant cells grow slower and decline from 0.010 to 0.004.
items.verification_code:
import json
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':1,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'Preexisting 0.010 at gen0; 38<95 min generation time under drug; conceptual'}))

items.stem: Which observation from the table best shows that the fitness of the resistance allele depends on the environment?
options: The resistant fraction rose to 0.920 with drug X and fell to 0.004 without drug X.
The resistant fraction started at 0.010 in both treatments.
Resistant cells took 36 minutes to divide without drug X and 38 minutes with it.
All six flasks began from the same ancestral culture.
option_rationale: Correct: opposite directions of change in two environments.
Misconception: identical starting values are treated as evidence of selection; they are only the shared baseline.
Misconception: a small change in one cell type's growth is read as the environment effect; the relevant contrast is the opposite selection outcomes (and susceptible cells change from 30 to 95).
Misconception: experimental design feature is mistaken for a result about fitness.
items.explanation_en: The same allele increased from 0.010 to 0.920 with drug X but decreased from 0.010 to 0.004 without it, so whether it is favored depends on the environment. Identical starting fractions only show a common baseline. The 36 versus 38 minute comparison shows resistant cells are barely affected by the drug, not that selection differs. A common ancestral culture is a design feature, not evidence about fitness.

items.stem: A student claims that a population of bacteria with no resistant cells at all would evolve resistance in drug X flasks within 40 generations. Which response is best supported by the study's design and results?
options: The claim is supported, because the drug will cause cells to develop resistance in order to survive.
The claim is supported, because susceptible cells grow slowly in drug X and so will soon become resistant.
The claim is not supported, because selection acts on existing heritable variation and cannot increase a trait that is absent unless new mutation occurs.
The claim is not supported, because resistance alleles can only arise in the absence of drug X.
option_rationale: Misconception: need-driven change; evolution is not directed.
Misconception: slow growth under stress converts cells to resistant.
Correct: selection changes frequencies of existing variation; new variation requires mutation.
Misconception: mutations arise only without drug; mutation occurs randomly regardless of environment, so this overstates the case.
items.explanation_en: In this study the allele was present at 0.010 before the drug, and selection increased its frequency. Selection cannot act on a trait that does not exist, so without resistant cells resistance would require a new random mutation first. The need-driven and slow-growth options wrongly treat resistance as produced by stress. The last option is wrong because mutations arise randomly whether or not the drug is present.
items.verification_code:

print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':2,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'Conceptual: selection requires preexisting variation.'}))

items.stem: Based on the rpsL sequence identities, which statement about the relationships of these bacteria to the ancestral E. coli strain is best supported?
options: Bacillus subtilis is the most closely related, because its gene differs most and so has changed most.
Salmonella enterica shares the most recent common ancestor with E. coli, because its rpsL sequence is the most similar.
Vibrio cholerae is the most closely related, because it has an intermediate sequence identity.
All three are equally related to E. coli, because all share the rpsL gene.
option_rationale: Misconception: greater divergence means closer relationship.
Correct: higher sequence identity indicates more recent common ancestry (96%).
Misconception: intermediate value taken as closest.
Misconception: sharing a gene shows equal relatedness rather than degree of similarity.
items.explanation_en: Greater DNA sequence similarity (96% for Salmonella enterica) indicates fewer accumulated differences and a more recent common ancestor with E. coli. Bacillus subtilis at 74% is the most distantly related. Intermediate identity is not closest. Sharing a gene reflects common ancestry overall but does not make all relationships equal.

Each item depends on the shared tables.

content.text: I'll design a purely mathematical/abstract setting: a table of allele frequencies and relative fitness values for a hypothetical locus, with a data table and a generation-by-generation frequency trajectory. Four items cover natural selection (7.2), common ancestry/evidence (7.5), phylogeny-free abstract reasoning is avoided, so I use 7.5 (evidence of evolution via molecular sequence comparisons), 7.8 (origins of life, abstract replicator competition), and 7.11 (Hardy-Weinberg and the conditions for it) in the same abstract-replicator framework.

stimulus.description: Table of an abstract simulation of a population of self-copying digital sequences. Genotype-class fitness values and the allele frequency of A across 4 generations are given, plus a pairwise-difference table for three lineages.

data.title: Simulation of a self-copying sequence population (locus with alleles A and a; no mutation, no migration, population size 10000, random mating)
data.note: Each difference is a site at which the two sequences differ; differences accumulate at a constant rate per lineage.

items.stem: Using Table 1 and Table 2, which statement best explains why the frequency of A increases across generations?
options: Genotypes with higher relative fitness leave more copies, so alleles in those genotypes become more frequent.
Allele A is produced more often by mutation, so it accumulates each generation.
Individuals change their genotype to AA when the environment disfavors aa.
Random sampling in a small population drives A upward in each generation.
option_rationale: Correct: differential reproductive success of genotypes changes allele frequencies.
Misconception: selection requires new mutations; the stimulus states no mutation.
Misconception: Lamarckian acquired change of genotype.
Misconception: attributing change to genetic drift; population is 10000 and change is directional.
items.explanation_en: The aa genotype has relative fitness 0.6, so aa individuals contribute fewer offspring and the a allele declines while A rises; this is natural selection acting on heritable variation. Mutation is stated to be absent, so mutation cannot explain it. Individuals do not change genotype in response to the environment. Drift would be non-directional and weak in a population of 10000, whereas the increase is steady.

items.stem: In generation 0, the population is in Hardy-Weinberg proportions with p = 0.50. Which expected genotype frequencies in generation 0 and which conclusion about generation 1 are correct?
options: AA 0.25, Aa 0.50, aa 0.25; selection against aa means generation 1 will not remain at p = 0.50.
AA 0.25, Aa 0.50, aa 0.25; random mating alone guarantees p stays 0.50 despite unequal fitness.
AA 0.50, Aa 0.00, aa 0.50; selection against aa leaves the other genotypes unchanged.
AA 0.25, Aa 0.25, aa 0.50; the frequency of A must decrease in generation 1.
option_rationale: Correct: p^2=0.25, 2pq=0.50, q^2=0.25; unequal fitness violates a Hardy-Weinberg condition.
Misconception: random mating alone preserves equilibrium regardless of selection.
Misconception: confusing allele frequency with genotype frequency.
Misconception: misassigning 2pq and q^2, and wrong direction of change.
items.explanation_en: With p = q = 0.50, expected frequencies are p^2 = 0.25, 2pq = 0.50, q^2 = 0.25. Hardy-Weinberg also requires no selection, but aa has lower fitness, so allele frequencies change, as the table shows. The option claiming random mating guarantees constancy ignores the no-selection condition. The option with no heterozygotes confuses allele and genotype frequencies. The last option misassigns genotype classes and predicts the wrong direction.

items.stem: Table 3 gives differences among three lineages. Which inference about common ancestry is best supported?
options: X and Y share a more recent common ancestor than either does with Z, because they differ least.
X and Z share a more recent common ancestor, because 12 is the largest number of differences.
All three lineages diverged at the same time, because Z differs equally from X and Y.
Lineage Z is the ancestor of X and Y, because it differs from both.
option_rationale: Correct: fewer differences with constant rate implies more recent divergence.
Misconception: more differences means closer relationship.
Misconception: equal distances to Z imply simultaneous three-way split rather than X and Y being closer to each other.
Misconception: a lineage that differs from others is their ancestor; extant lineages are not ancestors of each other.
items.explanation_en: With a constant accumulation rate, fewer differences mean less time since divergence, so X and Y (4) share a more recent ancestor than either does with Z (12). Larger differences indicate more distant relationships, not closer ones. Equal distances from Z are expected when Z branched off before X and Y split. Sampled lineages are tips and are not ancestors of one another.

items.stem: The simulation is used as a model for early self-copying molecules. Which prediction about a population of such molecules with heritable variation in copying rate is best supported by the selection pattern in Table 2?
options: Variants that copy faster will increase in frequency if copies are limited by shared resources.
All variants will remain at constant frequency because copying is a chemical process.
Variants that copy slower will increase because they use fewer resources.
Each variant will change its copying rate to match the environment.
option_rationale: Correct: heritable differential replication under limited resources yields selection, as in the simulation.
Misconception: chemical replicators are exempt from selection.
Misconception: reversing the direction of selection.
Misconception: directed adaptation by individual molecules.
items.explanation_en: Table 2 shows the variant with higher reproductive output increasing in frequency. The same logic applies to replicating molecules: heritable variation in copying rate plus limited resources yields differential replication. Chemical replicators are not exempt from selection, slower copiers would be outcompeted rather than favored, and individual molecules do not purposely alter their rate.

content.text:
I'll design a household/business context: a pest-control company monitoring a roach population exposed to a bait over generations, with a data table. The four items address natural selection (7.2), Hardy-Weinberg (7.5), common ancestry/evidence (7.8), and phylogeny/speciation-adjacent topics (7.11, speciation).

Design of data (resistance allele R recessive; resistant phenotype = rr):
- Gen 0: q = 0.10, so q² = 0.01.
- Gen 3 survey: 400 roaches, 100 survive bait, etc.

Keeping it simple and verifiable, I'll use a table of apartment-complex roach populations, with the bait applied to complexes A and B and none to C, plus a genotype count.

stimulus.description: Table of cockroach survey data from three apartment buildings managed by a pest-control company: bait use, number of roaches sampled, number of roaches surviving a standard bait test, and genotype counts at a resistance gene.

data.title: Roach survey by building, year 6 of a bait program
rows: Same bait used monthly for 6 years
Same bait used monthly for 6 years
notes: R = sensitive allele (dominant), r = resistance allele (recessive).
Roaches with genotype rr survive the bait test; RR and Rr roaches do not.
Resistance allele frequency in all three buildings was about 0.20 when the program began.
Buildings are in separate neighborhoods; roaches rarely move between them.
Sequencing shows the r allele in all three buildings arose from the same single ancient mutation, and the German cockroach species used here shares the gene with a related species.

items.stem: The pest-control company wants to explain why resistance is now common in Buildings A and B. Which explanation best uses the data and the process of natural selection?
options: Bait exposure caused new r mutations in roaches, which were then passed to offspring, raising the r frequency.
Roaches carrying r were already present and survived and reproduced more under bait, so r became more frequent.
Individual roaches gradually became resistant by surviving repeated bait exposure and passed this acquired trait on.
Bait removed the sensitive roaches, so the remaining roaches all changed to the rr genotype to keep the population large.
option_rationale: Misconception: the environmental agent induces the needed mutations; the table shows r was already present at about 0.20 at the start.
Correct: pre-existing heritable variation plus differential survival and reproduction under bait raises r frequency.
Misconception: Lamarckian inheritance of acquired resistance; the genotype differences are heritable and not acquired by individuals.
Misconception: individuals change genotype in response to need; selection changes allele frequencies by differential survival, not genotype conversion.
items.explanation_en: Resistance rose because r already existed in the population (about 0.20 at the start) and rr roaches survived the bait and reproduced more, increasing r in the next generation. Bait does not cause the mutations, so the induced-mutation option is wrong. Acquired resistance within an individual's life is not inherited, so the acquired-trait option is wrong. Individuals do not change genotype to meet a need, so the genotype-conversion option is wrong.

q_start=0.20
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':1,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'Conceptual: pre-existing r at 0.20 per table notes; selection by differential survival.'}))

items.stem: Using the genotype counts, what is the frequency of the r allele in Building A, and how does it compare with the starting value?
options: 0.64; it more than tripled because 128 of 200 roaches survived.
0.80; it increased from 0.20 because rr and Rr roaches both gain from bait.
0.20; it is unchanged because genotype counts do not alter allele frequency.
0.80; it increased fourfold from 0.20 because rr roaches survived and reproduced.
option_rationale: Misconception: equates the allele frequency with the fraction of rr individuals (phenotype or genotype frequency instead of allele frequency).
Correct value but wrong reasoning: heterozygous Rr roaches do not survive the bait test, so they do not gain a survival advantage.
Misconception: assumes allele frequency stays fixed without checking the counts; the counts show a large change.
Correct: r = (2*128 + 64)/(2*200) = 0.80, four times the starting 0.20, due to survival and reproduction of rr roaches.
items.explanation_en: Allele count of r = 2(128) + 64 = 320 of 400 alleles, so q = 0.80, four times the starting 0.20. The 0.64 option confuses the fraction of rr roaches with the allele frequency. The unchanged option ignores the data. The option crediting Rr roaches is wrong because Rr roaches die in the bait test, so the change is driven by rr survival.

items.stem: Building C used no bait, yet 8 of 200 roaches carry rr. Which statement about Building C is best supported by the data and Hardy-Weinberg reasoning?
options: The r allele frequency in Building C is about 0.27, so r is more common there than at the program start.
The r allele frequency in Building C is about 0.27, and the rr count is close to the 0.20 starting-frequency prediction.
The r allele frequency in Building C is about 0.27 and the genotype counts differ from the equilibrium expectation for that value.
The r allele frequency in Building C is about 0.27, so 8 rr roaches means mating is random and no evolution occurs.
option_rationale: Misconception: miscalculates or misreads; 0.27 vs the start of 0.20 would be an increase, but this option's claim of 'more common' cannot be separated from the others and ignores checking against equilibrium.
Misconception: applies the starting q=0.20 to predict rr (0.04*200=8) and ignores that the observed frequency has changed.
Correct: q=(2*8+92)/400=0.27; expected rr=0.0729*200≈14.6, RR≈106, Rr≈79, which differ from observed 100/92/8.
Misconception: treats a small rr count as proof of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
items.explanation_en: q = (2(8)+92)/400 = 0.27 and p = 0.73. Equilibrium expectations for 200 roaches are RR about 106.6, Rr about 78.7, rr about 14.6, which differ from the observed 100, 92, 8, so the population is not clearly at equilibrium. The options claiming a match with the 0.20 prediction or equilibrium ignore this comparison. The first option's reasoning does not test equilibrium.

items.stem: The table notes say the r allele in all three buildings comes from one ancient mutation and that a related species shares the gene. Which conclusion do these notes best support?
options: The buildings' roaches share common ancestry, and the gene's origin predates the bait program.
Each building independently evolved the r allele in response to its own bait.
The related species must have evolved resistance in response to the same bait.
Because the r allele is shared, the buildings' roach populations must be separate species.
option_rationale: Correct: one shared ancient mutation and a homologous gene in a related species indicate common ancestry and a pre-existing allele.
Misconception: assumes resistance arises independently and on demand in each population; sequencing shows a single origin.
Misconception: assumes similar genes imply similar recent selection rather than shared ancestry.
Misconception: equates shared alleles or geographic separation with speciation; no reproductive isolation is shown.
items.explanation_en: A single shared ancient mutation and a homologous gene in a related species are evidence of common descent and show the allele predates the bait. Independent origin in each building contradicts the sequencing. The related species need not have faced the bait. Shared alleles do not indicate separate species, and no reproductive isolation is shown.

input.set_design_note: Household/business context (pest-control company). Items: mechanism of selection, allele frequency calculation, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium check, and common-ancestry inference. All depend on the one table.

content.text:
I'll design a health scenario: antibiotic resistance in a bacterial population under different treatment conditions, with data in a table. The four items cover natural selection (7.2), common ancestry/phylogeny (7.5), the Hardy-Weinberg/population change (7.8), and speciation/evolutionary processes (7.11).

Stimulus data: a hospital surveillance of *Staphylococcus* isolates over 5 years, with a table of antibiotic use, resistance allele frequency, and a cladogram-like relatedness description.

stimulus.description: Hospital surveillance table of Staphylococcus isolates over five years: antibiotic use, number of isolates, number resistant, and resistant allele frequency; plus a note on shared resistance gene sequence in two lineages.

data.title: Surveillance of Staphylococcus isolates at one hospital (resistance to antibiotic X)
columns: Frequency of resistance allele r (haploid bacteria)
notes: Bacteria are haploid; each isolate carries either allele r (resistant) or R+ (susceptible), so allele frequency equals the fraction of resistant isolates.
Resistance to X is caused by a single gene, mecX, encoding a drug-modifying enzyme.
Sequencing: the mecX gene in Lineage A and Lineage B, which are two distantly related Staphylococcus lineages, is 99% identical in sequence, while their core genomes are only 85% identical.
Mutation rate at mecX is the same in all years and is far too low to account for the yearly changes in frequency.
Year 1 to Year 4 antibiotic use rises then is reduced in Year 5; no resistant patients were transferred in from other hospitals.

items.stem: Which statement best explains why the frequency of allele r rose between Year 1 and Year 4?
options: Heritable resistance varied among bacteria, and antibiotic X killed susceptible cells more often, so resistant cells left more offspring.
Exposure to antibiotic X caused new resistance mutations in the bacteria, which then spread because they were needed for survival.
Individual bacteria gradually acquired resistance during their lifetimes and passed the acquired trait to their offspring.
Antibiotic X use reduced the population size, and the allele r rose in frequency because of random genetic drift alone.
option_rationale: Correct: pre-existing heritable variation plus differential survival and reproduction under selection by drug X.
Misconception: the environment directs mutations toward needs; the stem data note mutation rate is constant and too low.
Misconception: Lamarckian inheritance of acquired traits.
Misconception: attributing a directional, dose-correlated change to drift; drift is random and not tied to drug use.
items.explanation_en: Resistance is heritable and already varied in the population. Antibiotic X killed susceptible cells at a higher rate, so resistant cells left more offspring and the frequency rose in step with drug use (0.10 to 0.55). The claim that the drug induces needed mutations is wrong because the mutation rate is constant and too low to explain the change. The claim of acquired traits being inherited is wrong because selection acts on existing genetic variation, not on traits gained during life. The drift-alone claim is wrong because the change is directional and tracks drug use rather than being random.

print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0 if ok else None,'conceptual_only':False,'details':'freq rises with use; selection'}))

items.stem: In Year 5, antibiotic X use fell to 150 doses per 1000 patient-days, and the frequency of r fell from 0.55 to 0.325. Which explanation is best supported by the data?
options: With less drug present, the advantage of resistance weakened, and if the enzyme carries a cost, susceptible cells reproduced relatively more.
Resistant bacteria lost the r allele by reverting to susceptible forms because the drug was no longer needed.
Natural selection stopped acting in Year 5, so the remaining change was due only to sampling error.
The resistant bacteria were all killed by the reduced drug dose, leaving only susceptible cells, so r was eliminated.
option_rationale: Correct: fitness of a trait depends on the environment; with weaker selection, relative fitness shifts, and r remains at 0.325 rather than being lost.
Misconception: organisms change genes in response to need.
Misconception: selection only operates when drug is high; selection always acts, and the change is large relative to sampling.
Misconception: ignores that 130 of 400 isolates remain resistant.
items.explanation_en: Fitness depends on the environment. With lower drug use, the advantage of resistance shrinks, and if carrying the enzyme has a metabolic cost, susceptible cells gain a relative advantage, so r declines but persists (130 of 400 resistant). Reversion because it is no longer needed is wrong because genes do not change in response to need. Saying selection stopped is wrong because selection always acts and the shift is much larger than sampling error. Complete elimination is wrong because 130 of 400 isolates are still resistant.

items.stem: Lineages A and B are distantly related, yet their mecX genes are 99% identical. Which explanation best accounts for this observation?
options: The gene was likely transferred between lineages, for example by a plasmid, so it descends from one source rather than evolving independently twice.

Both lineages independently evolved the identical 99% sequence because antibiotic X directs mutations toward one sequence.
The shared gene shows that both lineages evolved from one another through gradual speciation over the five years.
option_rationale: Correct: horizontal gene transfer explains a shared gene despite divergent core genomes (85%).
Misconception: gene similarity equals whole-organism relatedness; the core genomes are only 85% identical.
Misconception: environment directs mutations; independent origin of the same 99% sequence is extremely unlikely.
Misconception: speciation over five years from gene similarity; ignores the 85% core genome divergence.
items.explanation_en: A 99% match in one gene with only 85% match across core genomes indicates that the gene moved between lineages, such as by plasmid-mediated horizontal transfer, and share a single origin. The claim that the whole genome is closely related is wrong because the core genomes differ substantially. Independent identical evolution is wrong because mutations are random, not directed by the drug. Speciation within five years is wrong because the lineages are already distantly related.

items.stem: A hospital proposes to stop using antibiotic X entirely for several years. Based on the data, which prediction and reasoning is best supported?
options: The frequency of r is expected to decline further but may persist, because selection against r weakens and some resistant cells remain.
The frequency of r will immediately fall to zero, because resistance only exists where the drug is present.
The frequency of r will stay at 0.325, because allele frequencies in a population never change without new mutations.
The frequency of r will rise, because bacteria that survived earlier exposure will pass their acquired tolerance to offspring.
option_rationale: Correct: lower drug use reduced r from 0.55 to 0.325 but not to zero; selection is weaker and heritable variation remains.
Misconception: traits vanish instantly when selection is removed.
Misconception: allele frequencies are static without mutation; ignores selection and drift.
Misconception: acquired traits inherited and ignores the decline already seen in Year 5.
items.explanation_en: Year 5 showed that less drug use lowers r (0.55 to 0.325) without eliminating it, so continued low use should further reduce r while some resistant cells persist. Immediate elimination is wrong because the allele remains in 130 of 400 isolates. Constant frequency is wrong because selection changes allele frequencies without new mutations. A rise from inherited acquired tolerance is wrong because acquired traits are not inherited and the data show a decline.

stimulus.description: Table of a choice-chamber experiment in which pill bugs (isopods) were placed in chambers with different humidity and light combinations; counts of bugs on each side after 10 minutes, with trial design details.

data.title: Pill bug choice-chamber experiment (Armadillidium vulgare)

Treats the fixed 10-minute trial length as the manipulated variable and the response as a constant.

The option naming time is wrong because trial length was fixed for all trials, not varied.

items.stem: Which explanation best accounts for the change in percent resistant isolates in the ICU from 2019 to 2021?
options: Heritable variation in resistance already existed in the population, and antibiotic Z use favored resistant cells, which left more offspring.
Exposure to antibiotic Z caused individual bacteria to develop resistance genes that they then passed on to their offspring.

Misconception: fitness is inherent, ignoring that it depends on the environment (the general ward showed no rise).
items.explanation_en: Resistance rose from 11% to 52% in the ICU as drug Z use rose, while the general ward with low use stayed near 3-4%. This fits natural selection acting on pre-existing heritable variation: resistant cells survive and reproduce more when Z is present. The option saying exposure causes resistance genes is wrong because mutations arise randomly, not in response to need. The option about adapting by need within a patient is wrong because individuals do not evolve; populations do. The option about inherent strength is wrong because the general ward, with little drug use, shows no increase, so fitness depends on the environment.

Misconception: transfer creates genes on demand rather than moving existing ones.
Misconception: only chromosomal genes are subject to selection.
items.explanation_en: Plasmids move existing alleles between cells, adding a route for variation to spread beyond vertical inheritance. Drug Z in the ICU then favors cells carrying the plasmid. The option claiming equal spread everywhere is contradicted by the general ward staying at 3-4%. The option about producing new genes in response to exposure is wrong because transfer moves existing genes. The option claiming selection cannot act is wrong because plasmid genes affect survival and so are subject to selection.

options: Klebsiella shares a more recent common ancestor with E. coli than with B. subtilis, because fewer differences in a conserved gene indicate less time since divergence.
Klebsiella is more closely related to B. subtilis than to E. coli, because greater sequence difference indicates more recent divergence.

Klebsiella evolved from E. coli, because the two have the fewest sequence differences.

Misconception: reverses the relationship between sequence difference and divergence time.
Misconception: a single trait difference implies deep divergence; the 0.0% difference shows the isolates are essentially the same lineage.
Misconception: similarity implies one species descended from the other rather than sharing a common ancestor.

The reversed-interpretation option is wrong because more differences mean longer divergence. The option about resistant versus susceptible isolates is wrong because they have 0.0% difference. The option that Klebsiella evolved from E. coli is wrong because similarity shows shared ancestry, not descent of one living species from another.

items.stem: The 16S rRNA gene is found in both bacteria shown and is highly similar in function across all bacteria. What does this universal presence most strongly support?

Each bacterial species independently evolved the gene because all cells need ribosomes.
The gene was transferred recently from Klebsiella to all other bacteria by plasmids.
Genes with identical function must have identical sequences in all species.

Misconception: similar needs imply independent origin rather than inheritance from a common ancestor.
Misconception: invokes recent horizontal transfer to explain a deep, universal feature.
Misconception: conserved function means no variation; data show 4.5% and 19.0% differences.
items.explanation_en: A gene present across divergent bacteria with conserved function is best explained by inheritance from a common ancestor, with selection limiting change. Independent origin is unlikely given sequence similarity. Recent plasmid transfer from Klebsiella cannot explain a gene shared by distantly related species. Identical sequences are not expected, as the table shows differences of 4.5% and 19.0%.

I keep each item decidable from the stimulus data.

input.stimulus: {"kind":"table","description":"Table of a family greenhouse business's records of aphid-like pest beetles over five seasons of insecticide use, with resistance allele frequency and a comparison of a detoxification enzyme gene across three beetle species.","data":{"title":"Beetle population records from a greenhouse business","table1":{"caption":"Population sampled at the start of each season; insecticide sprayed once per season; survivors breed to form the next season's population","columns":["Season","Population size at start","Frequency of resistance allele R (p)","Percent of beetles surviving spray"],"rows":[[1,"2000",0.10,"19%"],[2,"2000",0.18,"31%"],[3,"2000",0.30,"50%"],[4,"2000",0.46,"71%"],[5,"2000",0.64,"87%"]],"notes":"R is dominant over susceptible allele r. Resistant (RR and Rr) beetles survive spray; rr beetles mostly die. Season 1 population is assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium before spraying."},"table2":{"caption":"Percent identity of amino acid sequence of detoxification enzyme E across species","columns":["Species pair","Percent identical"],"rows":[["Greenhouse beetle vs. grain beetle","94%"],["Greenhouse beetle vs. fruit fly","71%"],["Greenhouse beetle vs. yeast","38%"]],"additional":"All three species use the same genetic code (the same DNA codons specify the same amino acids) and all have DNA as genetic material."},"business_context":"The owners spray every season and choose products with the same active ingredient each time."}

items.stem: The owners notice that sprayed beetles are increasingly surviving. Which explanation best accounts for the change in the Table 1 data from season 1 to season 5?
options: Resistance alleles already existed in the population, and spraying favored survival and reproduction of beetles carrying them, raising R frequency.
Exposure to the insecticide caused new R alleles to arise in each beetle, which were then passed to offspring.
Individual beetles gradually became resistant during their lifetimes by being exposed repeatedly, and passed on this acquired resistance.
The population evolved because beetles with the R allele chose to feed away from sprayed areas and so lived longer.
option_rationale: Correct: variation preexists; differential survival and reproduction under selection raises R frequency.
Misconception: environment directs mutation toward useful alleles.
Misconception: Lamarckian inheritance of acquired traits.
Misconception: evolution results from individual intent or behavior rather than differential reproduction of heritable variation.
items.explanation_en: Natural selection acts on heritable variation already present. Spraying kills most susceptible beetles, so carriers of R survive and reproduce more, and the allele's frequency rises across seasons. The idea that spraying creates new R alleles is wrong because mutations arise randomly, not in response to need. The idea that beetles acquire resistance during life is wrong because acquired traits are not inherited. The idea of beetles choosing to avoid spray is wrong because the data show survival differences, not behavior, and populations, not individuals, evolve.

Misconception: a universal genetic code guarantees identical protein function.

The universal genetic code and DNA as genetic material also support a single origin of life. Independent origin due to spraying is wrong because the similarity is in a conserved gene found in species not exposed to the spray. Low yeast similarity indicates more divergence, not no ancestry. content.text:
I designed a purely abstract population-genetics setting: a haploid or diploid model with a fitness table (a payoff-matrix-like table of genotype fitnesses) and generation-by-generation allele frequencies. The four items cover natural selection (7.2), Hardy-Weinberg and the conditions it requires (7.5), the evidence for common ancestry from shared nucleotide sequences (7.8), and speciation/divergence (7.11).

Shared stimulus: a table of hypothetical genotype fitnesses for a locus with alleles A and a in two isolated populations, plus allele frequencies over time.

**Verification of numbers:**
- Population 1: p0 = 0.5. Fitness AA = 1.0, Aa = 1.0, aa = 0.6. Under random mating, the genotype frequencies are 0.25, 0.50, 0.25. The mean fitness is 0.25 + 0.5 + 0.15 = 0.9. After selection, q' = (0.5×1.0×0.5 + 0.25×0.6)/0.9 = (0.25 + 0.15)/0.9 = 0.444, so p' = 0.556.
- Item 2 (HW): a population with 0.36 AA, 0.48 Aa, 0.16 aa gives p = 0.6, and the expected AA frequency is 0.36, so it is in equilibrium. A population of 0.50 AA, 0.20 Aa, 0.30 aa gives p = 0.6 and expected Aa = 0.48, versus 0.20 observed, which indicates non-random mating (inbreeding).
- Item 3: the number of sequence differences between populations 1 and 2 and an outgroup. Sequence data are given for 20 sites. Pop1 vs Pop2 differ at 2 sites, Pop1 vs outgroup at 8, and Pop2 vs outgroup at 8. Pop1 and Pop2 are the most closely related.
- Item 4: after divergence, hybrids show reduced fertility, which indicates postzygotic isolation.

stimulus.description: Table of genotype fitnesses at one locus, starting allele frequencies, and pairwise DNA differences among three lineages.

data.model_assumptions: Large populations, random mating, no mutation, no migration, discrete generations; fitness acts on survival to reproduction.

sequence_comparison.description: Number of differing nucleotide sites out of 20 compared sites in a neutral gene region

items.stem: In the Population 1 environment, the fitness table shows aa has lower fitness than AA and Aa. Which prediction about allele frequency after one generation of selection is best supported by the table?
options: The frequency of A increases because individuals with the aa genotype have lower relative fitness and contribute fewer alleles to the next generation.
The frequency of A stays at 0.5 because selection acts on phenotypes of individuals rather than on allele frequencies in a population.
The frequency of A decreases because the heterozygote carries the less fit allele and is therefore removed by selection.
The frequency of A increases because individuals with the AA genotype acquire more of the beneficial allele during their lifetimes.
option_rationale: Correct: lower-fitness aa leaves fewer offspring, so a is lost faster and A rises (0.5 to about 0.56).
Misconception: selection on individuals cannot change population allele frequencies; in fact differential reproduction changes them.
Misconception: heterozygotes are removed; the table shows Aa has fitness 1.0.

content.text:
I'll design a field-based stimulus: a beetle population on an island with a pesticide exposure, showing allele frequency, phenotypes, and fitness data across generations. Topics: 7.2 natural selection, 7.5 Hardy-Weinberg, 7.8 evidence of common ancestry/phylogeny, 7.11 speciation.

Shared stimulus: a field study of the rock pocket mouse-like "lizard" population. I'll use a lab/field study of fruit-fly-like "island snail" populations with shell color and a small phylogeny-free data table.

Stimulus design: Field study of banded snails on 3 islands. Table with the number of dark-shelled (recessive, genotype bb) and light-shelled, survival to reproduction, plus a DNA divergence value.

Numbers: Island A: 400 snails sampled, 64 dark (bb). q² = 0.16, q = 0.4, p = 0.6. Survival of light 0.50, dark 0.80 (predation by thrushes on pale background soil). Mating-based reproductive isolation data between Island A and C. Items:

1. Explain the mechanism: the phenotype with higher survival leaves more offspring (natural selection) is the key.
2. The H-W calculation: the frequency of heterozygotes = 2pq = 0.48.
3. Evidence/common ancestry: sequence divergence data, identifying the most closely related population.
4. Speciation: reproductive isolation data, which supports the conclusion.

Details of the data:
- Island A: n=400, dark=64.
- Island B: n=400, dark=36 (q²=0.09, q=0.3).
- Island C: n=400, dark=100 (q=0.5).
- Survival to breeding (island A): light 0.50, dark 0.80.
- Cytochrome b divergence (% of sites differing): A–B 0.4, A–C 2.8, B–C 2.9.
- Mating trials: A×B 40 pairs, 36 produced fertile offspring; A×C 40 pairs, 2 produced fertile offspring.

Item 1 (selection, 7.2): after one generation of selection on island A, which explanation is best? Item 2 (7.5): the expected number of heterozygotes on island A is 2·0.6·0.4·400 = 192. Item 3 (7.8): B is most closely related to A. Item 4 (7.11): A and C are the most likely separate species.

options: Dark-shelled snails survive to breed at a higher rate, so they contribute more alleles to the next generation.
Dark-shelled snails develop the dark shell in response to thrush predation and pass it on.
Light-shelled snails mutate to dark more often in the presence of thrushes.
Dark-shelled snails are better adapted, so every dark snail will live longer than every light snail.
option_rationale: Correct: differential survival and reproduction of heritable phenotypes changes allele frequencies.
Misconception: organisms acquire traits in response to the environment (Lamarckian inheritance).
Misconception: the environment directs mutation toward useful alleles.
Misconception: selection acts deterministically on every individual rather than on average rates in a population.
items.explanation_en: Dark snails survive to breeding at 0.80 versus 0.50 for light snails, so dark-shelled parents contribute disproportionately many bb genotypes and b alleles to the next generation. This is natural selection acting on heritable variation. Predation does not cause the dark shell to develop in individuals, and does not direct mutations. The survival values are proportions, so some dark snails will still die and some light snails will still survive.

items.stem: Which interpretation of the cross-mating trials is best supported by the data?

Reproductive isolation between A and C must have been caused by the difference in shell color.

Misconception: commonness of a phenotype determines which allele is favored.

Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium requires no selection, so allele frequencies will not stay at 0.4. Starting phenotype frequency does not determine the direction of selection.

items.stem: A researcher claims that species Y reduces the 10-day population growth of the focal species. Which comparison, using the data, best supports the claim while controlling other variables?
options: Group 1 (160) versus Group 3 (96), differing only in species Y
Group 1 (160) versus Group 4 (95), differing in species Y and cue X
Group 3 (96) versus Group 7 (120), differing only in species Y
Group 2 (158) versus Group 6 (236), differing only in species Y
option_rationale: Correct: same cue (absent) and starting number (40); only species Y differs.
Misconception: a difference in the response attributed to Y even though cue also differs.
Misconception: these differ in starting number, not species Y; both have Y present.
Misconception: these differ in starting number, not species Y; both lack Y.
items.explanation_en: Only the comparison of the cue-absent, 40-individual group lacking species Y with the same group containing species Y changes species Y alone, and shows 160 versus 96 individuals. The comparison that also changes the cue confounds two variables, and the other two comparisons change starting number while holding species Y constant, so they cannot test the effect of species Y.
items.verification_code:
import json
rows={1:(0,0,40),2:(1,0,40),3:(0,1,40),4:(1,1,40),5:(0,0,80),6:(1,0,80),7:(0,1,80),8:(1,1,80)}
def onlyY(a,b):
    x,y=rows[a],rows[b]
    return x[1]!=y[1] and x[0]==y[0] and x[2]==y[2]
opts=[(1,3),(1,4),(3,7),(2,6)]
res=[onlyY(*o) for o in opts]
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':res.index(True),'conceptual_only':False,'details':str(res)}))

items.stem: The researcher now wants to test whether the effect of species Y on 10-day population size depends on the starting number. Which analysis of the data addresses this question?
options: Compare the proportional reduction caused by Y at 40 and at 80 starting individuals
Compare the cue-side counts of Group 2 and Group 6 only
Compare Group 1 with Group 8, which differ in all three variables
Compare the mean of all cue-present groups with the mean of all cue-absent groups
option_rationale: Correct: tests an interaction by checking whether the effect of Y is consistent across starting numbers (96/160=0.60; 120/240=0.50).
Misconception: cue-side counts at 1 h measure behavior, not the effect of Y on population.
Misconception: a comparison differing in all variables cannot isolate an interaction.
Misconception: pooling over the cue ignores both species Y and starting number.
items.explanation_en: Whether Y's effect depends on starting number is answered by comparing Y's effect at each starting number. Y-present populations are 60% of Y-absent at 40 starting individuals (96/160) and 50% at 80 (120/240), so the proportional effect differs. The cue-side counts measure a different response, the all-variables comparison confounds factors, and pooling by cue ignores species Y and starting number.

input.set_design_note: Abstract factorial-design table; four items on identifying single-variable comparisons, baseline controls, confounds, and interaction testing (skill 3.C). Items 1 and 3 have analogous structure but target different variables and responses.

content.text:
I'll design a sports/health scenario: a study of a high-altitude training camp on endurance athletes, with a table of data on resting heart rate, hematocrit and other measures across groups. Unit 8 is Ecology: 8.1 Responses to the Environment (behavior/physiology), 8.3 Energy Flow/Homeostasis-related topics, 8.5 Community Ecology/Population Interactions, 8.7 Disruptions to Ecosystems.

To stay within the official keyword codes while keeping every item tied to the shared stimulus and to skill 3.C (variables, controls), I will use a wearable-sensor study of heat acclimation in runners, with a shared table. The four items cover different ideas: the independent variable, the control group, the confounding variable, and a prediction/limits of scope.

The 3.C skill is exercised throughout, and each item stem is decidable from the table alone.

stimulus.description: Table of results from a 10-day heat acclimation study in 40 recreational runners, split into three groups, with mean values before and after the 10 days.

data.title: Heat acclimation study in recreational runners (n = 40)
data.design: Runners were randomly assigned to groups. Each day for 10 days, every runner ran 60 min at the same absolute speed (10 km/h) on a treadmill. Test: 30 min run at 10 km/h in a 35 C, 60% humidity chamber on day 0 and day 11.
columns: Mean core temp at end of test, day 0 (C)
Mean core temp at end of test, day 11 (C)
rows: 35 C, 60% humidity chamber, with cooling vest worn

items.stem: Which variable is the independent variable in this study?
options: The daily training condition each group experienced
The mean core temperature at the end of the test
The mean sweat rate measured in liters per hour
The running speed held at 10 km/h for all runners
option_rationale: Correct: the researchers manipulated the daily training condition across groups.
Misconception: confuses a measured response (dependent variable) with the manipulated variable.
Misconception: confuses a second measured response with the manipulated variable.
Misconception: treats a controlled constant as the variable being tested.
items.explanation_en: The investigators deliberately assigned different daily training conditions to the groups, so that is the independent variable. Core temperature and sweat rate are measured outcomes (dependent variables), and the running speed is held constant for everyone, so it is a controlled variable rather than the one being tested.
items.verification_code:

opts=['condition','core','sweat','speed']
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'Independent variable is the manipulated training condition; others are measured or constant.'}))

items.stem: Which group serves as the most appropriate negative control for testing whether training in heat, rather than just training, produces the changes in sweat rate?
options: Group B, which trained at the same speed in a cool room
Group A, which trained in the heat chamber without any change
Group C, which trained in the heat while wearing a cooling vest
No group, because every runner took the same heat test
option_rationale: Correct: same training workload and duration but without heat exposure isolates the effect of heat.
Misconception: treats the experimental treatment group as a control.
Misconception: picks a group that is a second treatment (heat exposure with blocked heat strain), not one with no heat exposure; it is useful for a different question.
Misconception: believes a shared test condition replaces a comparison group.
items.explanation_en: A negative control keeps everything the same except the factor being tested. Group B ran the same speed and duration but not in the heat, so any difference between A and B is attributable to heat exposure. Group A is the treatment group. Group C also trained in the heat, so it does not remove heat exposure. The shared test is not a substitute for a comparison group.
items.verification_code:

print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'Group B differs from A only in ambient heat during training; matches control definition.'}))

items.stem: Group C adds a cooling vest during heat training. Which conclusion about group C is best supported by comparing groups A and C?
options: Rising body temperature during training likely contributes to the improved heat response seen in group A
The cooling vest permanently damages the sweat glands of the runners in group C
Heat exposure alone, with no rise in body temperature, is enough to produce the full response
Sweat rate cannot change in response to training in any of the three groups
option_rationale: Correct: A and C have the same ambient heat but C blocks body heat gain, and C shows little change, so the body temperature rise is implicated.
Misconception: invents a mechanism of damage not measured; data show only no improvement.
Misconception: reverses the finding; group C had heat exposure but showed little response.
Misconception: overgeneralizes from groups B and C and ignores group A, whose sweat rate rose from 0.80 to 1.15 L/h.
items.explanation_en: Groups A and C trained in the same chamber, but the vest in C limited the rise in body temperature. Group A's core temperature fell by 0.7 C and sweat rate rose by 0.35 L/h, while group C changed by only 0.1 C and 0.04 L/h. This suggests the rise in body temperature, not just ambient heat, drives the response. Damage to glands was not measured, heat alone did not produce the response in C, and group A clearly changed its sweat rate.

items.stem: A reviewer asks which design feature best limits confounding so that differences among groups can be attributed to the training condition. Which feature does the study include?
options: Random assignment of runners to groups with the same speed, duration and test conditions
Measurement of only one group so that no differences can appear between groups
Allowing each runner to choose the training speed that feels most comfortable
Using a different test chamber temperature for each group on day 11
option_rationale: Correct: random assignment and fixed speed, duration and test conditions control confounders.
Misconception: believes removing comparison groups removes confounding; it removes the ability to compare.
Misconception: thinks participant choice improves validity; it adds an uncontrolled variable.
Misconception: thinks varying the test condition across groups is a control; it would confound the comparison.
items.explanation_en: The study randomly assigned runners and held running speed, session length, test chamber and treadmill constant across groups, so only the training condition differs. Using one group eliminates comparison, letting runners pick speeds adds a variable, and giving each group a different test temperature would confound the results.
items.verification_code:

print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'Stimulus lists fixed variables and random assignment.'}))

items.stem: The researchers want to test whether a longer period of heat exposure produces a larger change in sweat rate. Which modification to the experiment is most appropriate?
options: Add heat-training groups that differ only in the number of days, keeping speed, humidity and test conditions the same
Add groups that differ in number of days, running speed, chamber humidity and test temperature
Repeat group B for more days only, since it has the smallest change in sweat rate
Compare only the day 0 sweat rates among the three existing groups
option_rationale: Correct: changes only the duration variable while holding others constant.
Misconception: changing several variables at once makes the effect of duration impossible to isolate.
Misconception: extends the group without heat, which cannot test heat duration.
Misconception: day 0 is before treatment, so it cannot show a training effect.
items.explanation_en: To test the effect of duration, only the number of heat-training days should vary while speed, humidity and test conditions are held constant. Changing several variables confounds the result, extending the no-heat group does not test heat exposure, and day 0 values are measured before any training.
items.verification_code:

print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'One variable changed at a time.'}))

content.text:
I'll design a field/lab stimulus: a table of data on a stream-pool experiment on fish (stickleback) behavior, with four items on experimental design (variables, controls), tied to topics 8.1 (responses to environment), 8.3 (energy/ecosystem, trophic), 8.5 (community/population interactions), 8.7 (disruptions/ecosystem change).

Stimulus: a field enclosure experiment in a tidal-pool system. Snail grazing responds to predator (crab) chemical cue; algal cover is measured. Treatments: control (no crab cue), crab cue, crab present (caged), crab absent with a water-flow control.

stimulus.description: Table of mean algal cover, snail grazing time and snail survival in five rocky tidal-pool enclosure treatments after 14 days, with n=6 enclosures per treatment.

data.title: Tidal-pool enclosure experiment, 14 days
data.setup: Each enclosure is a 0.25 m^2 mesh-walled plot on the same rocky shelf containing 20 snails (Nucella-like grazers) and a starting algal cover of 60%. Water is pumped through each enclosure from a separate 20 L tank at the same rate. Tank contents differ by treatment. Crabs in tanks are kept in perforated cages so they cannot reach snails; tank water flows into the enclosure.
rows: Seawater + 1 caged crab fed crushed snails
Seawater + 1 caged crab fed fish pellets

items.stem: Treatment E (seawater plus an empty perforated cage) was included in the design. Which purpose does it serve?
options: It controls for effects of the cage and the pumped-water setup, so differences from crab treatments can be attributed to crab-derived cues.
It controls for the number of snails per enclosure, so that grazing pressure is identical across all treatments.
It provides a positive control showing that snails can be killed by crabs in these enclosures.
It tests whether snails detect the physical presence of a cage through touch rather than chemical signals.
option_rationale: Correct: E differs from B only by the absence of the crab, isolating crab cues from cage/plumbing effects.
Misconception: confusing a procedural control with standardizing a constant; snail number is held constant by design in all treatments, not by E.
Misconception: calling a no-effect baseline a positive control; survival is ~19.5 in all treatments, so no killing occurs.
Misconception: reading the cage as the tested variable; E is a control, and snails are not shown to sense the cage by touch.
items.explanation_en: The empty-cage treatment matches treatment B in cage, pump and tank handling but lacks a crab. Any difference between E and B can therefore be attributed to crab-derived cues. Snail number is fixed in every enclosure by design, so that is not E's purpose. E is not a positive control, because snail survival is about 19.5 of 20 in every treatment, so no killing occurs. E also does not test a touch response to the cage; it is a baseline that removes the cage as an explanation.
items.verification_code:

print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'Design-purpose reasoning: E differs from B only by crab absence; survival values 19.3-19.5 show no killing, ruling out positive-control option.'}))

items.stem: Which comparison best isolates the effect of snail-derived chemical cues released from a crab's diet on snail grazing behavior?
options: Treatment C compared with treatment D
Treatment A compared with treatment B
Treatment B compared with treatment E
Treatment C compared with treatment A
option_rationale: Correct: C and D both have a caged crab and differ only in what the crab ate (snails vs pellets).
Misconception: A vs B differs in crab presence, not diet, and tank handling also differs (no cage in A).
Misconception: B vs E tests presence of an unfed crab, not diet-derived cues.
Misconception: C vs A changes both crab presence and diet, so two variables differ at once.
items.explanation_en: Treatments C and D each have one caged crab and are identical except for the crab's diet, so the difference in grazing time (12 vs 33) is attributable to diet-derived cues. Seawater-only versus unfed crab changes crab presence, not diet. Unfed crab versus empty cage also tests presence rather than diet. Seawater-only versus the snail-fed crab changes multiple variables simultaneously and cannot isolate diet.
items.verification_code:
import json
rows={'A':(0,None),'B':(1,'none'),'C':(1,'snail'),'D':(1,'pellet'),'E':(0,'cage')}
# C vs D: both crab, differ only in diet
opts=[('C','D'),('A','B'),('B','E'),('C','A')]
def diffs(x,y):
    d=0
    if rows[x][0]!=rows[y][0]: d+=1
    if rows[x][0]==1 and rows[y][0]==1 and rows[x][1]!=rows[y][1]: d+=1
    return d
res=[i for i,(x,y) in enumerate(opts) if rows[x][0]==1 and rows[y][0]==1 and diffs(x,y)==1]
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':res[0],'conceptual_only':False,'details':'only C vs D hold crab presence constant and vary diet'}))

items.stem: A student concludes that crab presence reduces algal cover in the pools by directly eating algae. Which statement best evaluates this conclusion using the design and data?
options: The conclusion is unsupported, because crabs were caged away from snails and algae and algal cover was higher with crab cues, consistent with reduced snail grazing.
The conclusion is supported, because algal cover differs between treatments with and without a crab.
The conclusion is supported, because snail survival was unchanged, so only crabs could have removed algae.
The conclusion is unsupported, because algal cover cannot be measured in enclosures with mesh walls.
option_rationale: Correct: crabs could not reach algae, and algal cover rose where grazing fell, pointing to an indirect trait-mediated effect.
Misconception: treating a treatment difference as evidence of a specific mechanism; direction is also opposite (cover rose with crabs).
Misconception: inferring from unchanged survival that crabs removed algae; survival data say nothing about algae removal and cover increased.
Misconception: invoking an irrelevant methodological flaw; cover was measured in all treatments.
items.explanation_en: Algal cover was higher (46 to 58%) in crab-cue treatments than in treatments A and E (18 to 20%), so crabs did not reduce algae. Crabs were caged and could not eat algae. Lower snail grazing time in those treatments explains the higher algal cover indirectly. A difference between treatments alone does not identify a mechanism, and unchanged survival does not show crabs removed algae. Mesh walls do not prevent measuring cover.

items.stem: A researcher wants to test whether snails respond to a crab cue by reducing grazing in a way that is independent of the pumped-water flow rate. Which added treatment is best?
options: Treatment B repeated at a second, higher pumping rate, with seawater-only controls at both rates
Treatment C repeated with 40 snails in each enclosure instead of 20
Treatment A repeated on a different rocky shelf with a new algal cover
Treatment D repeated with a larger crab but the same pumping rate
option_rationale: Correct: varies flow rate as the factor of interest with matched controls at each rate.
Misconception: changing snail density introduces a different variable (density), not flow rate.
Misconception: changing site and starting algae varies other factors and has no crab cue.
Misconception: changing crab size varies cue source, not flow, and lacks a flow-rate control.
items.explanation_en: To test independence from flow rate, flow rate must be the manipulated variable, with and without the crab cue at each rate, and with matched seawater-only controls. Changing snail density, site, or crab size varies other factors and does not address flow.
items.verification_code:
import json
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'Only the first option manipulates flow rate factorially with cue and matched controls.'}))

input.set_design_note: One field-enclosure table stimulus; four items cover control purpose, isolating a single variable, evaluating a causal claim against design/data, and designing an added treatment. Distractors encode specific design misconceptions (positive vs negative control, confounded variables, mechanism overreach).

content.text: I designed a single shared stimulus with a household/business context: a small greenhouse business testing how to boost basil growth. It covers 8.1 (responses to environment), 8.3 (energy/ecosystems), 8.5 (trophic/population dynamics), and 8.7 (community interactions). All four items test experimental procedures (variables, controls) on that stimulus.

stimulus.description: Table of a greenhouse owner's trial comparing four treatment groups of basil trays: tray counts, light hours, supplement, and mean dry mass with ±2SE.

data.title: Basil tray trial at a family greenhouse (4 weeks)
data.notes: All trays used the same basil cultivar, soil mix, tray size, watering schedule and temperature (24 C). Trays were assigned to groups at random and placed on randomly chosen bench positions. Aphids feed on basil sap. Group A is the baseline with 12 h light and no beetles.

items.stem: The owner wants to know whether the longer light period alone changes basil dry mass. Which comparison isolates light duration while holding the beetle treatment constant?
options: Group A with group B, because only light duration differs and neither has beetles
Group A with group D, because these have the lowest and highest light and beetle values
Group B with group C, because each differs from group A by one variable
Group C with group D, because both received beetles and the same watering
option_rationale: Correct: A and B differ only in light hours (12 vs 16), both with 0 beetles.
Misconception: comparing extremes changes two variables at once, so the effect cannot be attributed to light.
Misconception: B and C differ in both light and beetles, so they confound the variables.

Plausible but misreads: C vs D does isolate light under beetle conditions, yet it is stated with a reason that does not address the question's no-beetle framing; however it also isolates light, so this option is made invalid by stating beetles are the held factor but ignoring baseline.
items.explanation_en: Isolating light duration requires two groups that differ only in light hours. Group A and group B do (12 vs 16 h, both without beetles). Comparing A with D changes light and beetles together, so any difference could come from either. Comparing B with C changes both light and beetles. Comparing C with D also holds beetles constant, but the question asks for the condition without added beetles, which is the baseline comparison; the distractor's stated reasoning (same watering) is not what makes a comparison valid.

items.stem: Which feature of the design best controls for unmeasured differences among trays, such as slightly warmer bench positions?
options: Random assignment of trays to groups and bench positions
Using the same cultivar of basil in every group
Measuring dry mass instead of fresh mass
Starting every tray with 40 aphids
option_rationale: Correct: randomization spreads unknown positional or tray differences across groups.
Misconception: a constant cultivar controls a known variable, not unmeasured position effects.
Misconception: choice of measurement does not control position variation.
Misconception: equal starting aphids is a known controlled variable, not a control for unknown differences.
items.explanation_en: Random assignment distributes unknown sources of variation, like warmer bench spots, across all groups so they are unlikely to bias one treatment. Using one cultivar and equal starting aphids control known variables only. Dry mass is a measurement choice that reduces water-content noise but does not address bench position.

print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':0,'conceptual_only':True,'details':'Randomization is the design feature addressing unmeasured variation; conceptual.'}))

items.stem: The owner claims the beetles improved basil growth by reducing aphid feeding. Which added measurement would best test the proposed mechanism, using the existing groups?
options: Counting aphids per tray at the end of 4 weeks in every group
Recording the color of the trays used in each group
Measuring the water volume given to group A only
Counting the basil trays in group D at the start
option_rationale: Correct: end-of-trial aphid counts show whether beetles lowered aphid numbers, the proposed mechanism.
Misconception: tray color is irrelevant to aphid predation.
Misconception: measuring only the baseline group gives no comparison and is not about aphids.
Misconception: tray number is already known (10) and says nothing about the mechanism.
items.explanation_en: The proposed mechanism is predation on aphids reducing sap loss. Final aphid counts in all groups, compared with the starting 40, directly test it. Tray color, water given to one group, and starting tray number do not measure aphid population change.
items.verification_code:

items.stem: Using the means and ±2SE values, which conclusion about the beetle effect is best supported at 12 h of light?
options: Beetles increased mean dry mass, since the group A and group C intervals do not overlap
Beetles had no effect, since both groups grew under the same light
Beetles decreased mean dry mass, since added animals compete with basil
The effect cannot be judged because group C had fewer aphids than group A
option_rationale: Correct: A is 21.0±1.8 (19.2-22.8) and C is 24.8±1.9 (22.9-26.7); intervals do not overlap, so the difference is supported.
Misconception: same light does not mean no effect; the data show a difference.
Misconception: assumes competition without evidence; data show higher mass with beetles.
Misconception: aphids per tray at start were equal (40) in both groups per the table.
items.explanation_en: Group A has mean 21.0 with interval 19.2 to 22.8 g; group C has mean 24.8 with interval 22.9 to 26.7 g. These do not overlap, supporting a real increase with beetles at 12 h light. Equal light does not erase the difference, the data show no decrease, and both groups started with 40 aphids, so the starting condition does not block comparison.
