content.text: I'll design a short FRQ (4 points) on organism responses to the environment (a plant phototropism lab with a data table), testing identification of experimental variables and controls.

input.title: Blue Light and Seedling Bending in Oat Coleoptiles

stimulus.description: Table of mean coleoptile bending angle after 6 hours for four treatment groups of oat seedlings, each with n = 30 seedlings.

data.setup: Oat (Avena sativa) seedlings were grown in complete darkness for 4 days. Coleoptile tips are the region that detects light. Seedlings were then placed in identical growth chambers at 22 degrees C with equal moisture and exposed for 6 hours to light from one side only. Bending angle is measured from vertical (0 degrees = no bending toward the light).
columns: Light intensity (umol photons per m2 per s)
rows: Tip covered with opaque foil cap
Foil cap on region below tip only, tip exposed

units.intensity: umol photons per m2 per s

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in the experiment using the data in the table.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: the treatment/light condition (presence of blue light from one side and which part of the seedling is covered). Dependent variable: the mean bending angle toward the light (degrees).

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
required_elements: Independent variable: light exposure and/or which region is covered (treatment)
Dependent variable: bending angle toward light
common_errors: Naming light intensity as the independent variable even though it is constant at 20 or 0
Naming the seedling as the dependent variable
alt_solutions: Independent variable stated as presence versus absence of blue light and tip covered versus uncovered

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the negative control group and explain what it allows the researchers to conclude about the bending observed in group 1.
parts.model_answer: Group 2 (intact seedlings in darkness) is the negative control. Its near-zero bending shows that bending in group 1 is caused by the one-sided light and not by handling, growth, or the chamber conditions alone.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies group 2 and links it to attributing bending to light
required_elements: Bending in group 1 is due to the light rather than other factors
common_errors: Choosing group 3 as the negative control

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Describe what the comparison of groups 1, 3, and 4 indicates about which part of the coleoptile detects the light stimulus.
parts.model_answer: Covering the tip (group 3) eliminates bending, while covering only the region below the tip (group 4) leaves bending essentially the same as group 1 (36 vs 38 degrees, error ranges overlap). So the tip detects the light.

rubric_rows.criterion: Concludes the tip is the light-sensing region using the data comparison
required_elements: Tip covered gives little or no bending (about 3 degrees)
Tip exposed gives bending similar to intact (about 36 vs 38) so tip detects light
common_errors: Concluding the region below the tip detects light

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A student proposes adding a fifth group in which the tip is covered with a clear, transparent cap instead of opaque foil. Predict the result and justify why this group would be a useful control for the foil cap in group 3.
parts.model_answer: Predict bending similar to group 1 (about 38 degrees). The clear cap lets light reach the tip but includes the physical presence of a cap, so if bending still occurs, the loss of bending in group 3 is due to blocking light and not to the cap itself (weight, handling, or damage).

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts bending comparable to group 1 and justifies as controlling for the cap's physical effect versus light blocking
required_elements: Prediction: substantial bending, similar to group 1
Justification: controls for effects of the cap other than blocking light
common_errors: Justifying only as a larger sample size

parts.label: a

common_errors: Naming temperature or seedling age as the variable

If the cap itself prevented bending, Group 3 would show little bending like Group 2; instead it bends about 40 degrees, so blocking light, not the cap, prevents bending.

content.text: I'll design a short FRQ (4 points) on Unit 8 topic 8.1 (responses to the environment: phototropism/plant tropisms) in a household/business context: a greenhouse business owner deciding on LED lighting for basil seedlings. The stimulus is a table of seedling bending angles.

input.title: Window-Sill Herb Business: Do Basil Seedlings Bend Toward Light?

stimulus.description: Table of mean stem bending angle (degrees from vertical) of basil seedlings after 48 hours under three setups, with n=20 seedlings per group and ±2 SE.

data.intro: A small business sells potted basil. The owner wants to decide whether to buy a one-sided LED strip for shelves or an overhead LED panel. She sets up trays of 20 identical basil seedlings (same age, soil, water, and 22 degrees C) in light-tight boxes for 48 hours. Bending angle is measured from vertical; positive means bending toward the side where the light source was placed.
rows: One-sided blue LED strip on left wall
One-sided red LED strip on left wall
Overhead panel (blue light from directly above)
data.units: degrees from vertical
data.notes: All boxes kept at 22 degrees C; all seedlings watered equally.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in the owner's investigation.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: the light treatment (color and direction of the light source). Dependent variable: the stem bending angle of the seedlings (degrees from vertical).

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
common_errors: Lists temperature or water as the independent variable

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the group that serves as the negative control and explain what it allows the owner to conclude about the bending seen in the other groups.
parts.model_answer: Group 4 (dark box, no light) is the negative control. Because seedlings did not bend without light, bending in other groups can be attributed to the light treatment rather than to handling, gravity, or other conditions of the box.

rubric_rows.criterion: Names the no-light group and links it to attributing bending to light
required_elements: Identifies Group 4 / dark box / no light
States that bending in other groups is due to light (not other factors) because the control shows no bending
common_errors: Names the overhead group as the negative control
Says the control is the group with the greatest bending

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the data, state which light treatment caused the greatest bending toward the light source, and justify that the difference between the blue one-sided group and the red one-sided group is likely real.
parts.model_answer: One-sided blue light (38.0 degrees) caused the greatest bending. Its interval (34.0 to 42.0) does not overlap the red one-sided interval (3.0 to 9.0), so the difference is likely real, indicating blue light is more effective at producing the response.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies blue one-sided and uses non-overlapping ±2 SE intervals as justification
required_elements: Identifies one-sided blue LED as greatest bending (about 38 degrees)
Cites non-overlapping ±2 SE intervals (34-42 vs 3-9) or the large difference relative to error
optional_phrases: blue light is more effective than red
common_errors: Claims significance without referencing error bars

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The owner wants all plants on a shelf to grow straight up rather than leaning. Predict which purchase (one-sided LED strip or overhead panel) she should make, and justify your prediction using the data and the role of light direction in the plant's response.
parts.model_answer: She should buy the overhead panel. Overhead blue light gave about 1 degree of bending, indistinguishable from the dark control (intervals overlap), because light arriving evenly from above does not create a lateral difference in light, so auxin is not redistributed to one side and the stems do not bend (no phototropism toward a side).

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts overhead panel and justifies with data and light direction/auxin or even illumination
required_elements: Cites near-zero bending (about 1 degree, similar to dark control) AND explains that even/overhead light gives no lateral light gradient or uneven auxin distribution
common_errors: Chooses one-sided strip because it gave the largest response
Gives data only with no mechanism

content.text:
I designed a single-price monopoly (a local ferry operator) with linear demand and constant marginal cost. Item 1 asks for the profit-maximizing outcome, and item 2 asks about the deadweight loss relative to the efficient outcome (topic 4.4 on efficiency and DWL).

Numbers: P = 100 − 2Q, so MR = 100 − 4Q. MC = ATC = 20. Setting MR = MC gives Q = 20 and P = 60. Profit = (60 − 20) × 20 = 800. Efficient Q = 40 (where P = MC = 20). DWL = 0.5 × (60 − 20) × (40 − 20) = 400.

stimulus.description: Linear demand, marginal revenue and flat marginal cost/average total cost curves for a single-price ferry operator.

data.notes: The operator is the only ferry service and must charge every rider the same price.

items.stem: Based on the graph, which of the following describes the profit-maximizing choice of the ferry operator and the resulting economic profit?
options: Produce 20 crossings, charge $60, and earn economic profit of $800
Produce 40 crossings, charge $20, and earn economic profit of $0
Produce 20 crossings, charge $20, and earn economic profit of $0
Produce 25 crossings, charge $50, and earn economic profit of $750
Produce 20 crossings, charge $60, and earn economic profit of $1,200
option_rationale: Correct: MR = MC at Q = 20; price from demand is $60; profit = (60-20)*20 = $800.
Misconception: monopolist produces where P = MC like a perfectly competitive firm.
Misconception: reads the price at the MR = MC quantity off the MC curve instead of the demand curve.
Misconception: uses the quantity where MR = 0 (revenue maximization) instead of MR = MC.
Misconception: computes profit as price times quantity minus marginal cost only once, or uses revenue 60*20 = 1,200 without subtracting cost.

items.stem: Based on the graph, compared with the efficient outcome, the monopoly outcome results in a deadweight loss of how much, and why does it occur?
options: $400, because the operator restricts output to where MR = MC, so crossings valued above their marginal cost go unproduced
$400, because the operator earns positive economic profit, which is itself a loss to society

$200, because the operator sets price equal to marginal revenue and overcharges riders
$0, because the operator's profit is a transfer from riders and no value is lost
option_rationale: Correct: DWL = 0.5*(60-20)*(40-20) = $400; it arises because output of 20 is below the efficient 40 even though riders value those extra crossings above $20.
Right number but wrong reasoning: treats profit itself as the source of the loss rather than the unproduced mutually beneficial trades.
Misconception: confuses the profit rectangle (a transfer, $800) with deadweight loss.
Misconception: forgets the one-half in the triangle formula or misidentifies the base, and ties the loss to MR rather than to underproduction.
Misconception: believes that a transfer from consumers to the producer means no efficiency loss at all.

content.text:
I designed a lab/field setting: a university-run radiation-detector calibration lab that is the sole provider of certified calibration, with a linear demand curve and constant MC. Item 1 asks for the profit-maximizing outcome. Item 2 asks about perfect price discrimination, topic 4.4 (efficiency/deadweight loss).

Numbers: P = 120 − 2Q, so MR = 120 − 4Q. MC = 20, so Q = 25 and P = 70. Profit = (70 − 20) × 25 = 1250 with zero fixed cost. Efficient Q = 50 (where P = MC), so DWL = 0.5 × 25 × 50 = 625. Consumer surplus at the monopoly outcome = 0.5 × 25 × 50 = 625.

Option sets: for item 1, the key is Q = 25 and P = 70. The distractors are Q = 25 with P = 20 (price set at MC), Q = 30 with P = 60 (MR = P intersection error), Q = 50 with P = 20 (the competitive outcome), and Q = 25 with P = 120 (the vertical intercept). Item 2 asks why a perfectly price-discriminating lab would produce the efficient quantity.

stimulus.description: Linear demand curve for certified calibration runs at a university radiation lab that is the only certified provider, with a horizontal marginal cost line at $20 and a marginal revenue curve below demand.

data.notes: Fixed costs are zero, so ATC equals MC. The lab sells every run at one single price unless stated otherwise. Lab is a single seller with no close substitutes.

items.stem: Based on the graph, which outcome results when the lab, as a single-price monopolist, maximizes profit?
options: It produces 25 runs per month and charges $70 per run.
It produces 25 runs per month and charges $20 per run.
It produces 30 runs per month and charges $60 per run.
It produces 50 runs per month and charges $20 per run.
It produces 25 runs per month and charges $120 per run.
option_rationale: Correct: MR = MC gives 120 - 4Q = 20, so Q = 25; the price is read from demand: 120 - 50 = 70.
Misconception: sets quantity at MR = MC but then charges the MC value instead of reading the price from the demand curve.
Misconception: finds the quantity where MR hits zero (Q = 30) or confuses revenue maximization with profit maximization.
Misconception: monopolist produces where P = MC, as a perfectly competitive firm would.
Misconception: reads the price from the vertical intercept of demand rather than at the chosen quantity.
items.explanation_en: A profit-maximizing monopolist produces where MR = MC: 120 - 4Q = 20, so Q = 25. It then charges the highest price consumers will pay for that quantity, found on the demand curve: P = 120 - 2(25) = $70. Charging the marginal cost ignores that price comes from demand, not from MC. Producing where MR equals zero maximizes revenue, not profit, because MC is positive. Producing where price equals MC is the competitive outcome, which a single-price monopolist avoids because it would give up profit. Charging the vertical intercept price would not sell 25 runs.

import sympy as sp
Q=sp.symbols('Q')
q=sp.solve(120-4*Q-20,Q)[0]
p=120-2*q
opts=[(25,70),(25,20),(30,60),(50,20),(25,120)]
idx=opts.index((q,p))
print(json.dumps({'computed_key_index':idx,'conceptual_only':False,'details':f'Q={q},P={p}'}))

items.stem: Suppose the lab could instead charge each customer exactly the maximum that customer is willing to pay for each run (perfect price discrimination). Compared with the single-price outcome shown, which statement best explains the result?
options: Output rises to 50 runs because the lab keeps producing until the price of the last run equals its marginal cost, which eliminates the deadweight loss.
Output stays at 25 runs because the lab still produces where the original MR equals MC, so the deadweight loss is unchanged.
Output rises to 50 runs and consumers gain, because the lab must lower its price to $20 on every run it sells.
Output falls below 25 runs because the lab can raise the price on its most eager customers and sell fewer runs.
Output rises to 60 runs because the lab keeps selling until the demand curve reaches a price of zero.
option_rationale: Correct: with perfect discrimination, the extra revenue from each additional run is the price on demand, so MR = D and output expands to where P = MC (Q = 50); no deadweight loss remains, and the lab captures all surplus.
Misconception: believes the original MR curve still applies even when each unit is sold at its own price.
Misconception: assumes efficiency implies a single competitive price and that consumers gain; in fact the lab captures all consumer surplus.
Misconception: thinks price discrimination always reduces output as a monopoly restricts quantity.
Misconception: ignores marginal cost and extends output to where demand reaches zero price.
items.explanation_en: With perfect price discrimination, selling one more run does not require lowering the price on earlier runs, so marginal revenue equals the demand price. The lab expands output until demand equals MC: 120 - 2Q = 20, so Q = 50. The deadweight loss of 0.5 x 25 x 50 = $625 under single pricing disappears because every run valued above its cost is produced. Keeping output at 25 uses a marginal revenue curve that no longer applies. Lowering the price to $20 for everyone would be the competitive result, not discrimination, and the lab instead captures all consumer surplus. Reducing output would forgo profitable sales. Producing to 60 runs would mean selling units that cost $20 to produce for less than $20.

content.text:
I'll design a short FRQ (4 points) on behavioral responses to the environment (Unit 8, Topic 8.1) in a sports/technology context: heat acclimation and sweat/behavior response, with a focus on experimental procedures (variables, controls).

I chose a wearable-sensor study of heart rate and avoidance of heat in zebrafish-like animals? A sports context is more natural: runners in a heat chamber. I'm keeping it tied to 8.1: responses to environmental change (temperature) via physiological/behavioral responses and homeostasis.

input.title: Wearable Sensors and Heat Responses in Trail Runners
input.stimulus: {"kind":"table","description":"Table of mean core body temperature, sweat rate, and heart rate after 30 minutes of running at the same pace in three environmental conditions, for two groups of runners.","data":{"title":"Responses after 30 min running at 10 km/h (mean of 12 runners per group, ±2SE)","columns":["Group","Chamber temperature (°C)","Mean sweat rate (mL/min)","Mean core temperature (°C)","Mean heart rate (beats/min)"],"rows":[["Group 1: no heat training","20","8.0 ± 1.2","37.8 ± 0.2","148 ± 6"],["Group 1: no heat training","35","14.0 ± 1.8","38.9 ± 0.3","171 ± 7"],["Group 2: 10 days heat training","20","8.4 ± 1.3","37.7 ± 0.2","146 ± 6"],["Group 2: 10 days heat training","35","21.0 ± 2.0","38.1 ± 0.2","152 ± 6"]],"design_notes":"Humidity held at 40% in all trials; runners were matched for age, body mass and fitness; chamber order randomized; wearable sensors recorded core temperature (ingestible capsule) and heart rate (chest strap).","sensor_note":"Sensors were identical for both groups."}

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and one dependent variable in the comparison of Group 1 and Group 2 at 35°C.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: heat training (10 days of heat training vs. none) [chamber temperature is also acceptable as a second independent variable]. Dependent variable: any of sweat rate, core body temperature, or heart rate.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies an independent variable and a measured dependent variable
required_elements: Independent variable: heat training status (or chamber temperature)
Dependent variable: sweat rate OR core temperature OR heart rate
alt_solutions: Independent variable: chamber temperature; dependent variable: core temperature
common_errors: Naming sweat rate as the independent variable
Naming only a controlled variable such as humidity

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify two variables that were controlled in this investigation and explain why controlling one of them is necessary for a valid comparison of the two groups.
parts.model_answer: Controlled variables: humidity (40%), running pace (10 km/h), duration (30 min), matched age/body mass/fitness, and identical sensors. Controlling one, for example pace, is necessary because a faster pace would raise heat production and core temperature in one group regardless of heat training, confounding the effect of training.

rubric_rows.criterion: Names two controlled variables from the design AND explains why controlling one prevents a confounding effect
required_elements: Two valid controlled variables (e.g., humidity, pace, duration, fitness matching, sensor type)
Explanation that an uncontrolled difference could alter the dependent variable and be mistaken for the effect of heat training
alt_solutions: Humidity: higher humidity reduces sweat evaporation and would raise core temperature independent of training

parts.label: c

content.text:
I designed a purely abstract setting: a monopolist with a linear demand and a constant marginal cost, no real-world context. Topic 4.2 covers MR=MC pricing and deadweight loss. Topic 4.4 covers price discrimination, which here is perfect price discrimination.

Stimulus numbers: P = 100 - 2Q, MC = ATC = 20.

- **Single-price monopoly:** MR = 100 - 4Q. Setting MR = MC gives Q = 20 and P = 60. Profit is (60 - 20) × 20 = 800.
- **Efficient quantity:** P = MC gives Q = 40.
- **Deadweight loss:** 0.5 × (60 - 20) × (40 - 20) = 400.
- **Perfect price discrimination:** Q = 40, profit = 0.5 × 80 × 40 = 1600, consumer surplus = 0, DWL = 0.

Item 1 asks why the single-price monopolist produces 20 rather than 40. Item 2 asks what happens to output and surplus under perfect price discrimination.

stimulus.description: Linear demand curve P = 100 - 2Q with a constant marginal cost and average total cost line at 20. Marginal revenue is MR = 100 - 4Q. Axes: quantity 0 to 50 units, price 0 to 100 dollars.

data.firm: Single seller facing the demand curve above; no fixed costs

items.stem: A single-price monopolist faces the demand, marginal revenue, and cost curves shown. Which statement best explains why it produces 20 units rather than the 40 units a perfectly competitive industry would produce?
options: At 20 units, marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and the price of 60 on the demand curve exceeds marginal cost, so output is below the efficient level.
At 20 units, price equals marginal cost, which maximizes profit, and 40 units would force price below average total cost.
At 20 units, total revenue is maximized because marginal revenue is positive, so the firm stops there.
At 20 units, price equals average total cost, so the firm earns zero economic profit and has no incentive to expand.
At 20 units, marginal revenue equals price, because a monopolist sells each additional unit at the same price as the previous one.
option_rationale: Correct: MR=MC at Q=20 gives P=60 above MC=20, so output is less than the P=MC quantity of 40.
Misconception: believing monopolists set P=MC; also 40 units would price at 20 = ATC, not below it.
Misconception: confusing revenue maximization with profit maximization; revenue is maximized where MR=0 (Q=25).
Misconception: thinking monopoly profit is zero; at Q=20 ATC=20 and P=60, so profit is 800.
Misconception: believing MR=P for a monopolist; MR lies below demand because the price cut applies to all units.
items.explanation_en: MR = 100 - 4Q equals MC = 20 at Q = 20, and the demand curve gives P = 60, which is above MC. Because price exceeds marginal cost, some mutually beneficial units between 20 and 40 go unproduced. The P=MC option is wrong because a monopolist does not price at marginal cost. The revenue-maximizing option is wrong because revenue peaks at Q=25 where MR=0, and profit maximization uses MR=MC. The zero-profit option is wrong because P=60 exceeds ATC=20. The MR equals price option is wrong because MR is below price for a single-price monopolist.

items.stem: Suppose the same firm could perfectly price discriminate, charging each buyer the maximum that buyer is willing to pay. Compared with the single-price outcome, which result occurs?
options: Output rises to 40 units, consumer surplus falls to zero, and deadweight loss is eliminated, as profit rises from 800 to 1600.
Output stays at 20 units, consumer surplus falls to zero, and profit rises because each of the 20 units sells at a higher price.
Output rises to 40 units, consumer surplus is unchanged, and profit rises because more units are sold at the price of 60.
Output rises to 40 units, deadweight loss is eliminated, and profit stays at 800 because costs rise with output.
Output falls below 20 units because the firm raises prices to the highest buyers and ignores low-value buyers.
option_rationale: Correct: each unit up to Q=40 sells at its demand price, so MR=demand, output is where P=MC (40), CS=0, DWL=0, profit=0.5*80*40=1600.
Misconception: assuming the discriminator keeps the single-price quantity; extra buyers with value above MC are now served.
Misconception: thinking all units still sell at 60 and consumer surplus is untouched; the 60 price would not sell 40 units.
Misconception: believing profit is unchanged; MC and ATC are constant at 20, so costs do not eat the gain.
Misconception: believing discrimination restricts output more; it expands output to the efficient level.
items.explanation_en: With perfect price discrimination, marginal revenue equals the demand price, so the firm produces until P = MC = 20, which gives Q = 40. All surplus above cost goes to the firm: profit = 0.5 x (100-20) x 40 = 1600 versus 800 before. Consumer surplus is zero and deadweight loss is eliminated. The option keeping output at 20 is wrong because buyers valuing units above 20 are now served. The option with unchanged consumer surplus is wrong because 40 units cannot all sell at 60. The option with profit staying at 800 is wrong because average cost is constant at 20. The option with falling output is wrong because output expands.

content.text:
I designed a field setting: a single-vendor ferry service on an island, with a linear demand curve and constant marginal cost. Item 1 tests the profit-maximizing choice (MR=MC) and Item 2 tests the efficiency comparison from topic 4.4.

Numbers: P = 120 - 2Q, so MR = 120 - 4Q. MC = 20 (constant). Monopoly: 120 - 4Q = 20, so Q = 25 and P = 70. Efficient: 120 - 2Q = 20, so Q = 50 and P = 20. DWL = 0.5 × (70 - 20) × (50 - 25) = 625. The fixed cost of 300 makes ATC = 20 + 300/Q, so profit at the monopoly point = (70 - 20) × 25 - 300 = 950.

stimulus.description: Linear demand for ferry trips with a downward-sloping marginal revenue curve and a horizontal marginal cost line at $20, for a single-operator island ferry.

data.setting: Field study: the only ferry operator serving a remote island
data.notes: Operator charges one price to all riders. Average total cost = 20 + 300/Q.

items.stem: Based on the graph, which of the following explains how the ferry operator determines the profit-maximizing quantity and price?
options: Produce 25 trips, where MR equals MC, and charge $70, the price on the demand curve at that quantity
Produce 50 trips, where demand equals MC, and charge $20, the price on the demand curve at that quantity
Produce 25 trips, where MR equals MC, and charge $20, the marginal cost at that quantity
Produce 30 trips, where MR equals zero, and charge $60, the price on the demand curve at that quantity
Produce 40 trips, where demand equals MR, and charge $40, the price on the demand curve at that quantity
option_rationale: Correct: MR=MC gives Q=25, and the price is read from demand: 120-50=70.
Misconception: applying the perfectly competitive rule P=MC; a monopolist with downward-sloping demand does not do this.
Misconception: finding Q with MR=MC but then pricing at MC instead of reading the price off the demand curve.
Misconception: maximizing revenue (MR=0) rather than profit; ignores marginal cost.
Misconception: believing demand and MR intersect; they only meet at the vertical intercept (Q=0).
items.explanation_en: The operator maximizes profit where MR = MC: 120 - 4Q = 20, so Q = 25. The highest price consumers will pay for 25 trips is on the demand curve: P = 120 - 2(25) = $70. Producing 50 trips with P = MC is the competitive outcome, not the monopoly choice. Charging marginal cost at Q = 25 ignores that the monopolist can price off demand. Producing 30 trips where MR = 0 maximizes revenue, not profit, because MC is positive. Producing 40 trips where demand equals MR is impossible, as those curves do not intersect at a positive quantity.

Misconception: using the full rectangle (50*25) and omitting the one-half for a triangle.
Misconception: believing a monopolist sets P=MC; actually P=70 exceeds MC=20.
Misconception: equating positive profit with efficiency; efficiency requires P=MC.
items.explanation_en: The efficient quantity is where demand meets MC: 120 - 2Q = 20, so Q = 50. The operator provides only 25 trips, charging $70 against a marginal cost of $20, so output is too low. The deadweight loss is the triangle with base 50 - 25 = 25 and height 70 - 20 = 50: 0.5 x 25 x 50 = $625. Overproduction is wrong because output is restricted. The $1,250 figure forgets the one-half of the triangle formula. Price does not equal marginal cost for the monopolist. Positive profit (($70 - $40) x 25 = $750 after the fixed cost, or ($70 - $20) x 25 - $300 = $950 on a marginal-cost basis) does not make the outcome efficient, since P exceeds MC.

content.text:
I designed a shared stimulus: a monopolist (a local ferry company) with linear demand and constant MC, with a payoff on a perfectly price-discriminating alternative. Topic 4.2 covers the monopoly's pricing and output decisions; topic 4.4 covers the welfare effects.

Numbers: demand P = 100 − 2Q, so MR = 100 − 4Q. MC = ATC = 20 (constant).
- Single-price monopoly: MR = MC gives 100 − 4Q = 20, so Q = 20 and P = 60. Profit = (60 − 20) × 20 = 800.
- Competitive/efficient output: 100 − 2Q = 20 gives Q = 40. Deadweight loss = 0.5 × (60 − 20) × (40 − 20) = 400.
- Consumer surplus at the monopoly price = 0.5 × (100 − 60) × 20 = 400.

Item 1 (4.2) asks why the monopolist produces 20 and not 40. Item 2 (4.4) asks what a perfectly price-discriminating monopolist would do, where output is 40 and consumer surplus is 0.

stimulus.description: Linear demand, marginal revenue and flat marginal/average total cost curves for a single-price monopoly ferry operator. Quantity in crossings per day, price in dollars per crossing.

data.notes: The firm currently charges one price to all riders.

items.stem: Based on the graph, the ferry operator charges one price to all riders. Which statement best explains why it chooses 20 crossings per day rather than 40?
options: Beyond 20 crossings, marginal revenue is below the marginal cost of $20, so each added crossing lowers profit.
Beyond 20 crossings, the price falls below the average total cost of $20, so the firm would take a loss on every crossing.
At 20 crossings, the demand price equals marginal cost, so allocative efficiency is achieved.
At 20 crossings, total revenue reaches its maximum, so profit is also maximized.
At 20 crossings, average total cost is at its minimum, so the firm is producing at the efficient scale.
option_rationale: Correct: profit maximization requires MR = MC; at Q = 20, MR = 20 = MC and beyond that MR < MC.
Misconception: confuses price with MR; at Q = 40 price equals ATC = 20, so there is no loss per unit, and the reason to stop at 20 is MR < MC.
Misconception: applies the competitive P = MC rule; at Q = 20, P = 60 which exceeds MC = 20.
Misconception: equates revenue maximization with profit maximization; revenue peaks where MR = 0 at Q = 25.
Misconception: ATC is constant at 20, so there is no minimum point that explains the choice; the rule is MR = MC.
items.explanation_en: The monopolist maximizes profit where MR = MC. At 20 crossings MR = 100 - 80 = 20, equal to MC. Beyond 20, MR falls below MC because the firm must cut the price on all units to sell more, so each extra crossing adds less revenue than cost. The claim that price falls below ATC is wrong: at 40 crossings price equals ATC, and the firm would not lose money on each crossing. P = MC is not satisfied at 20 (price is 60). Revenue is maximized at 25 crossings where MR = 0, not at 20. ATC is constant at 20 and has no minimum that drives the choice.

options: Output would rise to 40 crossings, deadweight loss would fall from $400 to $0, and consumer surplus would fall from $400 to $0.
Output would stay at 20 crossings, and the operator's profit would rise because the price rises above $60.
Output would rise to 40 crossings, and consumer surplus would rise because the average price paid falls to $20.
Output would fall below 20 crossings because the operator restricts quantity to raise the price for each rider.
Output would rise to 40 crossings, and deadweight loss would fall from $400 to $200 because some inefficiency remains.
option_rationale: Correct: with perfect price discrimination MR equals demand, so output is where P = MC, Q = 40; DWL = 0.5*40*20 = 400 is eliminated and all surplus goes to the firm, so CS = 0.
Misconception: believes the monopolist still stops at the MR = MC output of the single-price case; with perfect discrimination there is no price cut on earlier units.
Misconception: assumes more output means consumers gain; riders pay their full willingness to pay, not $20.
Misconception: thinks discrimination always restricts output; it expands output to the efficient level.
Misconception: believes some deadweight loss remains; every rider with willingness to pay above $20 is served, so none remains.
items.explanation_en: With perfect price discrimination, each additional rider adds revenue equal to the price on the demand curve, so marginal revenue equals demand and the firm expands to where demand meets MC, 40 crossings. Deadweight loss of 0.5 x 40 x 20 = $400 disappears, but consumer surplus of 0.5 x 40 x 20 = $400 also goes to zero, since every rider pays the maximum they will pay. Output staying at 20 ignores that MR no longer falls below demand. Consumers do not gain because they pay their full willingness to pay rather than $20. Output does not fall. No deadweight loss remains, since all mutually beneficial crossings are served.

The second explains the output and welfare effects of perfect price discrimination (topic 4.4). All numbers appear in the stimulus data or follow from it.

content.text:
Design: a monopolist with linear inverse demand P = 100 - 2Q and constant MC = AC = 20. The stimulus is given as equations, and the setting is abstract.

Computations:
- MR = 100 - 4Q. Setting MR = MC gives 100 - 4Q = 20, so Q = 20 and P = 60.
- Profit = (60 - 20) × 20 = 800.
- Perfectly competitive outcome: P = MC = 20, Q = 40.
- DWL = 0.5 × (60 - 20) × (40 - 20) = 400.
- Perfect price discrimination: Q = 40, profit = 0.5 × 80 × 40 = 1600, DWL = 0, and consumer surplus = 0.

Item 1 (topic 4.2) asks why the monopolist produces Q = 20 rather than Q = 40. The key is that at Q = 40 the MR is -60, below MC, so reducing output raises profit.

Item 2 (topic 4.4) asks what happens under perfect price discrimination. The key is that output rises to 40, the DWL is eliminated, and the monopolist captures all surplus.

The verification code recomputes each key from the stimulus numbers.

stimulus.description: A single-price monopolist faces linear inverse demand P = 100 - 2Q and has constant marginal cost equal to average total cost of 20 (no fixed cost). P is in dollars, Q in units.

items.stem: Using the demand and cost information given, which statement best explains why the single-price monopolist chooses 20 units rather than 40 units?
options: At 40 units, marginal revenue is below marginal cost, so cutting output raises profit.
At 40 units, price is below average total cost, so the firm would earn a loss.
At 40 units, marginal revenue is above marginal cost, so output should still be reduced.
At 20 units, price equals marginal cost, so profit is maximized there.
At 20 units, total revenue is at its maximum, so profit is maximized there.
option_rationale: Correct: MR = 100 - 4(40) = -60, below MC = 20, so each unit past 20 lowers profit.
Misconception: assumes price below cost at the competitive quantity; here P = ATC = 20 at 40 units, so profit is zero, not a loss.
Misconception: misreads the MR-MC comparison; MR is below MC at 40, and a firm cuts output only when MR is below MC.
Misconception: applies the competitive P = MC rule to the monopolist; at 20 units P = 60, which is above MC.
Misconception: confuses revenue maximization with profit maximization; revenue peaks where MR = 0 at 25 units, not 20.
items.explanation_en: MR = 100 - 4Q. At Q = 40, MR = -60, below MC = 20, so reducing output raises profit. The profit-maximizing quantity is where MR = MC, which is Q = 20 and P = 60. It is not true that price falls below ATC at 40, since P = ATC = 20 there and profit is zero rather than negative. MR is not above MC at 40. P = MC is the competitive rule, but at 20 units the price is 60. Revenue is maximized at 25 units, where MR = 0, not at 20.

options: Output rises to 40 units, deadweight loss is eliminated, and the firm captures all surplus.
Output stays at 20 units, but the firm's profit rises because it charges each buyer a different price.

Output falls below 20 units because the firm restricts quantity to raise prices.

option_rationale: Correct: each unit is sold at the buyer's maximum willingness to pay, so MR equals demand and the firm produces where P = MC at 40 units. Profit is 0.5(80)(40) = 1600 and deadweight loss is 0.
Misconception: assumes discrimination leaves output unchanged; the firm now expands until the last buyer's price equals MC.
Misconception: assumes that more output means more consumer surplus; under perfect discrimination consumer surplus is zero.
Misconception: assumes discrimination raises prices by restricting output; there is no reason to cut output when each unit sells at its own price.
Misconception: assumes the monopoly deadweight loss of 400 persists; the added units between 20 and 40 are now sold, eliminating it.
items.explanation_en: With perfect price discrimination, the marginal revenue from each unit equals the demand price. The firm therefore expands until P = MC, which is Q = 40. All mutually beneficial trades occur, so deadweight loss (400 under a single price) falls to 0. Profit rises from 800 to 1600 and consumer surplus falls to 0. Output does not stay at 20, since the firm gains from selling additional units. Consumer surplus does not rise. Output does not fall below 20. Deadweight loss does not remain at 400.

content.text:
Design: a monopoly seller of a wearable glucose-monitor sensor (health/technology) with linear demand and constant MC. Stimulus is a table of the demand schedule plus cost data. Topic 4.2 covers monopoly profit maximization and 4.4 covers deadweight loss and regulation or price discrimination.

Numbers: P = 100 - 2Q, so MR = 100 - 4Q. MC = ATC = 20 (constant, no fixed cost, to keep it simple). Setting MR = MC gives Q = 20 and P = 60. Profit = (60 - 20) × 20 = 800. Perfectly competitive outcome: P = MC = 20 gives Q = 40. Deadweight loss = 0.5 × (60 - 20) × (40 - 20) = 400. A regulated price cap at P = 20 gives Q = 40 and profit 0. A cap at P = 40 gives Q = 30, with demand at 40 equal to 30 and 40 > MC, so profit = 20 × 30 = 600.

Item 1 asks why the monopolist chooses Q = 20. Item 2 asks for the effect of a price ceiling at $40.

Item 2 options for a ceiling at $40:
- Q = 30, profit 600, DWL falls to 100. The cap makes MR = 40 for Q up to 30, which is above MC = 20, so the firm produces 30.
- Q = 20, unchanged. This distractor ignores that the cap is binding.
- Q = 40, the efficient quantity.
- Q = 30 with a shortage. This is wrong because the firm supplies exactly the quantity demanded at $40.
- Q = 30 with profit 800. This is wrong because profit is (40 - 20) × 30 = 600.

DWL at Q = 30: 0.5 × (P at Q = 30, which is 40, minus 20) × (40 - 30) = 0.5 × 20 × 10 = 100.

stimulus.description: Demand schedule, marginal revenue and constant marginal cost for a monopoly seller of wearable glucose-monitor sensors.

data.title: Sensor market (monthly, quantity in thousands, price in dollars per sensor)
data.firm_structure: single seller, no close substitutes, one uniform price

items.stem: The firm sells at one uniform price. Which statement best explains why it produces 20 thousand sensors rather than 40 thousand?
options: At 20 thousand, marginal revenue equals marginal cost; beyond that, each extra sensor adds less to revenue than to cost because the firm must lower the price on all units sold.
At 20 thousand, price equals marginal cost, so the firm is allocatively efficient and earns zero economic profit.
At 20 thousand, average total cost is at its minimum, and the firm always produces at minimum average total cost.
At 20 thousand, total revenue is at its maximum, and maximizing revenue maximizes profit.
At 40 thousand, price exceeds marginal cost, so producing there would reduce profit relative to 20 thousand.
option_rationale: Correct: MR = MC at Q = 20 (MR = 20 = MC); MR falls below the price because lowering price applies to all units.
Confuses monopoly with perfect competition: at Q = 20, P = 60 exceeds MC = 20 and profit is 800.
Mistakes ATC for the rule; ATC is constant at 20 and does not determine the choice.
Confuses revenue maximization (where MR = 0, Q = 25) with profit maximization.
At 40, price equals MC (20), not exceeds it; the real reason is MR < MC there.
items.explanation_en: Profit is maximized where MR = MC: 100 - 4Q = 20 gives Q = 20 thousand and P = 60. Because the monopolist must cut the price on all units to sell more, MR lies below demand, so MR drops below MC beyond 20. The price-equals-MC claim describes perfect competition, where output would be 40. ATC is constant, so minimum ATC does not pin down output. Revenue is maximized where MR = 0 (Q = 25), not at 20. At 40 thousand price equals MC, and the reason not to produce there is that MR is -60, below MC.

items.stem: Regulators impose a binding price ceiling of $40 per sensor. Compared with the unregulated outcome, what happens?
options: Output stays at 20 thousand because the monopolist still sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost.
Output rises to 30 thousand, profit falls from 800 to 600 thousand dollars, and deadweight loss falls from 400 to 100 thousand dollars.
Output rises to 40 thousand, the efficient quantity, and the firm earns zero economic profit.

Output rises to 30 thousand and profit stays at 800 thousand dollars because the firm sells more units.
option_rationale: Ignores that the ceiling makes marginal revenue equal to 40 up to 30 thousand units, above MC, so the firm expands output.
Correct: at $40 the firm sells up to 30 (demand at 40 is 30); profit = (40-20)*30 = 600; DWL = 0.5*20*10 = 100.
Assumes any ceiling yields the efficient outcome; only a ceiling at $20 gives Q = 40 and zero profit.
Believes a ceiling always creates a shortage; here quantity demanded at $40 is exactly 30, equal to quantity supplied.
Ignores the lower price per unit: profit is (40-20)*30 = 600, not 800.
items.explanation_en: With a $40 ceiling, the firm's marginal revenue is $40 for output up to 30 thousand, where the ceiling meets demand. Since 40 exceeds MC of 20, it produces 30 thousand. Profit is (40 - 20) x 30 = 600 thousand, down from 800. Deadweight loss is 0.5 x (40 - 20) x (40 - 30) = 100, down from 400. Output does not stay at 20 because the cap changes marginal revenue. It does not reach 40 because that requires a $20 ceiling. There is no shortage because quantity demanded at $40 equals the 30 thousand supplied. Profit does not stay at 800 because the price per unit fell.

content.text:
I designed a monopoly set on a wearable health-sensor patch maker, using a table stimulus. Item 1 covers the profit-maximizing output and the reason MR=MC is the rule. Item 2 covers price discrimination (topic 4.4), where a perfectly price-discriminating monopolist produces the efficient quantity.

Numbers: inverse demand P = 100 - 2Q, so MR = 100 - 4Q. MC = 20 (constant). The profit-maximizing quantity is 20, since 100 - 4Q = 20 gives Q = 20, and the price is 60. The efficient quantity is 40, where P = MC (100 - 2Q = 20). The deadweight loss is 0.5 × (60 - 20) × (40 - 20) = 400.

Item 1 asks why the monopolist does not produce at Q = 30, a quantity that appears in the table, and the answer rests on MR < MC beyond Q = 20. Item 2 asks what happens to output and deadweight loss under perfect price discrimination.

stimulus.description: Table of quantity, price, marginal revenue and marginal cost for a monopoly maker of wearable health-sensor patches.

data.title: Wearable health-sensor patch monopolist (single-price demand)

input.items: [{"stem":"The firm charges one price to all consumers. Using the table, which statement best explains why the firm does not produce 30 thousand patches, where price ($40) still exceeds marginal cost ($20)?","options":["Beyond 20 thousand patches, marginal revenue is below marginal cost, so each additional patch lowers total profit.","At 30 thousand patches, price is below average revenue, so the firm would earn negative accounting profit.","At 30 thousand patches, the firm would produce where price equals marginal cost, which is not profit maximizing.","Producing more than 20 thousand patches would raise marginal cost above the price the firm can charge.","Producing more than 20 thousand patches would eliminate the deadweight loss, which lowers the firm's profit."]
option_rationale: Correct: a monopolist adds output only while MR >= MC; past Q=20, MR is below the constant MC of $20 so profit falls.
Misconception: confuses price with average revenue (they are equal for a firm with a single price) and assumes a loss without comparing price to average cost.
Misconception: applies the perfectly competitive P = MC rule to a monopolist; Q=30 is not where P = MC either (that is Q=40).
Misconception: believes marginal cost rises with output; MC is constant at $20 in the table.
Misconception: thinks the firm cares about deadweight loss; the firm maximizes profit, and DWL is not a cost to it.
input.explanation_en: The profit-maximizing rule is to produce where MR = MC. At Q = 20, MR = $20 = MC. Beyond that quantity, MR falls below MC (at 30, MR = -$20 versus MC = $20), so each added patch reduces profit even though price still exceeds MC. The price-equals-marginal-cost option applies the competitive rule, which does not hold for a monopolist because MR < P. The option about negative profit confuses price with average revenue. The option about rising marginal cost contradicts the constant MC in the table. The deadweight loss option ascribes a goal the firm does not have.

items.stem: Suppose the firm could instead charge each consumer the maximum price that consumer is willing to pay (perfect price discrimination). Compared with the single-price outcome in the table, which describes the result and why?
options: Output rises to 40 thousand patches because the firm's marginal revenue equals the demand price, so it sells until price equals $20, and deadweight loss disappears.
Output stays at 20 thousand patches because the firm still equates marginal revenue and marginal cost on the single-price marginal revenue curve.
Output falls below 20 thousand patches because charging higher prices to some consumers reduces the quantity demanded.
Output rises to 40 thousand patches, and deadweight loss disappears because consumer surplus increases to its maximum.
Output rises to 30 thousand patches, where price is halfway between the single-price monopoly price and marginal cost.
option_rationale: Correct: with perfect discrimination each extra unit sells at its demand price, so MR = P along demand; the firm expands until P = MC at Q=40, capturing all surplus and eliminating DWL.
Misconception: assumes the downward-sloping MR curve (MR = 100 - 4Q) still applies even though lowering price no longer requires cutting price on earlier units.
Misconception: thinks price discrimination restricts output because some consumers pay more.
Misconception: reaches the right quantity but claims consumer surplus is maximized; under perfect discrimination consumer surplus falls to zero.
Misconception: believes output lands at an arbitrary midpoint; no such rule exists and Q=30 has P above MC.
items.explanation_en: A perfectly price-discriminating monopolist charges each buyer their willingness to pay, so selling one more unit does not force a lower price on earlier units. Marginal revenue equals the demand price, and the firm expands output until P = MC: 100 - 2Q = 20, so Q = 40 thousand, up from 20. Every mutually beneficial trade occurs, so deadweight loss (0.5 x $40 x 20 thousand = $400 thousand under single pricing) disappears; the firm captures all surplus. Staying at 20 uses the wrong MR curve. Falling output ignores that discrimination lets the firm sell more. The consumer-surplus option misstates that consumer surplus becomes zero. The 30 thousand option has no economic basis.

I designed a technology scenario: two data-throughput rate curves for a server, the area between them, and a solid with square cross-sections (topic 8.7) plus a washer-type volume (topic 8.8). Let me verify the numbers first.

input.stimulus: {"kind":"graph","description":"Graph of two curves for x from 0 to 6 cm in the first quadrant: the upper curve y=f(x)=4+2 sin(x/2) and the line y=g(x)=x/2+1. content.text:
I designed a field-setting FRQ about a stream channel cross-section, where two curves bound the region. It covers area between curves (8.4), volume of a solid with known cross-sections (8.7), and volume by discs/washers (8.8).

Setup: the channel bank is f(x) = 4 - 0.25x^2 (top) and the channel bed is g(x) = 0.5x - 1 (bottom). Intersection: 4 - 0.25x^2 = 0.5x - 1 gives 0.25x^2 + 0.5x - 5 = 0, so x^2 + 2x - 20 = 0 and x = -1 ± sqrt(21), i.e. x = -5.583 and x = 3.583. The verification script computes the area, the square cross-section volume, and the washer volume about y = -8.

content.text:
Design: f(x)=x^2+1 and g(x)=5-x^2 on [-2,2] (abstract). They intersect where x^2+1=5-x^2, so x=±√2. The region R is bounded by the two curves. Part (c) sets up a volume with a horizontal-line revolution. Part (d) uses a vertical-line revolution or a cross-section choice.

Computations:
- (a) Area = ∫_{-√2}^{√2} (4-2x^2) dx = 2(4√2 - 2·2√2/3) = 2(4√2 - 4√2/3) = 16√2/3 ≈ 7.542.
- (b) Cross-sections are squares perpendicular to the x-axis with side equal to the vertical distance: V = ∫(4-2x^2)^2 dx over [-√2, √2].
- (c) Revolve R about y=-1: washers with outer radius g+1 = 6-x^2 and inner radius f+1 = x^2+2, so V = π∫[(6-x^2)^2 - (x^2+2)^2] dx.

Check on (c): (6-x^2)^2 - (x^2+2)^2 = (36-12x^2+x^4) - (x^4+4x^2+4) = 32-16x^2. So V = π∫(32-16x^2) dx = π·2(32√2 - 16·2√2/3) = π·2·(32√2 - 32√2/3) = π·2·64√2/3 = 128√2π/3 ≈ 189.5. Part (c) is verified in the code below.

content.text:
Design: A household/business context. A solar-panel installation vs. a grid electricity cost: the savings rate is the gap between two rates, so area between curves gives accumulated savings (8.4). Topic 8.7 (volumes with cross sections) and 8.8 (disc/washer method) are drawn on through a storage tank design: a water tank for a small farm business with region between curves rotated about an axis.

I'll keep it coherent with one stimulus: a region bounded by $f(x)=4+\sin(x)$... Simpler is a cost-rate stimulus for (a), and a tank shape for (b) and (c).

Stimulus: a decorative planter business makes a planter whose cross-section region R lies between $f(x)=2+\sqrt{x}$ (outer) and $g(x)=\frac{x}{2}+1$ (inner) in the first quadrant, x in [0,4], in units of decimeters. At x=0: f=2, g=1. At x=4: f=4, g=3. They never cross, since f−g = 1+√x−x/2, which is 1 at 0 and 1+2−2 = 1 at 4, and positive between.

- (a) Area = ∫0^4 (1+√x−x/2) dx = 4 + (2/3)(8) − 4 = 16/3 ≈ 5.333 dm².
- (b) Volume with square cross-sections perpendicular to the x-axis = ∫ (f−g)² dx. Expanding (1+√x−x/2)² = 1 + x + x²/4 + 2√x − x − x√x = 1 + x²/4 + 2√x − x^{3/2}. Integrating from 0 to 4: 4 + (64/12) + (4/3)(8) − (2/5)(32) = 4 + 5.3333 + 10.6667 − 12.8 = 7.2, i.e. 36/5.
- (c) Volume when R is rotated about the x-axis (washers) = π∫(f²−g²) dx. f² = 4+4√x+x, and g² = x²/4+x+1. The difference is 3+4√x−x²/4. Integrating: 12 + (8/3)(8) − (64/12) = 12 + 21.3333 − 5.3333 = 28, so the volume is 28π ≈ 87.965.

The verification code recomputes these.

content.text:
I designed a household solar-and-battery decision: two continuous rate curves for electricity cost, with the area between them as the total savings, a revenue-style region, and a volume of a solid with square cross-sections (a storage tank).

**Model.** Over $0\le t\le 12$ months, the old plan costs $R(t)=120+10t$ dollars per month. The new plan costs $S(t)=60+30t-2t^2$ dollars per month. Setting $R=S$ gives $-2t^2+20t-60+... $, which I rework below so the curves cross cleanly.

$R-S=(120+10t)-(60+30t-2t^2)=2t^2-20t+60$. Its discriminant is $400-480<0$, so there is no crossing. I change $S$ to make a crossing.

Take $S(t)=40+30t-2t^2$. Then $R-S=80-20t+2t^2$, with discriminant $400-640<0$, so there is still no crossing. Try $R(t)=100+10t$ and $S(t)=40+34t-2t^2$.

Then $S-R=-60+24t-2t^2=-2(t^2-12t+30)$, with roots $t=6\pm\sqrt6\approx 3.551,\ 8.449$. So $S>R$ on $(3.551, 8.449)$ and $R>S$ outside that interval.

**Part (a)** asks for the crossing times, calculator required (1 point).

**Part (b)** asks for the total area between the curves on $[0,12]$ as a sum of integrals, with the value (3 points).

**Part (c)** gives a storage tank (a solid) whose base is the region between the curves on $[t_1,t_2]$ and whose cross-sections perpendicular to the $t$-axis are squares. This asks for the setup and value of the volume (3 points).

**Part (d)** asks which plan is cheaper on average, a justification using the average value (2 points).

For the values, with $f=S-R=-2t^2+24t-60$ and $a=6-\sqrt6$, $b=6+\sqrt6$, the antiderivative is $F=-\tfrac23t^3+12t^2-60t$. The middle area is $\int_a^b f\,dt$, and the outer area is $\int_0^{12}|f|\,dt$, computed in the verification code.

input.title: Comparing Two Household Energy Plans
input.stimulus: {"kind":"graph","description":"Graph of two monthly cost-rate curves for a household over 12 months: old plan R(t)=100+10t (line) and new plan S(t)=40+34t-2t^2 (parabola). content.text:
I designed a purely abstract setup: region between f(x) = x^2 + 1 and g(x) = 5 - x^2 (curves cross at x = ±√2), plus area, a solid with square cross-sections, and a disc/washer rotation about a horizontal line.

Area: ∫_{-√2}^{√2} (4 - 2x^2) dx = 2(4√2 - (2/3)·2√2) = 2(4√2 - 4√2/3) = 16√2/3 ≈ 7.542.

Square cross-sections perpendicular to the x-axis: side = g - f = 4 - 2x^2, so V = ∫(4 - 2x^2)^2 dx ≈ 28.5 (computed in code).

Rotation about y = -1: washer with outer radius g + 1 = 6 - x^2 and inner radius f + 1 = x^2 + 2, so V = π∫[(6 - x^2)^2 - (x^2 + 2)^2] dx. The integrand is (36 - 12x^2) - (4 + 4x^2) = 32 - 16x^2, so V = π(64√2 - (32/3)·2√2·... ) is evaluated in code.

input.title: Region Between Two Parabolas: Area and Two Volumes

stimulus.description: Two curves f(x)=x^2+1 and g(x)=5-x^2 enclose a region R.

data.region_R: bounded by the graphs of f and g between their two intersection points

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the x-coordinates of the points of intersection of the graphs of f and g, and write an integral expression for the area of R. Then use your calculator to find the area, to three decimal places.
parts.model_answer: Intersections at x=-sqrt(2) and x=sqrt(2). Area = integral from -sqrt2 to sqrt2 of (4-2x^2) dx = 16*sqrt(2)/3 ≈ 7.542.

rubric_rows.criterion: Intersection limits
Integral setup with top minus bottom
alt_solutions: 2*integral from 0 to sqrt2 of (4-2x^2) dx

rubric_rows.criterion: Area value

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Region R is the base of a solid. For each x, the cross-section perpendicular to the x-axis is a square. Write an integral expression for the volume of the solid and find its value using your calculator.
parts.model_answer: Side = 4-2x^2, so V = integral from -sqrt2 to sqrt2 of (4-2x^2)^2 dx ≈ 28.476 (exactly 256*sqrt(2)/15 ... see verification).

rubric_rows.criterion: Side length is the vertical distance
Squared integrand with correct limits
common_errors: integrating the side instead of its square
using area of a circle or semicircle

rubric_rows.criterion: Volume value

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Region R is rotated about the horizontal line y = -1. Write an integral expression for the volume of the resulting solid and find its value using your calculator.
parts.model_answer: Washers: outer radius (5-x^2)+1 = 6-x^2, inner radius (x^2+1)+1 = x^2+2. V = pi * integral from -sqrt2 to sqrt2 of [(6-x^2)^2-(x^2+2)^2] dx = pi * integral of (32-16x^2) dx ≈ 126.3 (see verification for value).

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct radii measured from y=-1
common_errors: radii measured from the x-axis (5-x^2 and x^2+1)

rubric_rows.criterion: Washer integral setup
Volume value

input.design_note: Abstract setting. Three parts require choosing the right integral rule (area between curves, known cross-sections, washers about a non-axis line). Calculator required. Model answer values are fixed by the verification script.

content.text: I designed a short 4-point FRQ on community ecology (competition and predator-prey effects) set in a health/technology context: a probiotic-based gut microbiome study in mice. Part (c) uses a Gause-style competition prediction, and the verification code recomputes the data readings.

input.title: Probiotic Strain Competition in the Mouse Gut Community

stimulus.description: Table of mean gut bacterial abundance (CFU per gram of stool, in millions) on day 14 for four groups of germ-free mice colonized with a harmful bacterium (Strain P) and/or a probiotic bacterium (Strain L). n = 10 mice per group.

data.title: Day-14 stool abundance (millions CFU per gram, mean +/- 2SE, n=10 mice per group)
rows: Standard diet plus heat-killed Strain L
data.notes: All mice were germ-free males of the same age and inbred line, housed in identical sterile cages, and given the same total food mass. Strain L and Strain P both use the same dietary fiber as their main food source. Group 4 received heat-killed (non-living) Strain L in place of living Strain L.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in the comparison of Group 1 and Group 3.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: presence or absence of living Strain L (colonization with Strain L). Dependent variable: abundance of Strain P (CFU per gram of stool) on day 14.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
common_errors: Naming Strain P abundance as independent

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Group 2 and Group 1 were each colonized with only one strain. Explain the purpose of including these two groups as controls in this investigation.
parts.model_answer: They show how each strain grows alone, without the other strain, giving a baseline abundance so that reduced growth of Strain P in Group 3 can be attributed to the presence of Strain L rather than to the mouse environment or an inability to grow.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that single-strain groups provide a baseline for each strain's growth without the other strain, for comparison with the mixed group
required_elements: Comparison to the mixed-strain group to attribute change to the other strain

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the data, calculate the percent decrease in mean Strain P abundance in Group 3 compared with Group 1, and state whether the difference is likely to be meaningful based on the 2SE values.
parts.model_answer: (480 - 150) / 480 x 100 = 68.75%, about 69%. The 2SE intervals (440-520 and 125-175) do not overlap, so the difference is likely meaningful.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct percent decrease and interval-overlap conclusion
required_elements: 2SE intervals do not overlap, so difference likely real

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Group 4 received heat-killed Strain L. Explain what this group tests and justify what its result indicates about how Strain L reduces Strain P.
parts.model_answer: It tests whether living, growing Strain L is required, as opposed to the mere presence of Strain L material or its nutrients. Strain P stayed high (470, similar to Group 1) and no living Strain L remained, so reduction of Strain P requires living Strain L competing for the shared fiber resource; dead cells did not reduce Strain P.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies that the group tests the need for living Strain L and justifies using Strain P staying high (about 470, similar to Group 1)
required_elements: Tests whether living Strain L is needed
Strain P remained high, similar to Group 1, so live competition for shared resource is supported
common_errors: Claiming heat-killed Strain L proves Strain L is harmless to humans

content.text:
I'll design a short FRQ (4 points) in a purely abstract/mathematical community-ecology setting: a Lotka-Volterra-style simulation experiment on two competing species, testing identification of variables and controls.

Design: a simulation study where the competition coefficient α (effect of species B on species A) is varied. Data table: final population of species A after 40 generations for α values with and without species B, 3 replicate runs.

Data (computed in the verification script): K = 200, r = 0.5, N0 = 20. Without B, A reaches about K = 200. With B (B fixed at 100 individuals as a constant competitor), the equilibrium for A is K − α·B.

- α = 0.0: 200
- α = 0.5: 150
- α = 1.0: 100
- α = 1.5: 50

The parts are ordered describe/explain, then read data, then predict, then justify.

input.title: Modeling Interspecific Competition: Identifying Variables and Controls

stimulus.description: Table of simulated final population size of species A after 40 generations at four competition coefficients, with species B held constant at 100 individuals, plus a control with no species B.

data.model: Discrete logistic growth with competition for species A: N(t+1) = N(t) + r*N(t)*(1 - (N(t) + alpha*B)/K)
columns: Competition coefficient alpha (effect of one B individual on A, in A-equivalents)
Final population of species A at generation 40 (individuals)
data.units: individuals

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this simulation investigation.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: the competition coefficient alpha (the strength of the effect of species B on species A). Dependent variable: the final population size of species A at generation 40.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
required_elements: Dependent variable = final population size of species A
common_errors: Naming the population of species B as the independent variable (it is held constant)

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The control run has no species B. Explain what this control allows a researcher to conclude about the results of runs 1 through 4.
parts.model_answer: The control shows the population A reaches with no competitor (200 = carrying capacity), providing a baseline. Any reduction of A below 200 in runs 2-4 can be attributed to competition from species B rather than to the other fixed parameters.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains the control as a no-competitor baseline for comparison
required_elements: Reductions below baseline attributed to competition from B
common_errors: Saying the control tests the effect of alpha

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the table, state the quantitative relationship between alpha and the final population of species A, and predict the final population of A if alpha were 2.0 with all other conditions unchanged.
parts.model_answer: Final A decreases by 50 individuals for each 0.5 increase in alpha (final A = 200 - 100*alpha). At alpha = 2.0, final A = 0 individuals (A is competitively excluded).

rubric_rows.criterion: Describes inverse linear trend and predicts 0 at alpha = 2.0
required_elements: Final A decreases as alpha increases (about 100 per unit alpha)
alt_solutions: Final A = K - alpha*B, so 200 - 2.0*100 = 0
common_errors: Predicting 25 or 50 by assuming a nonlinear leveling off

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A student proposes testing whether the size of species B matters by changing B from 100 to 50 individuals in run 3 only, while also changing r for species A to 0.8. Justify why this design is flawed and describe how to fix it.
parts.model_answer: Two variables (B population size and r) change at once, so any difference in final A cannot be attributed to B's size (confounded). Fix: change only B's population (e.g., 50 vs 100) while keeping r = 0.5 and all other parameters constant, ideally across the same alpha values.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies confounding from changing two variables and proposes changing only one
required_elements: More than one variable changed, so effect cannot be attributed to B's size
Keep r and other parameters constant, vary only B
common_errors: Claiming the flaw is too few generations
Saying only that sample size is small

input.design_note: Abstract Lotka-Volterra-style competition model; tests 3.C (variables, controls, confounds) within topic 8.5 using a no-competitor control and a confounded redesign.
input.verification_code:
import json
r=0.5;K=200;B=100
def sim(alpha,Bv):
    N=20.0
    for _ in range(400):
        N=N+r*N*(1-(N+alpha*Bv)/K)
        N=max(N,0)
    return N
vals=[sim(0,0)]+[sim(a,B) for a in (0,0.5,1.0,1.5)]
exp=[200,200,150,100,50]
ok=all(abs(v-e)<1 for v,e in zip(vals,exp))
p2=sim(2.0,B)
print(json.dumps({"checks":[{"part":"c","pass":bool(ok and abs(p2)<1),"detail":str(vals)+" alpha2="+str(p2)}],"conceptual_parts":["a","b","d"]}))

content.text:
I'll design a short FRQ (4 points) on community ecology (interspecific interactions, competition/predation) with a field/lab setting, emphasizing identifying variables and controls.

Scenario: a rocky intertidal field experiment on a predator (sea star) removal and barnacle/mussel/limpet community, using plots with different treatments and data on species counts.

Data (mean species richness and mussel cover after 12 months):
- Control (sea star present, no cage): 8 species, mussel cover 22%
- Sea star removal: 4 species, mussel cover 71%
- Cage control (cage with sides open, sea star present): 8 species, mussel cover 24%

Calculation: the % change in richness for removal vs. control = (4-8)/8 = -50%.

input.title: Predator Removal in an Intertidal Community

stimulus.description: Table of mean species richness and mean mussel cover after 12 months in three types of 4 m^2 rocky intertidal plots (10 plots per treatment).

data.title: Results after 12 months (mean of 10 plots per treatment)
columns: Mean number of species per plot
Mean mussel cover (% of plot area)
rows: Sea stars left in place; plot marked with stakes only
All sea stars removed by hand every 2 weeks; plot marked with stakes
Sea stars left in place; plot surrounded by a mesh fence with openings that sea stars can pass through
data.setup: Plots of equal size (4 m^2), same shore height and wave exposure, randomly assigned to treatments; sea stars are the main predator of mussels; mussels are a dominant competitor for space.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and one dependent variable in this experiment.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: presence or absence of sea stars (predator removal). Dependent variable: number of species per plot (or percent mussel cover).

rubric_rows.criterion: Names both the independent variable (sea star presence/removal) and a valid dependent variable (species richness or mussel cover).
required_elements: dependent variable = species number or mussel cover
common_errors: Naming plot size or shore height as the independent variable

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the treatment that serves as the control for the sea star removal and explain what it allows the researchers to compare.
parts.model_answer: Treatment A (sea stars left in place) is the control. Comparing it with treatment B shows the effect of removing sea stars while all else is unchanged.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies treatment A (unmanipulated, sea stars present) as the control and states that it provides a baseline for comparison with removal.
alt_solutions: Treatment C may also be accepted as a control for the fence if the response states it controls for the fence and compares to B
common_errors: Choosing treatment B as the control

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Treatment C was included even though sea stars were not removed. Explain what experimental problem treatment C addresses, and use the data to state whether that problem affected the results.
parts.model_answer: Treatment C controls for effects of the fence/structure itself (shading, altered water flow, disturbance), separate from sea star removal. Because richness (8 vs. 8) and mussel cover (24% vs. 22%) are nearly the same as in A, the fence had little effect.

rubric_rows.criterion: States C controls for the fence/structure artifact AND uses data (similar to A) to conclude the fence had little or no effect.
required_elements: controls for effect of fence/structure rather than predator removal
cites similarity of C to A (8 vs 8 species or 24% vs 22%)
common_errors: Saying C tests a different predator

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Using the data, explain how removing sea stars changed species richness, and justify with a community ecology concept.
parts.model_answer: Removal lowered richness from 8 to 4 species (a 50% decrease). Sea stars are a keystone predator: they keep mussels, the dominant competitor, from monopolizing space (cover rose from 22% to 71%), so without the predator competitive exclusion reduced diversity.

rubric_rows.criterion: States richness decreased (8 to 4) and links it to predation limiting a dominant competitor (keystone predator / competitive exclusion) as supported by increased mussel cover.
required_elements: predator limits dominant competitor mussels / keystone species / competitive exclusion

input.design_note: Short 4-point FRQ ordered identify variables, identify control, explain procedural control with data, then interpret with a community ecology concept. Primary skill 3.C (variables, controls). Setting is a field experiment.

content.text:
I'll design a sports/technology scenario: two cyclists' power-output rate curves, with the area between them, then a volume with square cross-sections, and a disc/washer setup.

Design: a trail ramp profile in a skate park. Upper curve f(x) = 4 + 2 sin(x/2)... To keep it clean: f(x) = 6 - 0.1x², g(x) = 0.5x on a ramp cross-section, 0 ≤ x ≤ intersection. Intersection: 6 - 0.1x² = 0.5x gives x² + 5x - 60 = 0, x = (-5 + √265)/2 ≈ 5.6394.

- (a) Area between curves (3 pts)
- (b) Volume with square cross-sections perpendicular to the x-axis (3 pts)
- (c) Volume when the region is revolved about the line y = -2 (3 pts)

Total of 9 points.

input.title: Skate Park Ramp Cross-Section: Area and Volumes
input.stimulus: {"kind":"graph","description":"Region in the first quadrant bounded above by the parabola y=6-0.1x^2, below by the line y=0.5x, and on the left by the y-axis. Units in meters.","data":{"x_axis":{"label":"x (meters, horizontal distance)","min":0,"max":7,"tick":1},"y_axis":{"label":"y (meters, height)","min":0,"max":7,"tick":1},"curves":[{"name":"f","equation":"y = 6 - 0.1*x^2","role":"upper boundary (top surface of the ramp)","points":[[0,6],[2,5.6],[4,4.4],[5.6394,2.8197]]},{"name":"g","equation":"y = 0.5*x","role":"lower boundary (sloped ground)","points":[[0,0],[2,1],[4,2],[5.6394,2.8197]]}],"boundary_vertical":{"x":0,"label":"y-axis"},"intersection":{"x":5.6394,"y":2.8197,"note":"f(x)=g(x), x>0"},"shaded_region":"between g and f for 0<=x<=intersection x","units":"meters"}

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: A skate park ramp has a vertical cross-section modeled by the region shown, bounded above by $f(x)=6-0.1x^2$, below by $g(x)=0.5x$, and on the left by the $y$-axis, with $x$ and $y$ in meters. Find the $x$-coordinate $k$ of the point where the graphs of $f$ and $g$ intersect for $x>0$, and write and evaluate an integral expression giving the area of the region.

rubric_rows.criterion: Intersection x-value
Setup: integral of upper minus lower with correct limits
alt_solutions: ∫_0^k (f(x)-g(x))dx with f and g substituted

rubric_rows.criterion: Area value with units

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The ramp is a solid whose base is the region described in part (a). Each cross-section perpendicular to the $x$-axis is a square. Write an integral expression for the volume of the solid and find its value. Include units.
parts.model_answer: V = ∫_0^k (6 - 0.1x^2 - 0.5x)^2 dx ≈ 69.62 cubic meters (see verification).

rubric_rows.criterion: Side length of square is f(x)-g(x)
Integral with limits
Value with units

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A designer models a curved concrete bowl by revolving the region from part (a) about the horizontal line $y=-2$. Write an integral expression for the volume of the resulting solid and find its value. Then explain in one sentence why the washer method, not the disc method, is appropriate.
parts.model_answer: V = π∫_0^k [(6-0.1x^2+2)^2 - (0.5x+2)^2] dx ≈ 539.9 cubic meters. Washers are needed because the region does not touch the axis of revolution, so each cross-section has a hole (outer radius f(x)+2, inner radius g(x)+2).

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct radii
common_errors: using f(x) and g(x) without shifting

rubric_rows.criterion: Integral setup and value
Justification for washers
required_elements: region does not touch/abut axis y=-2 so cross-sections have a hole (two radii)

input.design_note: Tests choosing among area-between-curves, known cross-section, and washer rules (8.4, 8.7, 8.8) from one region; calculator required for the irrational intersection and integrals. Points separate setup, value/units, justification.

g=lambda x:0.5*x

V=quad(lambda x:(f(x)-g(x))**2,0,k)[0]
W=np.pi*quad(lambda x:(f(x)+2)**2-(g(x)+2)**2,0,k)[0]
print(json.dumps({"checks":[{"part":"a","pass":abs(k-5.639)<0.001 and abs(A-20.108)<0.002,"detail":f"k={k},A={A}"},{"part":"b","pass":abs(V-69.62)<0.01,"detail":f"V={V}"},{"part":"c","pass":abs(W-539.9)<0.1,"detail":f"W={W}"}],"conceptual_parts":[]}))
