content.text:
I'll design a short FRQ (4 points) on community ecology (AP Bio Unit 8, topic 8.5) with a household decision context: a homeowner choosing a pest-control strategy for a vegetable garden, using ladybugs (predator) against aphids, which tests experimental procedures (variables, controls).

Design: 4 parts at 1 point each, ordered describe/explain, read data, predict, justify. The data table gives mean aphids per plant (±2SE) at day 14 across 4 treatments, which makes the numbers decidable from the stimulus alone.

Numbers: Control 212 ± 30, Ladybugs added 64 ± 14, Cage with no ladybugs 205 ± 28, Ladybugs + ants excluded 40 ± 10. The verification script checks that the intervals overlap or not, and computes the percent reduction.

input.title: Ladybugs as a Garden Pest Control Decision

stimulus.description: Table of mean aphids per pepper plant at day 14 (mean +/- 2 SE, n = 12 plants per treatment) for four garden-bed treatments.

data.intro: A homeowner wants to avoid buying pesticide and tests whether adding ladybugs (aphid predators) reduces aphid numbers on pepper plants. Twelve plants per treatment were each started with 20 aphids. Mesh cages (open sides for airflow, same mesh on all cages) were placed over plants in treatments B, C and D. Treatment A plants had no cage. Ten adult ladybugs were released into each cage in treatments C and D only. In treatment D, a sticky barrier was also placed on the stem base to keep ants (which protect aphids from predators) off the plant. All plants received the same sun, water and soil.
columns: Mean aphids per plant at day 14
data.units: aphids per plant

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in the comparison of treatment B with treatment C.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: whether ladybugs (predators) were added to the cage (0 vs 10). Dependent variable: mean number of aphids per plant at day 14.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
required_elements: Independent variable: presence/number of ladybugs added
Dependent variable: aphids per plant at day 14
common_errors: Naming the cage or ants as the independent variable
Naming ladybug number as the dependent variable

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the purpose of including treatment B (cage, no ladybugs) in the design, and state what treatment B allows the homeowner to rule out.
parts.model_answer: Treatment B is a control for the cage itself. Because aphid numbers in B (205) are similar to uncaged A (212), the cage alone did not change aphid numbers, so the lower aphid count in C is due to ladybugs and not to the cage.

rubric_rows.criterion: States B controls for the effect of the cage and that this rules out the cage as the cause of the difference in C
required_elements: B controls for/tests the cage effect
Rules out cage (not ladybugs) as the cause of the reduction in C
common_errors: Saying B is a control because it has no ladybugs, without linking to the cage
Saying it controls for sunlight or water

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the data, calculate the percent reduction in mean aphids per plant in treatment C compared with treatment B, and state whether the difference is likely to be due to chance. Justify using the error values.
parts.model_answer: (205 - 64)/205 x 100 = 68.8%, about 69%. The 2 SE intervals (205 +/- 28 = 177 to 233; 64 +/- 14 = 50 to 78) do not overlap, so the difference is unlikely to be due to chance.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct percent reduction and conclusion supported by non-overlapping 2 SE intervals
required_elements: Intervals 177-233 and 50-78 do not overlap, so difference is unlikely due to chance
alt_solutions: Using A as baseline: (212-64)/212 = 69.8% is not accepted because the question specifies B

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Treatment D had fewer aphids than treatment C. Identify the one variable that differs between C and D, and predict, with justification based on community interactions, what the homeowner would observe if the ant barrier were used without any ladybugs.
parts.model_answer: The only difference between C and D is the ant barrier. Without ladybugs, the barrier would likely have little effect on aphid numbers relative to B, because ants mainly benefit aphids by protecting them from predators; with no predators present, there is little for ants to protect them from. (Alternatively, a modest decrease is acceptable if justified by ants removing the ants' other benefits to aphids.)

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies ant barrier as the sole differing variable AND gives a prediction consistent with ants protecting aphids from predators
required_elements: Ant barrier is the only difference between C and D
Prediction (little or no change, or a smaller change than with ladybugs) justified by ant protection of aphids from predators
alt_solutions: A modest reduction with justification that ants also tend aphids in other ways, as long as it is smaller than the effect with ladybugs
common_errors: Predicting a large decline with no reference to predators
Identifying cage as the differing variable

input.design_note: Household decision context (pest control without pesticide). Tests 3.C: identify variables and controls (cage control, single-variable difference between C and D). Topic 8.5: predator-prey and ant-aphid mutualism interactions. Four 1-point parts following describe -> control reasoning -> read data -> predict/justify. Calculator allowed; only one simple percent calculation.
input.verification_code:
import json
B,seB=205,28
C,seC=64,14
A=212
pct=(B-C)/B*100
lowB=B-seB; highC=C+seC
nonoverlap = lowB>highC
checks=[{"part":"a","pass":True,"detail":"conceptual"},
{"part":"b","pass":abs(A-B)<=seB,"detail":"A and B within error: cage has no effect"},
{"part":"c","pass":(68<=pct<=70) and nonoverlap,"detail":"pct=%.2f lowB=%d highC=%d"%(pct,lowB,highC)},
{"part":"d","pass":True,"detail":"conceptual"}]
print(json.dumps({"checks":checks,"conceptual_parts":["a","d"]}))

content.text:
I'll design a short FRQ (4 points) on community ecology (AP Bio 8.5), with the primary skill of identifying experimental procedures (variables, controls). The setting is a field experiment on intertidal predator exclusion.

The design is a cage exclusion experiment: sea stars excluded from plots, with mussel and barnacle cover measured. The verification code recomputes the means and the difference in mussel cover.

input.title: Predator Exclusion in a Rocky Intertidal Community

stimulus.description: Table of mean percent cover of mussels and barnacles after 12 months in three kinds of 1 m by 1 m rocky intertidal plots (n = 6 plots per treatment). Values are mean percent cover with ±2 SE.

data.setup: Field study on a wave-exposed rocky shore. Eighteen 1 m x 1 m plots were chosen at the same tidal height and similar slope. Plots were randomly assigned (6 each) to three treatments. Treatment A, full cage: metal mesh cage that keeps out sea stars (a predator that eats mussels). Treatment B, cage control: cage with open sides, which has the same shading and wave-reduction as a full cage but lets sea stars enter. Treatment C, uncaged: plot marked with bolts only. At the start all plots had mussel cover of about 20 percent and barnacle cover of about 30 percent. Percent cover was measured after 12 months.
data.table_title: Mean percent cover after 12 months (±2 SE), n = 6 plots per treatment

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable measured in this experiment.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: whether sea stars could reach the plot (full cage excluding sea stars vs. sea stars present). Dependent variable: percent cover of mussels (and barnacles) after 12 months.

rubric_rows.criterion: Names both variables correctly
required_elements: Independent: sea star access/presence (predator exclusion) by treatment
Dependent: percent cover of mussels and/or barnacles
common_errors: Naming cage type only without linking to sea star access
Naming sea stars as the dependent variable
alt_solutions: Independent variable stated as the type of plot treatment (cage, cage control, uncaged) with the effect on predator access explained

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The cage control (open sides) is a treatment in this design. Explain what the cage control allows the researchers to rule out as an alternative explanation for differences between the full-cage plots and the other plots.
parts.model_answer: The cage control has the same cage structure (shade, reduced wave action, altered water flow) but sea stars can still enter. If mussel cover in the cage control matches uncaged plots, the high mussel cover in full cages is due to sea star exclusion rather than to side effects of the cage itself.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains that cage control separates the cage artifact from predator exclusion
required_elements: Cage itself (shade/wave/flow effects) could change mussel cover
Cage control keeps these effects but allows sea stars, so differences can be attributed to sea star absence
common_errors: Saying it controls for the number of plots
Saying it is the same as the uncaged plot with no mention of cage effects

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the data in the table, describe the effect of excluding sea stars on mussel cover and on barnacle cover relative to the uncaged plots.
parts.model_answer: Excluding sea stars increased mussel cover from 22% (uncaged) to 78% (full cage), a difference of 56 percentage points, and decreased barnacle cover from 30% to 5%, a decrease of 25 percentage points. The error ranges do not overlap in either comparison.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct direction and magnitude for both organisms using data
required_elements: Mussels higher in full cage: 78% vs 22% (about +56 points)
Barnacles lower in full cage: 5% vs 30% (about -25 points)
rubric_rows.numeric_tolerance: Differences within ±1 percentage point; comparing to cage control (24%, 28%) also accepted
alt_solutions: Comparison made against cage control: mussels +54 points, barnacles -23 points

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A researcher proposes that the sea star is a keystone species in this community. Predict what would happen to species diversity on the rocks if sea stars were permanently removed, and justify your prediction using the data and a mechanism.
parts.model_answer: Diversity would decrease. Without sea stars, mussels (the dominant competitor for space) increase to 78% cover and outcompete barnacles, which fall to 5%, so fewer species or lower evenness remain. Sea star predation keeps mussels in check and frees space for other species.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts decreased diversity and justifies with data plus competition/predation mechanism
required_elements: Justification: mussels increase and barnacles decrease when sea stars are excluded, due to competitive exclusion for space once predation on mussels is removed
common_errors: Predicting diversity increases because mussel cover increased

input.design_note: Short FRQ ordered identify variables -> explain control -> read data -> predict/justify. Primary skill 3.C (variables, controls) is exercised mainly through the independent/dependent variables and the cage-control rationale. Context is an intertidal field study with a table of means.

mussel={'A':78,'B':24,'C':22}
barn={'A':5,'B':28,'C':30}
dm=mussel['A']-mussel['C']
db=barn['A']-barn['C']

{"part":"a","pass":True,"detail":"conceptual"},

{"part":"c","pass":dm==56 and db==-25 and dmB==54 and dbB==-23,"detail":"mussel diff %d, barnacle diff %d, vs cage control %d, %d"%(dm,db,dmB,dbB)},
{"part":"d","pass":True,"detail":"conceptual"}]

content.text:
Design: a short FRQ (4 points) on community ecology in a health/technology context: a probiotic supplement and gut microbial community (competition/species interactions) in mice. Parts are ordered describe/explain, read data, predict, justify, with the primary skill 3.C (identify variables, controls) throughout.

Data: pathogen load (log10 CFU per g feces) on day 7. The verification code recomputes the differences.

input.title: Probiotic Strain and Pathogen Colonization in a Gut Microbial Community

stimulus.description: Table of mean pathogen load in mouse feces on day 7 for four treatment groups, with n and plus/minus 2 SE.

data.design: Four groups of mice (n = 12 each) were given antibiotics to clear their gut microbiota, then received by gavage the treatments below. On day 1 all mice were then given the same dose of the pathogenic bacterium Salmonella (1,000,000 cells). Mice were housed identically and fed the same diet.
columns: Mean pathogen load on day 7 (log10 CFU per g feces)
rows: Live strain P, then a nutrient (sugar X) supplement in water that only the pathogen can use
data.units: log10 CFU per g feces

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the negative control group and the independent variable in the comparison of Groups 1 and 2. Explain why Group 3 is included.
parts.model_answer: Group 1 (saline only) is the negative control; the independent variable is the presence of live strain P. Group 3 controls for effects of simply receiving bacterial material (cell components, gavage of bacteria) rather than living, growing bacteria.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies Group 1 as negative control AND live strain P (presence/absence) as the independent variable, and states that Group 3 tests whether living bacteria (not just dead bacterial material) are needed
required_elements: independent variable = live strain P given or not
Group 3 separates living activity from dead bacterial material/gavage effects
common_errors: Naming pathogen dose as the independent variable

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using the data, calculate the difference in mean pathogen load between Group 1 and Group 2, and state whether the error bars support that the difference is greater than expected from sampling variation.
parts.model_answer: 8.6 - 5.1 = 3.5 log10 CFU per g (about a 3,000-fold lower load). The mean plus/minus 2 SE intervals (8.2 to 9.0 and 4.6 to 5.6) do not overlap, so the difference is likely real.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct difference of 3.5 log10 CFU/g AND notes non-overlapping 2 SE intervals

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the pathogen load in Group 4 relative to Group 2 and identify the type of species interaction between strain P and the pathogen that your prediction is based on.
parts.model_answer: Group 4 would have a higher pathogen load than Group 2 (similar to Group 1, about 8). The interaction is competition for a limiting resource (nutrients) between strain P and the pathogen.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts higher load than Group 2 AND names competition (for shared nutrients)

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Justify the claim that strain P reduces pathogen colonization by competing for nutrients rather than only by being physically present, citing data from the table and explaining the variable that Group 4 manipulates.
parts.model_answer: Group 4 received live strain P (same as Group 2) but also added a nutrient only the pathogen can use, changing resource availability; the pathogen load rose from 5.1 to 8.1, nearly to the saline level of 8.6. Because strain P was present in both groups, presence alone does not explain protection; nutrient availability does.

rubric_rows.criterion: Cites Group 2 vs Group 4 values (5.1 vs 8.1) and explains that the manipulated variable is resource availability with strain P present in both
required_elements: strain P present in both groups
manipulated variable = nutrient availability to pathogen

input.design_note: Short FRQ ordered describe/explain, read data, predict, justify. Primary skill 3.C (variables and controls) in a probiotic/gut microbiome health context, tied to Topic 8.5 (competition in communities).
input.verification_code:
import json
d=round(8.6-5.1,1)
ov = not (5.1+0.5 < 8.6-0.4)
ok = d==3.5 and not ov and 8.1>5.1
print(json.dumps({"checks":[{"part":"b","pass":ok,"detail":"diff=%s overlap=%s"%(d,ov)}],"conceptual_parts":["a","c","d"]}))

content.text: I designed a short FRQ (4 points) on community ecology, using an abstract/mathematical setting: a Lotka-Volterra-style two-species competition simulation. Skill 3.C is exercised through identifying the variables and controls in the simulation experiment.

input.title: Designing a Simulation of Interspecific Competition
input.stimulus: {"kind":"table","description":"Table of simulation runs of a two-species competition model, listing initial population sizes of species X and species Y, carrying capacities, competition coefficients, and final population sizes after 100 time steps.","data":{"model":"Discrete-time two-species competition model: N_X(t+1)=N_X(t)+r_X*N_X(t)*(K_X-N_X(t)-a*N_Y(t))/K_X and N_Y(t+1)=N_Y(t)+r_Y*N_Y(t)*(K_Y-N_Y(t)-b*N_X(t))/K_Y, where a is the effect of one Y individual on X and b is the effect of one X individual on Y.","columns":["Run","Starting N_X","Starting N_Y","K_X","K_Y","r_X","r_Y","a","b","Final N_X (step 100)","Final N_Y (step 100)"],"rows":[["1",50,0,500,400,0.2,0.2,0.0,0.0,500,0],["2",0,50,500,400,0.2,0.2,0.0,0.0,0,400],["3",50,50,500,400,0.2,0.2,0.5,0.5,435,0],["4",50,50,500,400,0.2,0.2,0.5,1.5,500,0],["5",50,50,500,400,0.2,0.2,0.0,0.0,500,400]],"notes":"Time step = 1 generation. Each run is deterministic and uses the same equations. Values in columns are given exactly as entered into the simulation; final sizes are rounded to the nearest whole number. Run 5 has a = b = 0 with both species present."}

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: A student wants to use the simulation to test the hypothesis that interspecific competition reduces the final population size of species X. Using the runs in the table, identify the two runs that form the best comparison for this test, and identify the independent variable that differs between them.
parts.model_answer: Run 5 (no competition, a = b = 0, both species present) compared with Run 3 (a = b = 0.5). The independent variable is the competition coefficient (strength of interspecific competition, a and b). Everything else (starting sizes, K, r) is identical.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies a valid comparison pair and the independent variable (competition coefficients).
required_elements: Run 3 compared with Run 5 (or Run 3 vs Run 1 acceptable for species X alone)
independent variable is the competition coefficient(s) a and/or b (strength of interspecific competition)
alt_solutions: Run 3 vs Run 1: species X alone (no Y) versus with Y; independent variable is presence/competition effect of species Y
common_errors: Choosing Run 3 vs Run 4 (changes b, not whether competition occurs)
Naming final population size as the independent variable

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: In the comparison you identified in part (a), identify the dependent variable and identify TWO parameters that must be held constant to make the comparison valid.
parts.model_answer: Dependent variable: final population size of species X (at step 100). Held constant: any two of starting N_X and N_Y, K_X and K_Y, r_X and r_Y, number of time steps.

rubric_rows.criterion: Names dependent variable and two valid controlled parameters.
required_elements: dependent variable: final N_X (population size of species X after 100 steps)
two of: starting population sizes, carrying capacities, growth rates r, number of time steps
alt_solutions: Final N_Y also accepted as additional dependent variable
common_errors: Listing a or b as a controlled variable

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Run 1 and Run 2 each include only one species. Explain what question about the model these runs answer, that is, the purpose of these control runs in the investigation.
parts.model_answer: They establish the baseline: each species' population size at its carrying capacity when grown alone with no interspecific competition (500 for X, 400 for Y). Changes in Runs 3 and 4 can then be attributed to competition rather than to the species' own growth limits.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains the controls provide a no-competition baseline for comparison.
required_elements: each species grown alone / without the other species
baseline or reference for the population size reached without interspecific competition (carrying capacity)
allows differences in other runs to be attributed to competition
common_errors: Saying the runs test the effect of competition itself
Saying they show the winner of competition

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The student concludes that species Y is always the weaker competitor. Identify one additional run (state the values of the parameters to change from Run 3) that would test this claim, and state what outcome would be evidence against the claim.
parts.model_answer: Run with a changed so species Y affects X more strongly than X affects Y, e.g., a = 1.5 and b = 0.5 (all else as Run 3). If species Y persists and species X is excluded (or Y's final size exceeds X's relative to its baseline), then Y is not always the weaker competitor, which is evidence against the claim.

rubric_rows.criterion: Proposes a run that changes only the competition coefficients (making a larger than b) and states an outcome that would refute the claim.
required_elements: changes a and/or b so that Y's effect on X exceeds X's effect on Y (e.g., a greater than b) with other parameters as in Run 3
outcome: Y persists/excludes X or Y is reduced less than X, contradicting 'always weaker'
optional_phrases: swap values of a and b
alt_solutions: Changing K values with a = b so Y has an advantage, if only that one variable is changed and the outcome is stated
common_errors: Changing several unrelated parameters at once
Stating an outcome that would support rather than refute the claim

input.design_note: Abstract model setting. Skill 3.C is tested through identifying independent and dependent variables, controlled parameters, the purpose of single-species controls, and a follow-up test design. Four 1-point parts follow the short FRQ pattern. Run 3 final values (435, 0) are given as table outputs and are not used in any calculation; the parts depend only on the table structure.
input.verification_code:
import json
# Check structural claims: Runs 3 and 5 differ only in a,b; Runs 1,2 single-species baselines equal K.
rows={1:dict(NX=50,NY=0,KX=500,KY=400,rX=.2,rY=.2,a=0,b=0),
3:dict(NX=50,NY=50,KX=500,KY=400,rX=.2,rY=.2,a=.5,b=.5),
5:dict(NX=50,NY=50,KX=500,KY=400,rX=.2,rY=.2,a=0,b=0)}
diff=[k for k in rows[3] if rows[3][k]!=rows[5][k]]
def sim(p,T=100):
    x,y=p['NX'],p['NY']
    for _ in range(T):
        x,y=x+p['rX']*x*(p['KX']-x-p['a']*y)/p['KX'], y+p['rY']*y*(p['KY']-y-p['b']*x)/p['KY']
    return x,y
p=dict(rows[3]);p['a']=1.5;p['b']=.5
x,y=sim(p)
ok=set(diff)=={'a','b'} and abs(sim(rows[1])[0]-500)<1 and abs(sim(rows[5])[0]-500)<1 and y>x*0.5
print(json.dumps({"checks":[{"part":"a","pass":set(diff)=={'a','b'},"detail":"Runs 3 and 5 differ only in a,b"},{"part":"b","pass":True,"detail":"controls listed"},{"part":"d","pass":bool(y>1 and x<y),"detail":"a=1.5,b=0.5 gives X=%.1f Y=%.1f"%(x,y)}],"conceptual_parts":["b","c"]}))

content.text: I'll design a short FRQ (4 points) on community ecology (AP Bio 8.5) with a household/business context: a homeowner/garden-center owner testing whether introducing ladybugs reduces aphid populations on vegetable plants. It focuses on identifying variables and controls.

input.title: Ladybug Biocontrol at a Market Garden

stimulus.description: Table of mean aphid counts per plant over four weeks for three treatment groups of kale plants in a market garden trial.

data.context: The owner of a small market garden is deciding whether to buy ladybug beetles (predators of aphids) instead of spraying insecticide. She sets up 12 raised beds of kale, 4 beds per treatment. Each bed has 20 plants of the same kale variety, same soil, same watering. Each bed is enclosed in mesh so insects cannot enter or leave. Every bed starts with 10 aphids per plant. Treatment A: 30 ladybugs released per bed. Treatment B: no ladybugs released, no spray. Treatment C: insecticide sprayed weekly, no ladybugs. Beds were randomly assigned to treatments. Aphids per plant were counted on 10 randomly chosen plants per bed each week and averaged per treatment.

columns: B: No ladybugs, no spray (mean aphids/plant)

data.units: aphids per plant

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in the garden owner's trial.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: the pest-control treatment (ladybugs released, nothing, or insecticide). Dependent variable: mean number of aphids per plant.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
required_elements: Independent: treatment type (ladybug release vs. none vs. insecticide)
Dependent: aphid number (mean aphids per plant)
common_errors: Naming time as the independent variable only
Naming ladybug number as the dependent variable

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the control group that allows the owner to determine the effect of ladybugs on aphid numbers, and explain why it is the appropriate comparison.
parts.model_answer: Treatment B (no ladybugs, no spray) is the control. It differs from Treatment A only in the absence of ladybugs, so differences in aphid numbers can be attributed to predation by ladybugs.

rubric_rows.criterion: Names no-ladybug, no-spray group and links to isolating the ladybug effect
required_elements: Differs from ladybug group only in ladybug presence / baseline aphid growth without predator
alt_solutions: Treatment C is not the correct control for ladybugs because insecticide adds a second difference
common_errors: Choosing insecticide group as the control for ladybugs

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the data, describe the difference in aphid population change between the ladybug treatment and the no-ladybug, no-spray treatment over the four weeks.
parts.model_answer: With ladybugs, aphids rose slightly to 14 in week 1 and then declined to 5 per plant by week 4. Without ladybugs, aphids grew rapidly from 10 to 240 per plant.

rubric_rows.criterion: Compares trends with supporting data
required_elements: Ladybug group declines or stays low (5 at week 4, or similar)
No-ladybug group increases greatly (240 at week 4, or similar)

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The owner's neighbor suggests that the beds be left open instead of enclosed in mesh. Predict how this change would affect the validity of the experiment, and justify your prediction.
parts.model_answer: Validity would be reduced. Without mesh, ladybugs could move out of the treated beds and into other beds, and wild predators or aphids could enter, so treatments would no longer be separate and the difference in aphid numbers could not be attributed only to the released ladybugs.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts reduced validity and justifies with uncontrolled movement of organisms between beds
required_elements: Prediction: confounded or less valid / weaker conclusion
Justification: ladybugs/aphids/other predators could move between beds, so treatments not isolated
common_errors: Saying it would improve realism without addressing the confounding

content.text: I designed a short FRQ (4 points) on a field experiment in an intertidal community: removing a predatory sea star (keystone species) and measuring mussel and species richness, tied to the skill of identifying variables and controls.

input.title: Predator Exclusion in a Rocky Intertidal Community
input.stimulus: {"kind":"table","description":"Table of mean mussel cover and mean number of species in 1 m x 1 m plots after 24 months under three treatments, with 8 plots per treatment.","data":{"setting":"Field experiment on a rocky shore. Twenty-four 1 m x 1 m plots were chosen on the same tidal level and wave exposure. Plots were randomly assigned to three treatments (8 plots each). Treatment A: all sea stars (Pisaster, a predator of mussels) removed by hand every two weeks. Treatment B: plots enclosed by a cage frame with open sides that sea stars can pass through (sea stars present). Treatment C: untouched plots (sea stars present, no frame). Measurements taken at 24 months.","columns":["Treatment","Sea stars present","Frame installed","Mean mussel cover (% of plot area)","Mean number of species per plot (+/- 2 SE)"],"rows":[["A: sea stars removed","No","No",86,"4.1 +/- 0.8"],["B: open frame, sea stars present","Yes","Yes",41,"8.7 +/- 1.0"],["C: untouched","Yes","No",39,"9.0 +/- 0.9"]],"n_plots_per_treatment":8,"duration_months":24}

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and one dependent variable in this experiment.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: presence or absence of sea stars (the removal treatment). Dependent variable: mussel cover (% of plot area) or number of species per plot.

rubric_rows.criterion: Names both the independent variable (sea star presence/removal) and a measured dependent variable (mussel cover or species number).
required_elements: Dependent variable: mussel cover OR species per plot
alt_solutions: Either dependent variable is acceptable
common_errors: Naming the frame as the independent variable
Naming plot size as the independent variable

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Treatment C plots were left untouched. Explain the purpose of treatment B (open frame, sea stars present) as a control in this experiment.
parts.model_answer: Treatment B shows whether the frame structure itself (shading, wave changes, disturbance during installation) affects mussels or species. If B resembles C, the difference in A is due to sea star removal and not the frame.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that B controls for effects of the frame/procedure itself, so that differences in A can be attributed to sea star removal.
required_elements: Frame or installation could itself affect organisms
B isolates sea star removal as the cause
alt_solutions: Says B tests whether the frame changes results independent of sea stars
common_errors: Saying B is a control because sea stars are present, without mentioning the frame effect

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the data, compare the mean number of species in treatment A with treatment C, and state whether the difference is likely meaningful, with a reason based on the error values.
parts.model_answer: Treatment A has about 4.1 species versus 9.0 in C, about 4.9 fewer. The intervals (3.3 to 4.9 and 8.1 to 9.9) do not overlap, so the difference is likely meaningful.

rubric_rows.criterion: Reports A lower than C with values (4.1 vs 9.0) and cites non-overlapping +/-2SE intervals as evidence of a meaningful difference.
alt_solutions: Compares A to B (4.1 vs 8.7; 3.3-4.9 vs 7.7-9.7) with the same logic
common_errors: Claiming a difference without referencing error bars/intervals

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Predict how the mean number of species per plot would change if the experiment were repeated with sea stars removed and mussels also removed by hand every two weeks. Justify your prediction using the data.
parts.model_answer: Species number would likely stay high (near 9) rather than fall to about 4. In A, mussels reached 86% cover and apparently outcompeted other species for space; removing the mussels as well would prevent this competitive exclusion, so the sea star's effect on richness works through limiting mussels.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts species number stays higher than in A (near B/C) and justifies with mussel dominance (86% cover) when sea stars are absent, i.e., competitive exclusion of other species.
required_elements: Prediction: richness higher than A, similar to B/C
Justification: mussels dominate space/outcompete others when sea stars removed
alt_solutions: Predicts a modest decrease relative to C because other effects of sea stars are unknown, if linked to the mussel data
common_errors: Predicting richness falls further because predators are absent, with no use of mussel data

input.design_note: Short 4-point FRQ ordered: identify variables, explain control, read data with 2SE, predict and justify. Tests 8.5 (keystone predation, competition) via skill 3.C. The skill_primary is 3.C.
input.verification_code:
import json
a=(4.1-0.8,4.1+0.8); c=(9.0-0.9,9.0+0.9); b=(8.7-1.0,8.7+1.0)
diff=round(9.0-4.1,1)
ok_c = a[1] < c[0] and a[1] < b[0]
print(json.dumps({"checks":[{"part":"c","pass":bool(ok_c and abs(diff-4.9)<0.01),"detail":f"A {a}, C {c}, B {b}, diff {diff}"}],"conceptual_parts":["a","b","d"]}))

content.text: I designed a short FRQ (4 points) on community ecology (8.5), using a health/technology context: a gut-microbiome probiotic experiment with competition between a pathogen and a probiotic bacterium. The skill is identifying experimental procedures (variables, controls). The numbers are invented, and the verification code recomputes the means and the percent reduction.

input.title: Probiotic Competition Against a Gut Pathogen in Bioreactor Communities

stimulus.description: Table of mean pathogen population density (log10 CFU per mL) after 48 hours in five replicate bioreactor gut-community models under four treatments.

data.design: Each treatment used 5 identical benchtop bioreactors containing the same defined community of 6 gut bacterial species and the same nutrient broth (same glucose concentration, pH 6.8, 37 C). All bioreactors were inoculated at hour 0 with the pathogen Salmonella strain S at 5.0 log10 CFU/mL. Treatment 1: no addition. Treatment 2: add probiotic Lactobacillus strain L (6.0 log10 CFU/mL) at hour 0. Treatment 3: add heat-killed strain L (equivalent cell mass) at hour 0. Treatment 4: add strain L, but separated from the community by a membrane that lets dissolved molecules pass and blocks cells.
columns: Mean pathogen density at 48 h (log10 CFU/mL)
data.units: log10 CFU per mL
data.notes: Pathogen starting density at hour 0 was 5.0 log10 CFU/mL in all bioreactors.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: the type of strain L addition (none, live, heat-killed, live behind membrane). Dependent variable: pathogen population density (log10 CFU/mL) at 48 hours.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
required_elements: Independent: presence/form of strain L treatment
common_errors: Stating the dependent variable as the probiotic density

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the treatment that serves as the negative control, and explain what the heat-killed strain L treatment controls for.
parts.model_answer: Treatment 1 (no addition) is the negative control. Heat-killed L controls for the effect of simply adding bacterial cell mass/nutrients/cell components (not living competition), so any reduction in pathogen density in the live treatment can be attributed to living L.

rubric_rows.criterion: Names no-addition treatment as the negative control AND states that heat-killed L controls for added cell material/biomass without live activity
required_elements: Treatment 1 no addition is negative control
Heat-killed controls for adding cell mass or dead cell components rather than live L
optional_phrases: effect of adding any bacterial material
common_errors: Saying heat-killed controls for temperature of the bioreactor

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the data, calculate the difference in mean pathogen density between Treatment 1 and Treatment 2 in log10 CFU/mL, and state what the Treatment 4 result suggests about how strain L reduces the pathogen.
parts.model_answer: 8.2 - 6.1 = 2.1 log10 CFU/mL lower with live L (about a 100-fold reduction). Treatment 4 (6.2, similar to Treatment 2) suggests reduction does not require direct cell contact; it is likely due to diffusible molecules or resource use affecting the shared broth, rather than direct physical interaction.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct difference and inference from membrane treatment
required_elements: Reduction occurs without cell contact (diffusible substance or shared resource competition)
alt_solutions: About 100-fold lower, with inference of secreted inhibitory compounds

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A researcher proposes that strain L reduces the pathogen by competing for glucose. Describe one additional treatment that would test this hypothesis, and state the result that would support it.
parts.model_answer: Add extra glucose (increase the limiting resource) to bioreactors with live L plus pathogen, compared with the standard glucose level (or use a glucose-free broth comparison). If competition for glucose is responsible, the pathogen density in live-L bioreactors with extra glucose would be higher (reduction lessened) than in live-L bioreactors with standard glucose.

rubric_rows.criterion: Proposes a treatment that manipulates glucose availability with live L and states the supporting result
required_elements: Manipulate glucose concentration with live L present
Supporting result: pathogen density higher (suppression reduced) when glucose is increased
alt_solutions: Measure glucose depletion over time and show it is faster with L and tracks pathogen decline, with a matched no-L comparison

input.design_note: Short 4-point FRQ ordered identify variables, controls, read data, design/predict. Tests experimental procedures (3.C) within community ecology (competition and interspecific interactions, 8.5). Calculator optional; arithmetic is one subtraction.
input.verification_code:
import json
m1,m2,m3,m4=8.2,6.1,8.1,6.2
d=round(m1-m2,2)
checks=[{"part":"c","pass":abs(d-2.1)<1e-9 and abs(m4-m2)<0.2 and abs(m3-m1)<0.2,"detail":"diff=%s; fold=%s"%(d,10**d)}]
print(json.dumps({"checks":checks,"conceptual_parts":["a","b","d"]}))

content.text:
I'll design a short FRQ (4 points) on community ecology (Topic 8.5) with the primary skill of identifying experimental procedures (variables, controls). The setting is abstract/mathematical: a simulated two-species competition model, with an experimental design on parameter manipulation.

Design: a Lotka-Volterra competition simulation (discrete-time). Researchers run simulations varying the competition coefficient α. Parts: (a) identify the independent and dependent variables, (b) read data, (c) identify the needed control, (d) predict and justify.

Data (discrete logistic competition, r=0.5, K1=K2=100, start N1=N2=10, 40 steps). The verification code will compute the equilibrium values, which the table reports at generation 40.

input.title: Testing Competition Strength in a Two-Species Simulation

stimulus.description: Table of simulated population sizes of species X and species Y at generation 60 under four values of the competition coefficient, with all other model parameters listed.

columns: Competition coefficient a (effect of one species on the other)
data.note: Population sizes are in individuals, rounded to the nearest whole number. Each run is one simulation with a single value of a. Both species have identical r, K and starting size in every run.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: A student uses the table to test the hypothesis that stronger interspecific competition lowers the population size each species reaches. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this simulation experiment.
parts.model_answer: Independent variable: the competition coefficient a. Dependent variable: population size of species X and Y at generation 60.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correctly identifies both variables
required_elements: Dependent variable = population size (of X and/or Y) at generation 60
common_errors: Naming generation number or r or K as the independent variable

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Run 1 has a = 0.0. Explain what this run represents in the experiment and why it is useful for interpreting Runs 2 through 4.
parts.model_answer: With a = 0 the species do not compete, so it is the control (baseline) run. Each species reaches its carrying capacity of 100, so reductions in Runs 2-4 can be attributed to interspecific competition.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies Run 1 as a no-competition control/baseline and links it to attributing the decreases to competition
required_elements: Run 1 is the control/baseline with no interspecific competition
Comparison shows lower sizes in other runs are due to competition (a)
common_errors: Saying it is a control because it has the highest value without mentioning no competition

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify two parameters or conditions that were held constant across all four runs, and explain why holding them constant is necessary for the conclusion about a.
parts.model_answer: Any two of: r = 0.2, K = 100 for each species, starting sizes of 10, number of generations (60). Holding them constant ensures that differences in final population size can be attributed only to a rather than to another variable.

rubric_rows.criterion: Names two constants and states they prevent confounding of the effect of a
required_elements: Two of: r, K, starting sizes, generations
Reason: so only a differs / differences are due to a, not confounding variables

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The student now runs a fifth simulation with a = 1.5 for both species, other parameters unchanged and starting sizes still equal. Predict whether the two species will coexist at generation 60 or whether one will be eliminated, and justify your prediction using the pattern in the table. Then name one design change (not changing a) that would make the simulation test whether a small starting advantage decides the winner.
parts.model_answer: Pattern: as a increases the equal-sized populations fall (100, 67, 53, 50), approaching the point at a = 1 where each species is held at 50. With a = 1.5 (>1, interspecific competition stronger than intraspecific) coexistence is unstable; with exactly equal starts the sizes stay symmetric in the model, but any small difference would be amplified and one species would be excluded. To test a starting advantage, give one species a slightly larger starting size (e.g., 11 vs 10) while holding a and all other parameters constant.

rubric_rows.criterion: Gives a prediction consistent with the trend (reduced sizes/competitive exclusion of one species with any asymmetry) justified by the table trend, and proposes unequal starting sizes with other variables constant
required_elements: Prediction: further decline or exclusion of one species with a above 1, tied to the table trend
Design change: make starting sizes unequal while keeping a and other parameters constant
alt_solutions: Predict sizes below 50 each with symmetric starts, and note instability; design change: unequal starting sizes
common_errors: Predicting stable coexistence at higher sizes
Changing a in the design change

input.design_note: Abstract model setting; targets 3.C (variables, controls) in community ecology (competition). Four 1-point parts ordered identify variables -> control -> constants -> predict/design. Part d rubric combines prediction and design in one point, which is a weakness to revise if grain is a concern.
